Turns out, sharing headspace with Gollum is murder on your sleep schedule.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been quoting Gollum's "my precious" voice for more than two decades, usually to annoy someone within earshot. Andy Serkis has spent considerably more time inside the character's head, and apparently, Middle-earth's most obsessive resident has started interfering with his sleep. Considering he is returning to play Gollum while also directing The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, I suppose there's no escaping him now.

The actor opened up to The Times about revisiting the role he first took on 26 years ago. The new film is headed for the 2027 movie schedule, and while fans have plenty of reasons to be excited to see him back in a motion-capture suit, Serkis admitted the reunion has been doing a number on his already restless mind. Here's how he described it:

I’ve just lived with Gollum for such a long period. I’m a terrible sleeper. My mind is pretty active, and it has been insane going back to the character I started playing 26 years ago, and so I’m waking up at night. Actually, I don’t know if I’m asleep or awake, but I think, Am I directing you, Gollum? Or you me? Are we arguing?’ My mind is…busy.

I'm sorry, but imagining Serkis getting into a middle-of-the-night argument with Gollum is kind of hilarious. It gets even funnier when you remember that Peter Jackson compared the movie's psychological approach to Joaquin Phoenix's Joker. Apparently, getting inside Gollum's head is proving a little more complicated than anyone anticipated. This is a character who famously argues with himself, after all. Now he's apparently taking that talent into his actor's sleep schedule. I'd have enough trouble directing a movie without one of its stars trying to conduct a meeting inside my skull at 3 a.m.

Of course, a lot is riding on this particular trip back to Middle-earth. The Star Wars veteran actor first appeared as Gollum in 2001's The Fellowship of the Ring, and his performance-capture work helped change what audiences expected from digital characters, although Peter Jackson and the crew weren't entirely sure what to make of him at first. He returned in The Hobbit movies, but The Hunt for Gollum gives him a bigger responsibility than ever. He's stepping behind the camera for a film centered on the very character he helped make famous.

That means revisiting the voice, movements and personality that have become second nature over the years. We previously covered how writer Philippa Boyens was impressed by Serkis' physical commitment when she saw him back in his motion-capture suit. He's 62 now, and getting down on all fours to play that creature sounds exhausting enough before you factor in the sleepless nights.

I actually wrote last year about Serkis admitting he "cannot escape" Gollum. At the time, I took that as a career observation. Apparently, it also applies at bedtime. While promoting his new memoir, My Pressures, he discussed how playing a role can change an actor and how hard it can be to leave a character behind. Gollum has occupied a corner of his professional life for over a quarter-century. No wonder returning to that mindset is taking some adjustment.

At least he'll have some familiar faces around. Peter Jackson is producing alongside Fran Walsh and Boyens, while Ian McKellen and Elijah Wood are returning as Gandalf and Frodo. Wood has even said he thinks Serkis is the perfect person to direct a movie about Gollum.”

I'm excited to see what the mo-cap pioneer does with Gollum now that he's calling the shots, but I hope he gets a decent night's sleep before opening weekend. After 26 years, the poor man deserves a few hours without hearing "precious" in his head.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3573. Yellowstone's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

There was a time when "Yellowstone" was on top of the world, so far as mainstream television was concerned. What started as a somewhat unassuming Western TV show on an upper-tier cable channel became a breakout hit, in no small part thanks to the participation of Oscar-winner Kevin Costner in the lead role as John Dutton. "Yellowstone" set a huge record as the most-watched show of 2022. It was massive. Then, it all came crashing down.

"Yellowstone" Season 5 became its last, with a massive gap between "Part 1" and "Part 2" of that season. Series creator Taylor Sheridan decided to focus more on the show's spin-offs, as well as his other projects, with the series finale airing in December 2024. That was that. But where, exactly, did it all go wrong? When was the downfall of this once mighty TV titan? Frankly, it's not that hard to figure out.

To put my cards on the table, I've not seen a single episode of the show. I'm merely someone who writes about this stuff professionally and pays attention to the business. Anyone who does that can tell you with confidence that the behind-the-scenes drama between Sheridan and Costner is without a doubt what doomed "Yellowstone." Once Costner checked out, however that actually went down, the writing was on the wall.

Indeed, it was reported in May 2023 that Costner was leaving "Yellowstone" after Season 5. That raised eyebrows and sounded alarms. Any time a lead actor leaves a show, that's to be expected. But as the headlines continued to swirl, it became clear that this wasn't just a guy stepping away from a series. There was much more to the story.

To this day, it's still not entirely clear how everything went down. What we know for sure is that Taylor Sheridan became the busiest man in showbusiness, with a ton of series on the air, all of which he was chiefly responsible for. Kevin Costner, meanwhile, had other projects he wanted to do while also fronting "Yellowstone." Tension mounted. It even came to light that Costner was "very upset" with "Yellowstone" Season 2, long before his departure.

The gap between the end of "Part 1" of "Yellowstone" Season 5 and "Part 2" is where things really started to go south. Costner wanted to go make his long-planned Western movie saga "Horizon," which he did. But that conflicted with the planned schedule for the show, which caused issues. Not for nothing, we still don't know what's going on with "Horizon: An American Saga — Chapter 2" after the first movie bombed in theaters. But that's another story.

Sheridan has explained Costner's surprising "Yellowstone" exit, suggesting that the actor stayed on the show even longer than he wanted to in the first place:

"Even though Kevin was ready to go —he had other things he wanted to do — he stayed on for another two seasons, and that was just because the show was such a behemoth and such a huge hit that the notion of giving up a hit before it had run of juice to squeeze is very foreign to a network."

But it's not that simple. Costner explained his "Yellowstone" exit and said he'd "probably go to court" over it in 2023. It wasn't an amicable parting of ways. The main point is that Costner leaving and the feud that went on undoubtedly derailed the show. It's that simple.

It's also worth pointing out that even when Kevin Costner was still on the show, things were far from rosey. Costner's clash with a co-star reportedly left "Yellowstone" lead Kelly Reilly in tears, and while Costner has a bit of a reputation for being difficult to work with in general, reports like this are still a bad look. At a certain point, even wildly popular TV shows are forced to buckle to external pressures, particularly when they involve their leading men.

Be that as it may, Taylor Sheridan and Paramount have made the most out of the situation. It's a real lemons/lemonade deal they've got going on. Spoilers, but "Yellowstone" Season 5 dealt with John Dutton by revealing he's dead. The show moved on and got to its finale without him. More than that, Sheridan has made the most of the greater "Yellowstone" universe he established by not only developing prequels such as "1883" and "1923" but spin-offs as well.

First and foremost is "Dutton Ranch," which is getting a Season 2. What happens beyond that remains to be seen, but its protagonists Beth Dutton (Reilly) and Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) have effectively picked up where John Dutton left off. There's also "Marshals," which has brought Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton to network TV, resulting in a big hit on CBS. So, even without Costner, the "Yellowstone" franchise has thrived. It wasn't a happy marriage or a happy divorce, but the dust settled, and everyone figured out a path forward.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3571. The Crow Star Bill Skarsgård Knows Exactly What Went Wrong With The Remake

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The world waited 30 years for a remake of "The Crow," and to say it wasn't worth the wait would be an understatement. Now, that movie's star, Bill Skarsgard, has opened up about the experience. When it comes to what went wrong, Skarsgard has a pretty good idea.

A lot of actors almost played the Crow before Skarsgard got stuck with it, but the movie focuses on soulmates Eric and Shelly who are brutally murdered. Eric is given a chance to save the love of his life and has to traverse the worlds of the living and the dead in search of revenge. Rupert Sanders ("Snow White and the Huntsman") wound up in the director's chair.

That partnership wasn't fruitful. "The Crow" was dubbed a "dull, lifeless, meaningless remake" by /Film at the time. It also wasn't a success commercially. On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Skarsgard reflected on the 2024 movie's failure. What it really comes down to is a rush job that went into production without a finished script:

"I think the lesson was that I'm not signing on to anything without a finished script. But it's surprising how common it is that something gets green-lit and then you're struggling with finishing the script because the dates are already set and the studio's already locked everything in motion. And it's like, 'Oh, the script needed...'"

There is a long dark history behind "The Crow" franchise, most notably the death of the original movie's star Brandon Lee towards the end of production. To state the obvious, making a bad movie isn't anywhere near on that level, but there is something to be said for this seeming doomed from the outset.

"That was something that Rupert [Sanders] and I just struggled with," Bill Skarsgard added. "We were like, 'Okay, the first script came in two months before we started to shoot.' It was an insanely rushed process in that regard. But I don't regret any of the roles that I've done. And I think they could be good experiences; they could be bad experiences. But how you learn from them is really what it's about."

Hollywood had been attempting to remake "The Crow" for years before it finally happened. Many actors and directors came and went over the years. Nothing materialized. "Aquaman" himself Jason Momoa got very, very close to making it back in 2018. But days before filming was set to begin, it all fell apart. "The Crow" remake was dead again as both Momoa and director Corin Hardy exited.

It never totally died though and, eventually, it came around to Bill Skarsgard. On paper, he was a good fit for the role. But you can only polish a turd so well and, if the script is a turd, he can only do so much.

"The Crow" remake bombed at the box office, pulling in just $24 million worldwide against terrible reviews. At the very least, Skarsgard walked away with an important lesson and doesn't have any regrets. He's just very unlikely to sign on for a potential franchise role again if the script isn't airtight.

You can grab "The Crow" on Blu-ray or DVD from Amazon.

#3570. Nobody Said The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Was This Funny

Though I’ve never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time until now, I’ve heard people sing its praises for years. Mostly, this revolved around its impossibly high score of 99 on Metacritic, its influential open world and combat design, and its memorable dungeons. But none of those ardent fans bothered to tell me that this classic game has some genuinely hilarious moments. Because the game was originally released 28 years ago, a spoiler-free experience is pretty much off the table for me. But the goofs and gags? Those are all 100% fresh.

I love a zingy insult or quip as much as anybody else, but some of the best video game humor leans into the unique qualities of the medium. These gags go beyond writing to incorporate at least some element of interaction — or a conspicuous lack thereof. An early example of this in Ocarina of Time comes when you show a message in a bottle to King Zora, which reveals his daughter is currently stranded inside the massive fish Jabu-Jabu. The grateful king moves aside to allow you access to the entrance of the fish’s belly — very, very slowly. No button-mashing through this one. Just like you would for a real-life monarch (or older person), you must patiently wait for the scooting to be done. With each incremental booty-shuffle, he makes a little noise that sounds like “moo–ee.”

Once you venture inside the giant fish, Princess Ruto must be carried everywhere by Link, making it impossible for you to use your sword or shield while holding her on your shoulders and moving from room to room. Thankfully, you can use Ruto as a literal dead weight to press down switches to open doors. Better still, you can toss her at enemies like a rock, and she won’t take any damage. (She will complain about it, though.)

Later in the game, you‘re tasked with rescuing nine Gorons from the Fire Temple. Some of them will give you a small morsel of information about how to proceed through the dungeon. Others will simply wish you well. Either way, once freed from their cells, a lilting, cheerful flute ditty plays as they prance away with the dumbest possible expressions on their faces — leaving a stone-faced Link to continue grinding his way through the dungeon. This happens nine times in the Fire Temple alone. Ocarina repeats the bit as you’re freeing the four construction workers in the Gerudo Fortress, and it’s somehow even funnier the 13th time you see it.

I’m not the only one discovering the humor of this classic game for the first time. Folks on social media are gleefully posting about Moblin butts, the sphincter-like doors inside Jabu-Jabu’s dungeon, and the unique experience of discovering a cow in Link’s treehouse. Others are making their own fun, by sequence-breaking the game and creating the abomination that is tween Link, or playing "We Are Charlie Kirk" to the frogs near Zora’s Domain. Come for the generational video game experience, stay for the sweet, sweet memes.

The stunning adventure makes great use of capable hardware

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

It’s not just Ocarina, all of the Zelda games are deeply silly. It’s one of their defining features. And one of the biggest issues with the BotW/TotK was that the Mii-based character generator they used to quickly iterate NPC designs resulted in fewer ridiculously weird guys. Like in your average Zelda game, every NPC is typically a very weird little guy.

#3569. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 9. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice has been airing on the 2026 TV schedule for a hot minute, but Live Shows are finally underway in Season 30 of NBC’s long-running singing competition. This week they were paying tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s. Yes, it was Y2K week, and veteran coach Adam Levine, who I should note won Season 29 with Alexia Jayy, and The Voice newbie Queen Latifah saw their combined six singers take on songs by Aerosmith, Britney Spears, *NSYNC, Bon Jovi, Avril Lavigne, and even fellow coach Kelly Clarkson, each demonstrating the talent that has kept them in the competition until now.

The Top 13 of the season – the coaches’ picks plus fan-voted Kyle Davis, Team Kelly’s 61-year-old singer – kicked of the night by performing a version of “Everybody (Backstreet’s Back”) by the Backstreet Boys that made me want to get up and dance.

It wasn’t until everyone had sung their hearts out that I got mad about the fact that being on the West Coast (in Los Angeles) means that voting is already closed by the time the live shows air. Seriously, I watch this show religiously, and I'm not able to keep a deserving singer from going home? Bummer. People actively not voting for the contestant I think should go through? Yeah, I can get big mad.

One of the most noticeable aspects of the Live Shows is just how fast the episodes can breeze by. While showcasing six singers in rehearsal before their performances, which now includes band members and back-up singers, it only left room for their coach and one other to give feedback while the East Coast viewers were voting.

A fun fact about me is that I love a great Britney Spears cover that puts a spin on her songs that we all know so well. One of my favorites is the slowed down, deeply pained version of “Baby One More Time” from the Scottish rock band Travis. So, when Team Queen’s Lillie Kolich took on the Crossroads star’s 1999 hit “(You Drive Me) Crazy,” I got excited to hear what she was going to do with it. Her sultry take on the otherwise upbeat dance track felt interesting and new and full of swag, and really made Lillie stand out for me.

That’s why I was really surprised, and definitely unnerved, when she was eliminated from the reality competition. She delivered a performance that stood out for being something different that could showcase her artistry. As someone unafraid of putting her own stamp on a classic, I was excited to see what choices she would make moving forward and am now disappointed that I won’t get that chance. What happened with the votes y'all?

Look, I don’t want to take anything away from Queen Latifah’s two remaining singers. It took a lot of guts for Mia Knight to take on the Kelly Clarkson song “Miss Independent” in front of the O.G. American Idol winner herself. It’s not an easy song, but she handled the pressure to deliver with ease. Then, there was BigCountry, who had the liveliest performance of the night, rocking out to Bon Jovi’s “It’s My Life” with his big voice and big personality never letting the stage effects overpower him.

We have one more round of Y2K Week, as we get to hear Team Kelly and Team Riley duke it out before one of those singers is cut. Once the Season 30 winner is crowned in December, Keke Palmer will be taking on hosting duties for Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity. Until then, keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays (and if you're like me not voting) to see how this all plays out.

#3567. Avedon Director Ron Howard On Richard Avedon’s “Creative Courage,” and His Favorite Images From 'In the American West'

In his new documentary Avedon, director Ron Howard traces the vivid legacy of the influential photographer Richard Avedon, which premieres November 11 on Netflix. “The subjects he worked with on the commercial side of his career were dazzling and beautiful, and he was so entertaining and expressive in the way that he would shoot them. But I really had no idea how he applied his status, his influence, his access to tell this other kind of story about human beings that was honest, insightful, and more journalistic,” Howard tells Vanity Fair.

The glamorous heights of Avedon’s career were what first caught Howard’s attention. “I became aware of him really in the ’80s. Then it was even his TV commercials, like Brooke Shields [in Calvin Klein ads],” Howard said. Later, he realized a few of his favorite portraits were taken by Avedon. One of these was a portrait of a young Kareem Abdul-Jabbar at a playground in New York holding a basketball “and kind of casually standing there looking straight into the camera. It’s not against a white background…” notes Howard. “I know Kareem a little bit. It so captured the foundational strength of character and intelligence that Kareem carried with him along with his basketball talent.”

Initially, Howard, who spent three years making the film, thought it was going to be more focused on the fashion and celebrity worlds that Avedon inhabited. However, his fascination with photographs like “sad Marilyn” (Avedon’s 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe) grew into a respect for the full breadth of Avedon’s career, and his “creative courage as an artist.”

In the film, footage of Avedon and new interviews with Lauren Hutton, Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Joel Meyerowitz, Larry Gagosian, and Avedon’s son John, among others, paint a picture of a driven, curious, and sometimes mercurial artist. In the 1950s, Avedon’s career took off when he began shooting for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and Vanity Fair. He injected a sense of play and prewar European glamour into his images by drawing inspiration from the films of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. Eventually, he ventured into documentary assignments and more political subjects, including Nothing Personal (1964), a photobook with text by James Baldwin that captured the tensions of the Civil Rights era alongside a broader look at American life, a three panel portrait of anti-war protesters the Chicago Seven, and members of America’s political and financial elite at the time of the country’s bicentennial (“The Family”) for Rolling Stone. At the height of his career, he seemingly shifted quite easily from photographing celebrities to documenting anti-war protests and the counterculture of the 1960s, even when his work was met with mixed reactions.

Dovima with elephants, evening dress by Dior, Cirque d’Hiver, Paris, August 1955.

James Baldwin, New York, January 9, 1963.

Avedon (left) with Gloria Vanderbilt and Sidney Lumet at a party for the movie premiere of East of Eden (dir. Elia Kazan), 1955.

“We tried to reflect the risks he took and the transitions he made with his art and his career,” Howard shares. Had Howard made the documentary in Avedon’s lifetime, he would have liked to have asked him directly about the turning points in his career. “In all the interviews, he just kind of made it seem like it was a natural step. But to me, it's not a natural step to stop getting thousands and thousands of dollars an hour to shoot commercials and shoot for the world's most read magazines, and go to Vietnam where no one was really. He wasn’t on assignment initially… he just committed.”

In 1979, the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas, commissioned Avedon to capture a portrait of the West. He worked on this ambitious portfolio periodically through 1984, traveling across 17 states like California, Colorado, Iowa, North Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, with assistants and a researcher, Laura Wilson, who helped Avedon arrange 752 portrait sittings. (Wilson also documented the making of the project in her own remarkable photographs and writing.) In total, Avedon printed 124 photographs (some as large as four feet tall) and exhibited them at the museum in 1985. The result was In the American West—a turning point in Avedon’s career. Prior to the project’s completion, in 1983, Vanity Fair ran five photographs from the eventual series, showing coal miners covered in dust and one lone oil worker alongside a feature on Wagner’s operas and an excerpt of Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold.

“One of the reasons I was drawn to [In the American West] is because my family roots are in the Midwest,” Howard says. “I see a lot of truth in these images.”

Avedon conducting a portrait session for In the American West beside his 8x10 camera.

In a similar fashion to August Sander’s massive undertaking People of the 20th Century, Avedon went looking for “men and women who work at hard, uncelebrated jobs, the people who are often ignored or overlooked,” Wilson wrote. In doing so he joined a whole legion of photographers whose images have come to define broad swaths of middle and western America. But unlike common readings of Sander’s project at the time, Avedon was clear that his version of the West was totally subjective, more of a cinematic panorama than an objective record. He was emphatic that all photographs are filtered through the photographer’s eye, and become their interpretation. Through Wilson, he declared, “This is a fictional West. I don’t think the West of these portraits is any more conclusive than the West of John Wayne.”

Below, Howard reflects on five of his favorite photographs from Avedon’s In the American West.

“I asked if that was makeup, and I was assured that none of it was. [Avedon] set up, and just as workers were coming off their shift, he was getting them in front of the camera. I mean, wow, this is what these workers look like. This is what was in their lungs and their pores. I have cousins and uncles who worked in the oil fields. I never had any idea that they had their days looking like they’d been through what this guy has been through on his shift.”

“The boy with the rattlesnake was the first photo that [Avedon] took where he knew he was going to get at something deeper... He felt like this was almost religious iconography in a way, or mythic. [The subject] was a teenager. As Avedon says, he's a boy turning into a man, and here he's doing this kind of work, so it speaks to a transformation. It also speaks of that region as a very pragmatic region. My own dad, to try to get some spending money [in the ’30s], was hunting and trapping raccoons to sell skins to the junk dealer or possums they could eat. Absolutely just a pragmatic way of life there. So that image always resonated with me. It is also featured in the documentary because it was the proof in [Avedon’s] mind that he was going to be able to identify moments and individuals that would be arresting and mean a lot on an artistic level.”

“The beekeeper is, of course, a stunning image–one that doesn't have that much to do with the American West. I think [Avedon] could have found somebody like that in almost any corner of the planet, but it certainly is fascinating and a tribute to the research team that was working with him to help find him.”

“The maintenance worker who’s dressed up in a really flashy suit, suit jacket, tie and hat, that just looks very familiar to me. I mean, the jacket and all the embroidery on it, the flowers, I never saw anything like that with my family. They didn’t have that kind of flourish. This guy looks like he could be a country western singer or could be trying to be a country western star. But the hat, the tie, the gaze, the posture looks very, very familiar to me. That looks like a hardworking guy getting dressed up on the weekend.”

#3566. Sydney Sweeney Delivered One Of Her Best Performances In A Beloved HBO Miniseries

Most will know Sydney Sweeney for her performance as Cassandra "Cassie" Howard in "Euphoria" and for starring in Paul Feig's excellent wicked thriller "The Housemaid." Many will likely also be aware of her box office smash hit rom-com "Anyone But You" co-starring Glen Powell. But Sweeney is a deceptively diverse actor who has delivered some excellent performances over the last decade, as evidenced by her role in the HBO miniseries "Sharp Objects."

This eight-episode psychological thriller series is based on a novel by Gillian Flynn, who's best-known for having written "Gone Girl" (the 2014 David Fincher-helmed film adaptation of which saw the true crime trend coming well in advance). But four years after the "Seven" director put his spin on Flynn's material, "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" alum Marti Noxon took a shot at it with "Sharp Objects."

Noxon's adaptation of Flynn's 2006 novel took the form of a 2018 HBO miniseries starring Amy Adams as an alcoholic crime reporter who returns to her hometown to look into the murders of two young girls. There, she's forced to reckon with her past trauma. Sweeney appears in the show as a similarly troubled teen who meets Adams' character during her stay in a psychiatric hospital. It's one of the actor's best yet most overlooked performances.

Sydney Sweeney has had her share of hits, but she must also be used to some of her best work going overlooked. Indeed, Sweeney's 2025 film "Americana" was completely ignored at the box office and her psychological drama "Clementine" came and went without much fanfare amidst the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. But while it was nowhere near the cultural phenomenon that "Euphoria" was at the height of its success, "Sharp Objects" did receive widespread praise upon its debut in 2018, earning eight Emmy award nominations and garnering Sweeney significant attention for her portrayal of psychiatric patient Alice.

Alice shares a self-harm problem with Amy Adams' Camille Preaker — who, after returning to her hometown of Wind Gap, Missouri, finds herself reflecting on her time in treatment. In these flashbacks, we see her meeting Alice, who handles her own issues by retreating into her iPod. The pair formed a bond during their time in the facility, and it seems Sweeney managed to impress "Sharp Objects" director Jean-Marc Vallée while filming her scenes as well.

As the actor once told Harper's Bazaar, "[Vallée] kept bringing me back more and more for different scenes, and he'd add me in here and there, so really, he and I were able to build my character together." It seems that was a result of Sweeney's dedication to the role, which, as she told the outlet, involved going to hospitals "where there were patients that self-harmed" and spending time with them. Equally impressive was the fact that, as she previously told Nylon, she would film her "Sharp Objects" scenes on weekends before getting on a red-eye flight to Portland to film her scenes for Netflix's "Everything Sucks!" Both ended up being two of Sydney Sweeney's best projects.

"Sharp Objects" was met with critical praise upon its 2018 debut, earning an impressive 92% "certified fresh" rating on Rotten Tomatoes and garnering Sydney Sweeney attention for her portrayal of Alice. 2018 was, of course, the year before "Euphoria" began airing on HBO. As such, Sweeney had yet to break through with her portrayal of Cassie Howard. But with "Everything Sucks!," a role on Season 2 of "The Handmaid's Tale," and her appearance in "Sharp Objects," she had managed to build some serious momentum going into the show, ultimately paving the way to her becoming a household name.

"Sharp Objects," in particular, garnered praise from critics. Writing for Rolling Stone, Alan Sepinwall highlighted Sweeney's performance in what he referred to as a "versatile, era-spanning year" for the actor. Sepinwall added that both she and fellow "Sharp Objects" actor Eliza Scanlen were "names to watch," which turned out to be a particularly prescient observation. Years later, in 2023, Frank Bruni looked back on Sweeney's ascension in a piece for The New York Times, mentioning her appearance in "Sharp Objects" and noting how it had helped her become "prestige TV royalty."

Sadly, Alice isn't typically mentioned as one of Sweeney's best roles, but her quietly powerful performance was proof, even before she debuted as Cassie, that she was a versatile actor capable of nuanced portrayals. She'd prove as much once again in 2019 when she played the title role in the nerve-wracking dramatic thriller "Reality," which is well worth a watch in its own right. But if you missed "Sharp Objects" back in 2018, give it a go on HBO Max.

#3565. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

I really can't get over the end of the 1998 movie.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You've Got Mail is a movie that many consider one of the best rom-coms. However, because of how it ends, I do not. Now, that's not to say I totally dislike Nora Ephron's film. In fact, there's a lot to love about it. So, I am excited that it's going to get rebooted. However, in this new take, I will need them to fix the end.

Now, let me backtrack for a second to the news about this reboot. Jason Orley, who has directed I Want You Back and Big Time Adolescence, is attached to helm this reboot. It will be based on the 1998 movie You’ve Got Mail, and it’s being described as a “new take on the classic romantic comedy.” Per Deadline, no other details are available, which means we don't know if it will be a modernized version of this story (however, I am guessing it will be).

We do know it’s being written by Orley, and it's a new draft of a script originally written by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont.

Notably, You’ve Got Mail was inspired by the 1937 play Parfumerie, and there’s also the 1940 movie, The Shop Around the Corner. So, the movie led by Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks is a reboot in its own right, and served as a modern take on a classic tale. Now, I’m hoping for an even more modern take (technologically speaking). I’m also hoping for one major change to be made to the story.

While I know You’ve Got Mail is a highly rewatchable movie, and people go back to see Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks fall in love over and over again, I can’t do that because I hate the end. While this rom-com is a five-star film for the majority of its runtime, its conclusion totally ruins it, and I need the reboot to change it.

I mean, You’ve Got Mail ends with Joe and Kathleen confessing their love, and Kathleen just accepting that her store went out of business. Seriously, I still wonder why she’d want to be with a man who knowingly and actively just let her shop close so his big store could succeed. I don’t want my rom-coms to end with capitalism winning and people falling in love with someone who kept secrets and let that happen.

In this reboot, I need that not to happen. Instead, I’d like to see small businesses win, and even if it dosen’t I need her to at least fight for it. I also need the man she falls in love with to understand the harm he causes with his big business.

With all that said, I do like a lot of You’ve Got Mail (which you can stream for free on Pluto), and it’s always fun to see Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks work together. So, I am looking forward to this reboot that will hopefully feature two stars with undeniable chemistry like the two who came before them, a big battle of the bookstores, and an ending that does not culminate in the the owner of the smaller shop just accepting that big business won.

#3563. Exclusive: See Camila Morrone in Netflix’s Sexually Charged ‘The Age of Innocence’

When Edith Wharton was in her mid-40s, she had a sexual awakening. For decades, the celebrated novelist had been stuck in a dull, loveless marriage to Edward Robbins Wharton, a fellow patrician 12 years older than her. Then she met debonair journalist William Morton Fullerton and fell—hard.

“I have drunk of the wine of life at last,” she wrote on May 21, 1908, in the document Wharton scholars call her “love diary.” “I have known the thing best worth knowing, I have been warmed through & through, never to grow quite cold again til the end.” Years later, she’d finally divorce Teddy and move abroad, where she’d channel these transformative experiences into her most celebrated novel: The Age of Innocence, published in 1920.

“I was at a place where I said I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period,” says showrunner Emma Frost, whose résumé includes a trio of lavish historical series: The White Queen, The White Princess, and The Spanish Princess. But when Netflix asked if she might be interested in adapting The Age of Innocence, she reconsidered. Frost had read the novel and seen Martin Scorsese’s lush 1993 adaptation, starring Daniel Day-Lewis, Winona Ryder, and Michelle Pfeiffer. “I remembered it was the very first love story I ever engaged with that felt truly adult,” she says.

Then she learned that Wharton had actually written two alternate endings to her book—“and both the alternative endings have explicit sexual content.” It was a surprising development considering the published version of the novel, which is full of tortured yearning—there’s an achingly erotic moment concentrated on a character silently lifting a velvet ribbon to his lips—but contains no actual sex.

Her discovery led Frost to fall down a Whartonian rabbit hole. She learned everything about Wharton’s life-changing affair, devouring the 300 love letters the author had sent to Fullerton. “Once you actually delve into the Wharton archive, there’s all sorts of unpublished works that are explicitly about this experience of being a very sexual woman,” Frost says.

“The yearning, and the tension, and the longing, and the looks, and all of that delicious stuff is so important. I’ve been really obsessive in trying to capture that, and be very faithful to it.” But the sexy stuff in Wharton’s archive is what inspired Frost to make an Age of Innocence that’s not so innocent after all.

Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer, Kristine Froseth as May Welland, and Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska

As in the novel, her series—premiering on Netflix February 18—follows Gilded Age aristocrat Newland Archer, a gentleman lawyer preparing for a staid but satisfying life with his betrothed, well-bred ingenue May Welland. But his carefully planned future is thrown into disarray when May’s cousin, the independent-minded Countess Ellen Olenska, arrives in New York under a cloud of scandal, and with a highly unusual desire for this era: She wants to divorce her horrible husband.

Unlike the novel, Frost’s version also has nudity and graphic content: masturbation, voyeurism, a narratively important threesome. It’s not your grandmother’s Edith Wharton. But Frost would argue it’s very true to the spirit of its author.

And there’s more to her Age of Innocence than sex, of course. Wharton’s novel is told from Newland’s limited perspective; we only know what he knows, and see what he sees. Frost, though, wanted to make her version a true three-hander. “I think when you stay just with the male point of view, May becomes the antagonist, and Ellen becomes the thing to be won or saved or rescued. And that wasn’t something I wanted to do,” she says. “I wanted to have these two women really existing as flesh-and-blood women who we can care about.”

To accomplish this, she’d need a dynamic cast featuring The Witcher alum Ben Radcliffe as Newland, Kristine Froseth—who also stars in the Wharton-based Apple series The Buccaneers—as May, and Emmy nominee Camila Morrone as Ellen. Newland, says Frost, “doesn’t fit in with this society. He’s straining at the conventions. Ellen represents that other world, greater freedom”—the very freedom Wharton herself found when she ditched both New York City and her husband.

Radcliffe seemed to understand his character on a profound level. “There was a stillness that nobody else brought, and you could just see everything happening behind his eyes,” Frost says. Morrone, best known for playing a May Welland-esque character on Prime Video’s Daisy Jones and the Six, was similarly well-suited for hers: “She’s the most fearless actor I have ever met.”

Kristine Froseth as May Welland and Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska

And then there’s May, who might be the trickiest member of the trio for modern audiences to understand. Unlike her fiancé and her cousin, she likes occupying a prescribed role in buttoned-up 1870s society—and she’ll do what she must to protect her perch, without malice or cruelty. Froseth found a way to convey the character’s depth and dimensionality.

“I always felt quite indignant on May’s behalf. All she ever did was fall in love with a man who courts her, say yes to a man who proposes to her, do everything right—and then along comes her cousin, and suddenly her choices are be shamed, be dumped, or fight for him,” says Frost. “Kristine just brings this light into the room. You love her, and you want her to be happy, and not to be disappointed. And that was the essential quality for me with May.”

There’s no real antagonist in Frost’s Age of Innocence. “I think it felt complex and morally right to keep saying, ‘There’s three people here that have feelings. What is the right thing in this situation?’” she says.

Kristine Froseth as May Welland and Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer

Frost also wanted to flesh out the world of Wharton’s novel by adding mentions and subplots about real-world events its characters may have been aware of—like the Comstock Act of 1873, an anti-obscenity law that has never been repealed—and by introducing new settings like a boxing gym, where Newland goes to work out his aggression. In the series, that’s also where he befriends journalist Ned Winsett, a character from Wharton’s book reimagined here as a Black New Yorker played by Kel Matsena. “For me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters” in the series, says Frost. “They are the new ideas. They are the exciting conversations. They are the music that’s coming in.” Casting Argentine-American Morrone as the Countess Olenska, “making Ellen part of that influx, [also] felt right.”

As in any good period piece, the show’s costumes—designed by Daniel Orlandi, whom Frost calls a “bona fide genius”—and production design, overseen by Jean-François Campeau, are vital storytelling engines as well. “We always talked about these ridiculous little Victorians, trying so hard to believe they could live from the neck upwards—somehow divorce themselves from their animal nature and their bodies. The clothes and the sets were all part of that,” says Frost. “Weather and animals are really big motifs in the show. It’s about contrasting these people with the real, natural world and the weather that kind of goes, ‘Ha, ha, ha, you think you can somehow exist away from nature?’”

Camila Morrone as Ellen Olenska and Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer

Though Frost and her team paid careful attention to detail, she cautions that sticklers may find things to quibble about if they examine the costumes carefully: “Our bustles are slightly smaller than they should be in the period.” And that’s without even considering the sexual aspect of the series. “Oh, there will be some pearl clutching,” Frost laughs. “Totally, I’m sure.”

But an expert in period drama like Frost knows when embracing historical accuracy actually matters, and when to let it slide. Wharton did too. While writing The Age of Innocence, Frost says, the author discovered that famed Swedish soprano Christina Nilsson did not actually sing Faust in New York in the year she'd set her novel—even though a performance of Faust starring Nilsson was the catalyst for her book’s action. Wharton wrestled with whether she should include the scene anyway. “And then she wrote to her sister-in-law and said, ‘I don’t care. Atmosphere is more important than historical accuracy.’”

“So I’m like, ‘Okay, Edith. If it’s good enough for you, it is good enough for me.’”

#3562. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3561. James Gunn's DC Universe Is Being 'Dismantled' As DC Studios Prepares Another Reset (Report)

These DC reboots are starting to become a bit of a tradition. In the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, it seems the new guard is ready to tear down almost their entire cinematic project. At least, according to a new report.

Puck's Matthew Belloni claims to have heard that "plans are already afoot" for new DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham — who steps into the role of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026 — to scrap almost everything Gunn and Safran had planned post-"Man of Tomorrow," "The Batman: Part II," and an unnamed HBO series. As Belloni put it, "So DC goes back into reboot mode ... again."

This is the second major reset for DC's cinematic enterprise (third if you count the pre and post-Walter Hamada era), and it frankly seems like a dire state of affairs. When Gunn and Safran were brought in to head up the newly-christened DC Studios back in 2022, they had grand plans to revive the franchise following a disappointing end to the DC Extended Universe or "Snyderverse." This was supposed to be the moment DC turned things around and finally matched Marvel's cinematic success with an ambitious shared universe. Now, it's all come to a premature end as Skydance CEO David Ellison (who now oversees the newly merged Paramount and Warner Bros.) seemingly prepares to take a wrecking ball to Gunn and Safran's still fledgling DC Universe.

In his article, Matthew Belloni noted how James Gunn and Peter Safran reported to the Warner Bros. Discovery CEO, a post previously held by David Zaslav. The erstwhile head of Warners seemed perfectly happy to let his newly appointed DC Studios co-heads take full creative control. But, as Belloni noted, "Maybe it was too much freedom... hence 'Supergirl.'"

This is, of course, a reference to the box office flop that was this year's "Supergirl," a solo outing for Milly Alcock's Kara Zor-El that brought in just $126.5 million at the box office against a $170 million budget. And while /Film's own "Supergirl" review argued the movie has an aspirational and uplifting message and is nowhere near as bad as its box office returns may suggest, Belloni opined that David Ellison no doubt viewed the failure of "Supergirl" as a result of Gunn and Safran being given too much creative power. Hence, that simply won't be the case with Ellison now in charge.

This also means that while Jeremy Latcham is replacing the former DC Studios co-bosses, he will have nowhere near as much freedom and instead report only to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Depending on how you felt about Gunn's creative decisions, then, this is either a good or disappointing development. But even if you like the idea of Ellison and his studio heads calling the shots and keeping DC on a tight leash, none of this bodes well for the brand's cinematic fortunes moving forward — especially if Ellison and co. really do intend to discard Gunn's entire DC roadmap and start from scratch.

When James Gunn and Peter Safran were appointed co-heads of DC Studios, the franchise desperately needed a hard reset. A string of flops in 2023, which included the box office bomb of superheroic proportions that was "The Flash" (a movie which, as it happens, Gunn once called "probably one of the greatest superhero movies ever made"), marked an ignoble end for the DC Extended Universe, and it was Gunn's job to reset, regroup, and revitalize the entire thing. Instead, he opted for a soft reboot that retained several elements of the DCEU. Even at the time, it seemed misguided, and it feels like all the more of a misstep in hindsight.

Now, David Ellison and his executives are, according to Puck, rebooting the entire thing. But it seems like it's all too late. Audiences were never going to be won over by animated "Creature Commandos" series or a potential Mister Miracle animated show. By all means, take a few risks, but maybe save them for after DC has regained some respect among mainstream viewers. Instead, we're at a point where the whole thing is being scrapped yet again, and most people simply do not care about these behind the scenes developments. They just want good movies (which, at this point, have been in short supply).

As Matthew Belloni observed in his report, the last decade has really "only solidified Kevin Feige's run at Marvel [Studios] as all the more remarkable" when compared to DC's struggles. Of course, with Jeremy Latcham having spent many years as a Marvel Studios producer, there's a chance he might turn things around. But by now, audiences are surely tired of having to keep up with these reboots, soft or otherwise.

#3560. Big Walk AI Controversy Is a GOTY Awards Twist Sparking a Bigger Debate

An IGF voter stance marks a new hardline for the industry

Big Walk, one of the best-reviewed games of 2026 and by all measures a Game of the Year darling, faces a crossroads on the eve of awards season. Following a recent disclosure of AI use from its developer, Big Walk’s chances at one awards show seem fraught. And its shot at the big one (December’s Game Awards) might be impacted. But it’s not just a chapter in 2026’s awards show saga. In many ways, it’s a boiling over of a debate that’s been bubbling in the games industry for several years now.

On Monday, a group of 19 Independent Game Festival (IGF) jurors, including Immortality director Sam Barlow and Friends at the Table host Austin Walker, shared a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI tools in any capacity — including for code.

On Bluesky, Barlow said that this discussion among IGF jurors is always lively, but that this year’s “conversation was even more intense.”

Why? It did not take long for at least part of the reason to become clear: Big Walk used generative AI tools in development, developer House House revealed in its voluntary disclosure to the IGF. (In a follow-up statement, Barlow noted that the impetus for the conversation was more broadly about the volume of games that make use of generative AI, and that Big Walk was the "tricky edge case.")

In a statement to Aftermath (also cross-posted on the developer’s website), House House said that “well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code” had anything to do with generative AI tools, and those tools were used solely to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.” House House also noted that the studio used large language models (LLMs) to generate a baseline, which the team then “modified into game code.” House House’s statement gets into it in full, but the studio pointed to a lighting issue as an example of how LLMs helped with the final phase of Big Walk’s development, amounting to “about 10 lines of code.”

That might seem small in the grand scheme of things, but a hard line is only a hard line if you don’t cross it. And for 19 members of the IGF jury, that’s the line.

The group of jurors cite several reasons for its stance against generative AI, including the technology’s widely documented negative impacts on the economy, the labor market, the environment, and the global informational pipeline. They also say that AI use is “not a foregone conclusion” in the games industry, and, as independent developers, see this as an opportunity to take a stance that many people working at larger companies might not have the leeway to take.

Critically, the inclusion of code as part of the hardline is not something you see every day. Generally, the colloquial argument against generative AI use is reserved for disciplines that are considered more “creative” in nature: art, writing, composition, voice acting, and so forth. You often see people make exceptions for technical work, like programming. This stance from part of the IGF jury marks a clear public expansion of the tent among an influential games industry group, and it’s not lost among a subset of the community that isn’t always public-facing. Responses to Walker’s Bluesky post of the statement are full of programmers thanking the jurors for considering coding an art form.

The debate isn’t merely broken down among clean lines of “AI good” vs. “AI bad.” Some see it as a betrayal not just that House House used these tools but that it didn’t disclose that use upon release. If the use of an LLM was no big deal, the argument goes, why hide it? And if the company hid this instance, what else was hidden? (Though Steam requires a disclosure for generative AI use, it does not require that disclosure for the use of code or chatbots.)

For others, it’s just about the best case scenario for a worst-case situation. It’s a fairly minimal use, they say, and if strict delineations are made for the public disclosure of 10 lines of AI-generated code, wouldn’t that disqualify many video games? Plus, they say, House House seems reflective and open to change, pointing to the studio’s philanthropic efforts in the past as a sign of good will. (In 2020, following the release of Untitled Goose Game, House House pledged to donate 1% of its profits to organizations that help members of indigenous communities make rent.)

Will this ultimately affect Big Walk’s chances during awards season? Maybe! Though the statement was issued by fewer than 20 IGF jury members, it’s gained traction across both social and traditional media. And now that it’s become a matter of public interest and widespread discussion, there’s always the chance other voters are swayed by their arguments or otherwise hesitate to vote for Big Walk.

How this affects the Game Awards horse race is a cloudier issue. On Monday, Big Walk was all but a lock for a Game of the Year nomination, according to Polygon’s ongoing analysis of the race. But an indie game securing a GOTY nomination is always an uphill race — even without the albatross of controversy.

Yes, the technically indie game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 smashed records and swept the 2025 Game Awards, but it also broke into the mainstream in an undeniable way. Big Walk, despite its impressive critical reception, has not. To secure the nomination, it needs every vote it can get from nominating jurors who are part of the indie gaming community, which largely rejects generative AI. To wit: Clair Obscur may have run the tale during the 2025 awards circuit, but ultimately had its Game of the Year award from the Indie Game Awards (note: not the same thing as the IGF) stripped over inclusion of AI.

Beyond awards, the entire saga seems an inflection point for an industry that has struggled to grapple with the encroachment of generative AI. Developers of all strata — from the creator of The Last of Us to the studio behind the Wendy’s JRPG — have taken public stances against the technology, refusing to use AI whatsoever in any part of development. They stand in contrast to prominent firms like Embark Studios, which caught heat for using AI in its 2023 shooter The Finals and then immediately used the same tools for its 2025 shooter Arc Raiders, or Epic Games, which is run by a CEO whose stance on LLMs could fairly be summarized as “Claude = Jesus 2.0.”

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

All the while, AI tools have proven a third rail for large portions of the gaming audience, often prompting public apologies from developers that disclose their use. House House joins that club.

“Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure,” House House said in its statement. “We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.”

That’s good on House House. Stating some clearly defined rules for this sort of thing helps settle internal debate, and provides a north star for anyone working at the studio. It could even serve as a model for others in the industry to adopt. But the lack of policy shouldn’t land entirely on the shoulders of a small outfit in Melbourne — or any developer of any size, for that matter. At this point, generative AI tools have been publicly available for nearly half a decade. Until governments start taking the technology seriously and passing real regulations around what counts as acceptable use, this will keep happening.

Bruce Straley isn't all too fond of generative AI art
