#3543. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Review: Prime Video's Lord Of The Rings Series Still Falls Short

If there's one theme the latest installment of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" highlights above the rest, it's this: Time comes for us all. Whether it's the glacial pace experienced by immortal Elves or the nonstop blur the rest of Middle-earth's mere mortals have been doomed (or gifted?) to receive, this army's inevitable march is one that nobody — not even a Dark Lord — can hope to defeat.

Four years after the Prime Video series first made waves among a passionate, if divisive fanbase, it's clear co-showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have felt this pressure as keenly as anyone. An up-and-down debut season with glimpses of potential eventually found itself surpassed by a sophomore effort that went darker, bolder, and better than before. But, to date, fans have been left waiting for the moment when this J.R.R. Tolkien adaptation truly comes into its own.

Time, unfortunately, is a commodity that "The Rings of Power" doesn't have on its side this year. There's Amazon's head-scratching release strategy that (mostly) becomes clear in retrospect, with eight episodes of streaming television squeezed into three total weeks. More troublingly, the actual story does itself very few favors. There are simply too many far-flung locations to check in on, too many main characters and uninteresting supporting players to service, too much nerdy lore for casuals to digest (if any are even left) ... and, despite some of the most sluggish pacing in streaming, there's hardly enough space to let them breathe. It's an issue that rears its ugly, Balrog-shaped head again and again.

In short, Season 3 is an encapsulation of "The Rings of Power" as a whole: some incredibly high highs, several frustrating lows, and the creeping feeling that time is finally starting to run out.

Season 3's big claim to fame has been heavily teased as the creation of the legendary One Ring, which is the one doomsday event overshadowing over every single storyline this year. Five years after the conclusion of Season 2, as Galadriel's exposition-dump narration explains in the premiere, Sauron's armies wage war on the rest of Middle-earth. Only the Elves and their magical, untarnished rings remain capable of holding out. But when a suspicious Orc arrives (Adam Young as Marnûkh, easily one of the season's best new additions) bearing game-changing news of Sauron's plans, this kicks off a series of events that will either lead to good's greatest triumph over evil ... or as stunning a failure as anything in Tolkien's legendarium.

As a prequel, of course, "The Rings of Power" uses our knowledge of what's to come in "The Lord of the Rings" to its advantage. As a result, every moment Sauron is on screen trying (and failing) to forge his superweapon to rule them all absolutely soars. Whether he's cruelly bossing powerless underlings around, casually committing murder, arguing with the ghosts in his head, or generally sulking over his inability to seduce Galadriel to his cause, Charlie Vickers's Sauron will have you rooting for the villain every step of the way. He brings a delightful sense of theatricality and purpose to every evil act, while the long-awaited introduction of Galadriel's MIA husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower, another major highlight of Season 3) finally provides the third point of the unlikeliest love triangle in the canon.

But if Sauron is the main driving force behind the best narrative arc of them all, "The Rings of Power" fares far worse everywhere else.

This "Lord of the Rings" series has always had trouble finding the right balance among its varying subplots, separated by narrative relevance and theme just as much as by distance. Nowhere does that feel more glaring than in Season 3. The courtly intrigue and succession struggles taking place in the Dwarven realm of Khazad-dûm aim for "House of the Dragon"-like dramatics, but neither of the plucky performances by Owain Arthur's King Durin or Sophia Nomvete's Queen Disa can make this feel like anything less than a misguided detour.

Similarly, the brewing civil war in Númenór takes ages to click into place (and, even then, not because of any established locals, but because Robert Aramayo's ever-conflicted Elf Elrond finally gets involved). And don't forget there's another B-plot entirely in the desert of Rhûn, with Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard circling one another.

The further we get from Sauron's antics in Mordor, the less effective "The Rings of Power" undeniably becomes.

The five-year time jump should've allowed for J.D Payne, Patrick McKay, and co-writer Justin Doble to regroup strategically and reset the creative board a bit. And, to an extent, they do manage to cut things down to a more manageable size. A major character death or two helps trim an unwieldy ensemble that has only grown more so over the years, while others undergo some overdo changes in both personality and role. Even the lovable, pint-sized Harfoots have been written out completely this time around. But these are half-measures, at best. As this saga hits its midway point, viewers will be left with the impression that merely reshuffling the deck wasn't nearly enough.

These structural issues extend to the main conflict of Season 3, as well. In the early episodes, the creative team struggles with establishing the stakes of such an abstract threat as the One Ring. Season 1 had the (seemingly) unseen menace of Sauron working in its favor, while Season 2 organically built up to the epic siege of Eregion and the manipulation of Celebrimbor as its big emotional payoff. Season 3 pays lip service to the idea of Mordor's forces on the brink of total victory; but, other than a few minor skirmishes here and the aftermath of some battles there, we barely actually see this for ourselves.

It's a shame because, creatively and technically, the most expensive series on streaming has never looked better nor felt more cinematic. Directors Charlotte Brändström, Sanaa Hamri, and Stefan Schwartz depict a breathtaking level of scope and scale that modern viewers have almost become inured to these days. Together, J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay dream up some of the most spectacular fantasy concepts Tolkien nerds could only ever dare to imagine. As of the seven episodes out of eight made available for critics to review, it all builds up to the moment we've all been waiting for — one that, for a moment, absolutely lives up to the hype.

Is that enough? "Always is a long time," Galadriel suggests with a twinkle in her eye early on. With its five-season plan hopefully still in place, "The Rings of Power" doesn't have anywhere near that long to make up for lost time.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 premieres with four episodes November 11, 2026 on Prime Video.

#3542. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3541. Why Princess Diana Dressed William and Harry Identically, Even Though They Didn’t Like It

Princess Diana had a keen sense of style. It was a talent the late princess (who arrived at court at a very young age and was therefore still unfamiliar with the ins and outs of high fashion) developed over the years with the help of experts in the field—and which has repeatedly earned her the title of style icon.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her keen eye for new trends and her passion for the most sought-after pieces were also reflected in the fashion choices she made for her two children, Prince William and Prince Harry, whom she loved to dress alike from a very young age, no matter the occasion.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. July 1986.

Princess Diana, it must be said, was neither the first nor the last mother to choose identical outfits for her children, but it seems this habit was not merely a fashion game. According to a report by Marie Claire, the princess’s former butler, Paul Burrell, reportedly said that Diana’s choice to dress William and Harry identically was a way to reinforce the idea that, in her eyes, there was no difference between the two—even though everyone around her showed preferential treatment toward the eldest son, the future heir to the throne.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1986.

That’s why the princess waged her own battle, even choosing to dress her two sons in matching outfits, almost as if to convey a sense of unity and equality in their appearance. If these were indeed some of the reasons behind the brothers’ identical looks, it certainly wouldn’t be surprising. We know full well how Diana insisted on equal treatment for her two sons, who, for their part, apparently didn’t much care for their mother’s tendency to choose identical outfits. “The boys hated that, by the way; they didn’t want to be dressed the same,” Burrell added.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

This statement has also been confirmed by Prince Harry himself. In the 2017 television documentary, Diana, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy, which aired on the 20th anniversary of Princess Diana’s death, her two sons spoke openly about their mother. The younger son said with a smile: “I genuinely think she got satisfaction out of dressing myself and William up in the most bizarre outfits—normally matching. It was weird shorts and little shiny shoes with the old clip-on.”

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1989.

Bermuda shorts and patent leather shoes with straps—all the rage in the ’80s and ’90s—were, in fact, two of the key elements of the outfits Diana put together for her boys. The lineup also included matching shirts, polos, and sweaters. “Looking back at the photos, it just makes me laugh, and I think, ‘How could you do that to us?’” Harry added with a touch of irony.

As they grew up, the two, of course, began to rebel against this tradition—particularly William, who, according to Harry’s account, at one point refused to have anything to do with being his brother’s twin. “Funnily enough, we got to the age when William would turn round and go: ‘Oh, this is ridiculous. You know, I’m the older brother. Why do I have to be dressed the same as him?’” he recalled. “Hang on a second. If you’re going to dress differently, I’m not going to be the only person dressed like this. This is just ridiculous!” Harry replied.

As with any growing boy, things gradually began to change, and the two brothers started to develop their own independent style. But one can’t help but pause to consider how every choice—even the most trivial, like picking out an outfit—was a statement of intent for the beloved princess. Always in the name of love.

#3540. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3539. DC Studios Boss Jeremy Latcham Wants More Family-Friendly Movies In Hollywood

Remember when nobody cared who was in charge at movie studios and we just watched the actual films? Those days are long gone, as evidenced by the latest debacle at Skydance, where DC Studios co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran are out. The pair are set to be replaced by longtime Marvel Studios producer and Kevin Feige colleague, Jeremy Latcham,who has a more wholesome, family-friendly sensibility than his predecessors. In fact, he wants more family entertainment from Hollywood in general.

At this point, it remains to be seen just what the Marvel Studios alum, who will officially become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1, 2026, has in store for DC, or indeed how much creative control he'll have. What we do know about Latcham is that he's all for family-friendly fare. He previously spoke to The Christian Broadcasting Network in an interview entitled "Hollywood Producer Behind Massive Marvel Hits Loves Jesus."

The new face of DC we are cooked. RIP Peacemaker and anything rated R pic.twitter.com/W50CYpfBeO

In this interview from June 2026, Latcham refers to the "Grandma Test" he used during his Marvel tenure "When we were making the first Marvel movies, I'd always be like, 'I don't know if my grandma would like that, you know?'" he said, adding:

"And that became like a guiding light of like as we were developing the movies, I just had this sense of, 'I don't know if my grandma would like that,' and that became the stand-in [to determine if a movie] is going to work for regular people that are outside of the bubble of Hollywood. What does this [movie] say for a regular family?"

While we ponder how DC's cinematic future could be indirectly influenced by Jeremy Latcham's nana, it's worth noting that this "grandma test" is just one expression of Latcham's fondness for wholesome entertainment.

Jeremy Latcham has made no secret of his affinity for family-friendly movies that put heart and characters at the forefront. In another clip making the rounds on Twitter/X, the newly-appointed DC Studios head spoke about how studios have forsaken the most important elements of film in order to churn out empty spectacle.

The new DC Studios boss, Jeremy Latcham, talks about the importance of storytelling, making movies that connect with audiences, and creating memorable cinematic experiences.#DCU #DCComics #DCStudios pic.twitter.com/Wnnancri19

— Phil The Assyrian King (@PhilTheAssyrian) November 10, 2026

"The thing that I learned most at Marvel, and the thing that drives the movie, and it's something that I feel very strongly about, is heart, humor, and spectacle, in that order," Latcham said, before adding that most people in Hollywood get it wrong. "A lot of people in town say, 'We're making a spectacle film and the characters don't matter as much and the humor doesn't matter as much because it's all about the spectacle.'" According to him, however, spectacle is readily available in our society. What matters is heart and "characters that you can actually invest in." Doesn't seem like a bad point, does it?

Unfortunately, that perfectly reasonable assessment of the modern day movie industry recently led Latcham to produce one of the most forgettable movies of 2026 in "The Breadwinner," the family-oriented comedy starring Nate Bargatze that earned a 19% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. Otherwise, besides producing big Marvel hits such as "Iron Man," "Spider-Man: Homecoming," and, funnily enough, James Gunn's "Guardians of the Galaxy," Latcham has been involved with "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves" and "Bad Times at the El Royale." But "The Breadwinner" was most obviously aligned with Latcham's stated sensibilities, and that isn't the most reassuring fact.

Jeremy Latcham left Marvel Studios in 2017 and between producing mainstream movies has also been involved in several Christian projects, including the Biblical TV series "House of David." He previously appeared on the Bible Bros podcast where he talked about using his faith during his time at Marvel Studios. "It wasn't like instilling, like, faith per se," he said. "But it was like instilling redemptive qualities into these characters and seeing the growth that they could have." Latcham doesn't seem interested in injecting overt Christianity into DC's output. But his fondness for family-friendly entertainment obviously has a Christian basis.

The new DC Studios head went on to say, "There's not been a theatrical family comedy [...] in the theaters in, like, over a decade. They just abandoned it [...] And I was like, 'I think people will go see this movie if you make it.'" Sadly, "The Breadwinner" didn't prove his point. But clearly this guy wants more movies to be a lot more wholesome than they currently are.

Whether he'll use DC to try to shift things in that direction remains unclear. A new report claims that Skydance CEO David Ellison and his cohort plan on dismantling James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC Universe, clearing the way for a new take on the source material. But it's unlikely Latcham will have much creative freedom. Ellison, who runs the newly-merged Paramount and Warner Bros., is having Latcham report to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein rather than directly to him. As such, Latcham will have an extra level of oversight. Whether he'll actually get any closer to his vision of a family-friendly, PG-13 Hollywood utopia at DC is yet to be determined.

The Blade Runner saga is set to continue amid the 2026 TV schedule, thanks to an upcoming limited series. Blade Runner 2099 presents the next chapter in this science-fiction-infused tale of humans and replicants and puts new protagonists at the forefront. Given what’s come before, it’s only natural to wonder whether the show has direct connections to Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film and Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, 2049. Well, the showrunner is now shedding some light on that front.

If it weren’t already clear due to the title, 2099 picks up fifty years after the events of the critically acclaimed Blade Runner 2049. That film left quite a few plot threads on the table, including the revelation that the late Eldon Tyrell gave replicants the ability to reproduce. Heading up the new show is Silka Luisa, who is a longtime fan of the franchise. Luisa recently spoke with SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend and was asked if events from 2049 would come into play. With that, she gave a very clear answer:

No, [Blade Runner 2049] is not directly connected to the show. What was an important early mandate was that audiences could come to the show not having seen the films, and this could stand alone. This could be an introduction to the world of Blade Runner, and it wouldn’t be dependent on you having watched 2049, you having watched the first Blade Runner. In that sense, we had to divorce ourselves from the narrative.

Why Edward James Olmos Says He Owes His Battlestar Galactica Legacy To Blade Runner

Some fans may be a tad disappointed to learn that replicant reproduction won’t be expanded upon during the events of the show. Yet Luisa’s “mandate” does indeed make a lot of sense. What she and her collaborators ultimately want is a show that fits snugly into the continuity but also doesn’t require watching the movies. (Of course, both of those films are excellent and deserve to be watched regardless.) In short, the Shining Girls creator is promising a series that works on its own, and that could do away with any trepidation newcomers may have about jumping in.

Blade Runner 2099 takes viewers to a Los Angeles that’s now fully controlled by replicants, and humans must essentially live within the lower levels of society. At the center of the story is Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner (played by Michelle Yeoh) who is only days away from dying. She is eventually partnered with Marion Jessop to take on a case. However, unbeknownst to Olwen, “Marion” is actually a human named Cora (Hunter Schafer), who is only masquerading as a Replicant to achieve her own goals.

Per what’s been shared thus far, Yeoh and Schafer forged a strong bond on set not unlike Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling did while making 2049. However, as far as we know, Yeoh didn’t accidentally punch Schafer in the face like Ford did to Gosling. In fact, Yeoh was protective of her co-star amid production and, in a truly mom-coded move, she even bought Schafer a baby helmet.

The trailers for 2099 would suggest that such headgear was necessary, because a lot of intense moments have been teased thus far. Although fans won’t see any direct links to the Blade Runner films, Silka Luisa is aiming to dish out the action-infused thrills, heightened visuals and deep themes that have long permeated this franchise.

Check out Blade Runner 2099 when all eight episodes are released for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25. In the meantime, anyone who’s curious can stream the original movie for free on Pluto TV and check out 2049 on Prime as well.

#3537. PlayStation Officially Cancels Live-service Shooter Fairgames

Sony's latest game cancellation adds to a long list of failed GaaS projects

Sony has canceled Fairgames (aka Fairgame$) three years after the live-service shooter was announced, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. No one at its developer, Haven Studios, is getting laid off, and instead Haven will support other Sony Interactive Entertainment-owned studios, according to that report.

Farigames recently held a playtest and, according to an internal email reviewed by Bloomberg, feedback from that playtest didn't live up to PlayStation's expectations. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle said in the email. With "challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre," Sony decided to cancel the game.

Fairgames reportedly had been reworked multiple times since its 2023 reveal. It would have been the debut game from Haven, which was founded in 2021 by former Assassin's Creed producer and Google Stadia Games and Entertainment head Jade Raymond, who has since left the studio. Haven was acquired by Sony in 2022.

Back in 2022, Sony announced a huge push for live-service games, aiming to release at least 10 by 2026. While games like Helldivers 2 and Gran Turismo 7 have been steady live-service hits, Sony's push has largely failed. Concord is the most notable misfire, as it was actually released before Sony reversed course and shut it down shortly after launch in embarrassing fashion.

A live-service God of War game, a multiplayer The Last of Us game, and many others were canceled before they could see the light of day. PlayStation studios working on live-service games, including London Studios, Firewalk Studios, and Bluepoint Games, were all shut down in recent years. In June, Sony laid off most of the Destiny team at Bungie, as "Destiny 2 fell short of expectations" with players. Recently, Horizon Hunters Gathering was reportedly delayed so it can be rebooted in response to negative player feedback (which sounds not too dissimilar to the Fairgames situation).

#3536. No Reservations: Jessica Craig-Martin Serves Up a Rowdy, Inside Account of ’80s Indochine

No one is famous when they are at home. In New York in 1984, all it took to be famous was to leave the house with intent to commit fame. Beautiful youths were shot through the fame cannon at a rate that made Warhol’s fifteen minutes seem like a century. A cloud of new money hovered over the city, ominously gathering dollars, dropping sudden fortunes on those who knew how to make it rain. No veneer of philanthropy was needed to whitewash the excesses of the wealthy. Conspicuous consumption was the new normal. The new designer clothes all had giant shoulder pads. So did the buildings. The thick-walleted and soft-bellied moved around the city at night in chauffeur-driven carapaces. Eurotrash was the latest import. Fast-talking cocaine replaced nodding-out heroin. The words supermodel and art star fell from heavily glossed lips. Everyone wanted to see and be seen. But where? Studio 54 was closed, disco was dead. Brian McNally’s new restaurant, Indochine, was poised to become the epicenter of ’80s decadence.

Jessica and another waitress with Rupert E at Indochine, 1986.

Waitressing seemed like the best way to make money. I’d met Brian while traveling with the Mardens in France, and he’d mentioned he was opening a restaurant. I had left New York as a hip urban waif with short dark hair and pale skin. I returned curvy and brown-skinned, with long hair that had turned blond in the sun. I wore no makeup and had no interest in fashion, feeling I’d done all that as a teen. I wore vintage ’40s dresses from flea markets, and plastic jelly sandals. When I dropped by 420 Lafayette to ask for a job, Brian looked me up and down and gave me a sly wink. “Yeah, you’ll do.” The question of waitressing experience did not come up.

On opening day, I arrived to find the staff running around frantically with hammers and paintbrushes; stenciling palm leaves on the walls; putting up wallpaper; accepting deliveries of banana trees, ducks, orchids, MSG, and Champagne. There was no way in hell we were going to be ready. I grabbed a brush.

Indochine opened that night, walls still wet, with a private party for Julian Schnabel’s opening at the Mary Boone Gallery. Art dealer Pat Hearn sang Patsy Cline songs wearing a tight 1950s gold brocade dress. Warhol superstar, writer, and genius-about-town Taylor Mead got up on a table to give a hilarious impromptu speech. The crowd danced all night. With one private event after another, opening night lasted a month.

Brian was truly brilliant with people. He made everyone feel like they were in the right place at the right time, and that they were clever, sexy, witty, charming, or all of the above. He was just as comfortable with Henry Geldzahler as he was with Madonna. He could converse on any topic and did so with an easy British charm and lack of pretension that disarmed even the worst snobs.

Moira Hodgson gave us two stars, but other critics found the food “rather ordinary” or “unspectacular,” and everyone agreed that the service was appalling. Ironically, as Brian pointed out later, this became part of the charm of the place. Brian had a strict policy of never refusing a reservation, no matter how overbooked we were. He knew the frenzy at the bar and long waits for booked tables only increased our status as the most sought-after restaurant in town.

When Brian told me my shirt was wrinkled, I said, “Brian, chill out. This is linen. It’s supposed to be wrinkled.” In fact, the shirt could have done with a quick press, but I had only one white shirt and no intention of buying an iron or paying for dry cleaning. Fortunately the waitstaff started to add increased personal touches to the black-and-white dress code until it disappeared. Brian stopped objecting when he saw that the stylish staff was becoming one of the draws of the place. Soon most of us were unrecognizable as waitstaff, leading to many a black-suited banker being called upon for drinks or the check while navigating his way to the bathroom.

Taylor Mead became a nightly fixture at the bar, offering brilliant quips while dining on Dewar’s. Larissa slept on her barstool, her lit cigarette in an elegantly raised hand until someone said, “Larissa!” causing her to reanimate and flick her ash while shouting: “Dahhhh-ling!” She was a movie star who didn’t need movies. If Larissa came to Indochine to sleep, John F. Kennedy Jr. and Daryl Hannah came to break up and reunite, using the vestibule to break up and the bathroom for make-up sex. Carol Channing brought her own silver. Dolly Parton brought her own food. She was on a raw-vegetable and booze diet: “Just gimme the most expensive bottle in the house, honey.” Bianca Jagger ordered her meals in one low, unsmiling breath: “Steamed vegetables no soy sauce no hot sauce no sugar no salt no MSG.” What she didn’t know was that in the kitchen there were three tubs of white powder that went into every single dish: salt, sugar, and MSG.

Dead-eyed debutantes danced in their Manolo’s on tables strewn with platters of spicy beef salad, celebrating an addition to the Guinness dynasty. I wouldn't start using a camera for another eight years, but my mother says Indochine is where I became a photographer.

One night Lena Horne spat her gum directly into my hand. “Gum,” she’d said, after beckoning me over, after which I’d instinctively put my hand out. I gave it to my boyfriend Nick for his birthday. A strand of Cindy Crawford’s hair was the following year’s gift. (We never did get around to cloning her.) Saturday nights were Bridge and Tunnel. I opened the bathroom door to find a woman in high-heeled white boots giving a blowjob to some guy, his soft leather pants around his ankles. Laurie Anderson and I waited to pee while they finished. After that we referred to Saturdays as “White Boot Nights.” Warren Beatty leaned casually against a column, asking a waitress, “You’re a dancer, right? I can see the dance in your body.” A few months later, there he was, leaning against the column again. He asked the same waitress, Robin, “You’re a dancer, right?” Robert De Niro would sit at the end of the bar checking out the scene. Then he’d leave and call the restaurant from his idling limo. He’d ask the maître d’ to tell a woman he found attractive that he was on the phone. Sometimes women simply left their dates mid-meal to join him. One night the Beastie Boys brought a homeless man to dinner who’d asked them if they could spare some change. Even the odd exiled dictator made an appearance. The shah of Iran booked one table for himself and his wife, and three for his bodyguards. I noted their ankle holsters.

The waitstaff was made up of ambitious, creative young New Yorkers. Among them were Fidel Márquez, a painter; Masha Calloway, a fashion designer; and Darrell Maupin, who would open his own successful restaurant, Flamingo East. They and Robin Renzi, the dancer, became my close friends. Robin would later launch the jewelry line Me&Ro with Michelle Quan, who left Indochine for a modeling career. All I had going on outside of work were drawing classes at the New York Academy of Art a few days a week. I had not yet located any particular ambition. I went for dinner with friends, danced all night, and had sex all day. I remember being furious with Brian for a remark he made when I arrived at work: “You look like you just got fucked all day.” I was outraged, but it occurred to me later that he was absolutely right.

There was an ecstasy dealer who took to dropping by the restaurant around midnight. We’d take the pills toward the end of our shifts, hoping no customers would linger too long. After work we’d head to the clubs, needing catharsis and easily spending the money we had just spent hours earning. The Sisyphean irony of this went unnoticed. I was amused to discover that working at Indochine had a certain cachet. Waiters and waitresses were swept past the velvet ropes into all the clubs. I was initially surprised by the mini celebrity status conferred by waiting tables, but it says a lot about the era, which was all about tipping status on its head. Julian Schnabel was flipping burgers ten minutes before he became famous overnight with his broken-plate paintings. With his sensational-looking wife, Jacqueline, on his arm and New York at his feet, he seemed to be starring in his own biopic as he swept into Indochine night after night. “Jessica, get yourself a glass—have some of this Cristal,” he would say with a beneficent wave of his arm. It was the only restaurant in town where you could see Madonna, Sean Penn, Chris Walken, and Andy Warhol in one booth, John Waters and Divine in the next, and Henry Kissinger and his wife having a quiet dinner in another.

A certain high-powered lawyer was easily the restaurant’s most repugnant client, a considerable achievement. On one occasion he was approached by his waitress, Demetrious, a Black, bald, and beautiful torch singer who always wore huge brass earrings in the shape of Africa.

“Can I offer you something from the bar?” she asked him.

“Yes. I would like a different waitress,” he told her without looking up. She ignored him, went away, and returned calmly.

“I already told you, I want another fucking waitress,” he spat.

She shrugged. “I’m your waitress. I guess you’ll just have to deal with it.”

“GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM ME YOU UGLY BLACK BALD BITCH!”

She leaned in. “Sitthefuckdownandshutthefuckupyoudumbwhite-muthafucka,” she said in one breath. Beaten, he sat. I begged Brian to ban him, but Demetrious just shrugged it off. She was used to fighting her own battles and had already moved on.

At first, I was shocked by the overtly sexist behavior and banter at the restaurant. In the art world men did not compare the sex appeal of women in the presence of other women—or to their faces. There was rampant sexism and misogyny in the art world, of course, but it was generally more institutional and less visible to the naked eye. Men in the art world were less likely to openly grab one’s ass, or to make saliva-drenched comments about the run in your stockings inspiring in them an urge to bend you over a table. The art world had its share of knuckle-draggers—but the likelihood of being kneed in the balls by the objects of their desire kept them somewhat held in check. The women who raised me considered that feminism had “worked.” Their very existence was proof. No one thought the work was over—the ERA had failed to pass, after all—but the essential equality of women was beyond question, and the idea of acting coyly around men was considered absurd. However, the liberation train I’d been raised on had not reached restaurant culture. I was shocked to see so many women pushing out their tits, wiggling and giggling for their power-suited dates. Ironically, I’d been sheltered by my avant-garde upbringing.

I met Huy Chi Le on my first shift at Indochine. He was my age and had just arrived in New York from Vietnam. He spoke almost no English. Huy worked six nights a week at Indochine and seven days at another restaurant, working twice the number of hours to make the same amount of money as a waiter. When Huy was promoted at both venues to waiter, he kept both jobs, still taking just a half day off a week. He sent funds to his family and saved the rest. He established credit, obtaining an Amex gold card while we waiters were living out of tip envelopes and dancing all night. He bought a house in Brooklyn and sponsored his family to come over one by one. By the time Brian was ready to sell, Huy was poised to buy. He is now the owner of several businesses, a multimillionaire, and—with former manager Michael Callahan and former waiter Jean-Marc Houmard—co-owner of the still incredibly popular, and now legendary Indochine.

#3535. The Cat In The Hat Is Another Box Office Flop Warner Bros. Can't Afford

Another weekend, another bad result for Warner Bros. "The Cat in the Hat" looked like it could help get Warner Bros. back on track at the box office. Instead? It became the latest in a string of flops that has defined the studio's year. Family-friendly movies have been very safe bets in recent years, and on paper, Dr. Seuss is very good intellectual property to exploit for a PG animated movie. But this didn't pan out as anyone had hoped.

Director Erica Rivinoja's "The Cat in the Hat" opened to a very disappointing $20 million domestically. It also pulled in just $10 million internationally, giving it a soft $30 million global start. That was only good enough for the number two spot, since "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening. Normally, it would be much safer to bet on the PG family movie over the R-rated Japanese monster movie. But this wasn't a normal situation, and instead, the animated movie was left fighting for scraps, relatively speaking.

The new movie sees the title character (voiced by "SNL" alum Bill Hader) take on his toughest assignment yet for the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC): to cheer up Gabby and Sebastian, a pair of siblings struggling with their move to a new town. It carries a reported budget in the $90 million range.

This major disappointment comes mere weeks after the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was made official, with the mega-corporation Skydance now ruling over both studios. That corporation is lousy with debt and it needs Warner Bros. to deliver. Unfortunately for CEO David Ellison and his new film chiefs, they're walking into a messy situation. They've got a ship to right.

The storied movie studio had a stellar year in 2025, with massive hits like "Sinners" and "F1" to its name. Warner Bros. set a huge record that year with six movies in a row opening to at least $40 million, but 2026 has not been nearly as kind.

Skydance inherited a string of massive flops from the Warner Bros. deal, with its 2027 slate also looking a bit uneven. Things could get worse before they get better, as evidenced by the performance of "The Cat in the Hat." Granted, the year should end on a high note as "Dune: Part 3" is just around the corner, but even that can't make up for everything that preceded it.

A very rough rule of thumb for theatrical success has always been a movie making 2.5 times its budget, given that theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales. So just how bad has the year been for Warner Bros? The studio's bombs/disappointments include "The Bride!" ($90 million budget / $24 million worldwide haul), "They Will Kill You" ($10 million budget / $19 million worldwide), "Mortal Kombat II" ($80 million budget / $129 million worldwide), "Supergirl" ($170 million budget / $126 million worldwide), "The End of Oak Street" ($90 million budget / $121 million worldwide), "Practical Magic 2" ($75 million budget / $106 million worldwide), and "Digger" ($180 million budget / $50 million worldwide).

Yikes. Tom Cruise's "Digger" alone will lose as much as $250 million. Hits like "Wuthering Heights" and "Clayface," encouraging though they may be, can't come close to making up for losses that pile up for would-be blockbusters like "Supergirl." Unfortunately, this Dr. Seuss adaptation now joins this ever-growing list of crushing disappointments. Skydance and the new team has their work cut out for them.

#3534. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

At any point there are a number of upcoming book to screen adaptations on the way, but few are as wildly anticipated as the upcoming Harry Potter TV show that's coming to HBO (and will be streaming with a HBO Max subscription). The pressure is on for the show to deliver, especially with a new group of young actors playing the beloved characters. OG Ron Weasley Rupert Grint recently shared his "hope" for the next Ron, and now I'm getting emotional.

The Harry Potter cast grew up before our eyes, especially Grint, Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson. In an interview clip from ET's Twitter, he side stepped questions about a possible cameo in the Potter TV show, while also speaking about his relationship with new Ron Alastair Stout. As he put it:

I mean, it’s interesting. The kind of great stories get retold. Yes. I wrote a letter to Alistair. Who’s Ron, just a few words to have support, ’cause it was, I mean, just such a fun time for me. I really hope they’ve had the same experience.

I'm not crying, you're crying. Playing Ron in the Harry Potter movies made Rupert Grint a household name, and catapulted him into mega fame. Despite this, and the long hours that went into shooting those eight films, it sounds like the 38 year-old actor looks back fondly on his time in the Wizarding World. He had fun playing Harry's best friend Ron, and hopes that Stout has the same experience during his years at Hogwarts.

The pressure is on for the Harry Potter TV show to deliver, and the young actors who are playing the leads might be feeling this. After all, they've got some big shoes to fill. Luckily it sounds like the OGs are being kind to the young stars who will soon become household names.

This is only the latest example of the Harry Potter movie stars wishing well for those involved in the TV adaptation. Back in June of 2024 Daniel Radcliffe said he hopes the producers allow the kids to stay kids, despite their magical new roles. Grint wants the new Ron to have plenty of fun, which feels like a similar sentiment.

He'll play an adult version of his signature character in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Broadway, following in the footsteps of Tom Felton, who reprised his role as Draco Malfoy on the Great White Way. Of course, fans are hoping that this means the OG actors will sign up for an film adaptation of that stage play. Fingers crossed it happens eventually.

The Harry Potter TV show is set to premiere on December 25th as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Those who want to re-watch Grint's time as Ron can do so by streaming the movies over on HBO Max.

#3532. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3531. Stephen Miller Into the Breach: How Susie Wiles’s Failures Portend Miller’s Future

There’s a time-honored tradition for new White House chiefs of staff: The outgoing chief invites former holders of the office, Republicans and Democrats, to a get-together (usually in the West Wing), where the newcomer is offered advice. But Donald Trump’s new chief, Stephen Miller—appointed in a jaw-dropping Truth Social post on Friday—won’t be getting a party. First, because the tradition applies only to a president’s first chief. Second, because no Democratic chief would likely want to be caught dead with Miller, a longtime basher of the opposition party. Shortly after hearing that Trump had picked the hard-right firebrand as his new chief, James Carville sent me a text that summed up the prevailing attitude: “This is like Caligula’s appointment of his horse as consul.”

It was different when Susie Wiles came to town. On the evening of November 19, 2024, she was the guest of honor at a dinner party thrown by Jeffrey Zients, Joe Biden’s outgoing White House chief of staff. They were joined by eight of Zients’s predecessors. It was an occasion for bipartisan bonhomie, a tradition started in 2008 by George W. Bush’s chief Joshua Bolten. In a spirit of goodwill and generosity, Bolten had thrown a gathering in his West Wing office for Barack Obama’s incoming chief, Rahm Emanuel. The informal meetup was intended as a way to convey the chiefs’ collective wisdom and experience—and to offer, in miniature, a nuts-and-bolts version of the transition of executive power that is a hallmark of American democracy.

Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

On the night of the dinner for Wiles, however, a cloud hung over the occasion. Virtually no one at the table thought she could succeed as Donald Trump’s chief of staff.

For almost two years, Wiles was the second most powerful person in the West Wing. Had Trump been interested in governing, she might have helped him solidify a GOP majority in Congress for years to come. But she was unwilling, or unable, to save Trump from himself. On Wiles’s watch, he squandered his second term with a reign of revenge, retribution, and recklessness. Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

And if past experience is any guide, Wiles’s replacement, Stephen Miller, may well crash and burn in even more spectacular fashion.

There was no one the president relied on or trusted more than Wiles. From their first meeting in 2015 at Trump Tower to her impressive stint as his winning 2024 presidential campaign co-manager, the “ice maiden” had Trump’s back. And he had hers—until last Tuesday’s epic Democratic blowout. Wiles would resign two days later. Indeed, the Republicans’ midterm apocalypse was an extinction event that not even Wiles could have survived.

Ironically, Trump’s savvy political strategist was the architect of what turned out to be a big blue bloodbath. “We’re going to win the midterms,” Wiles told me boldly when I interviewed her for Vanity Fair just a year ago. Even then, three months before Trump initiated a war on Iran, that was a ridiculously rosy prediction. The president’s approval rating was in the gutter. He’d failed to address, much less solve, voters’ primary concerns: affordability, inflation, health care, and housing—and had still not released the remaining Epstein files. How could a battle-hardened political pro like Wiles be so starry-eyed? The answer, I believe, is that in the fog of MAGA-land, she’d lost touch with the real world.

In almost every presidency, the West Wing is a bubble where like-minded acolytes engage in groupthink. But in Trump’s West Wing this phenomenon is exponentially magnified. It’s a parallel universe, one in which the 2020 election was stolen, violent insurrectionists are “patriots,” and the prosecution of political enemies—with scant evidence—is a presidential perk. (“Who would blame him?” Wiles said to me of Trump’s campaign to settle scores.) That, to my mind, is why Wiles seemed so stunned by the firestorm that erupted when her words appeared in my 10,000-word Vanity Fair series last December. She had no idea they would land like bombs on planet Earth.

Wiles invested Trump with almost otherworldly powers. He would lead the GOP to victory in the 2026 midterms, she believed, because of his preternatural ability to rally his base. That’s why, on the eve of the midterms, Wiles was all-in on sending Trump almost everywhere all at once, admonishing people to “vote like I’m on the ballot.” The trouble was voters saw all too clearly what she apparently couldn’t see: Trump was deeply unpopular; on his watch, the country was coming apart.

A year ago, when Wiles made her electoral prediction, I challenged her. “I admire your confidence about the midterms,” I said, “but the stakes are huge, right? And history is not encouraging. Incumbents do stuff and there’s a reaction. And usually, as Obama said, you get shellacked.”

Wiles seemed to shrug off that possibility. “Can you ever imagine Donald Trump saying that?” she said. “No, no.”

Wiles was right. Trump could never say such a thing—because he could never accept the fact that his electoral magic had waned. Neither, it seemed, could Wiles. But as his chief of staff and top political strategist, she was paid to know better.

Even before the election debacle, Trump had reportedly started privately inquiring about her on phone calls, although he lashed out at accounts of such purported conversations. Then, once the carnage sunk in, the die was cast. Wiles offered her resignation. And Trump accepted it.

At the start of her West Wing tenure, I believed Wiles stood a chance of succeeding. If Trump would listen to anyone, I thought, it was the loyal, organized, no-nonsense Wiles. Yet during 10 conversations with her over 10 months, I watched as she abdicated the most important duty of the White House chief: telling the president hard truths. Wiles told me she’d read my book, The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, and she understood the importance of heeding Reagan chief James Baker’s advice. “You do not serve your president well if you are just a yes man,” he said. In a phone call, she told me, Baker “reminded me that my job wasn’t to be a fangirl.” I asked Wiles, “Have you had any gut check moments where you had to tell the president something he didn’t want to hear?” She paused. “I probably have one a day,” she said. “But they’re over little things, not big.”

Wiles should have known that the midterms would spell disaster. She carried around a list of her priorities, on an index card. Number five: “Don’t forget about organized labor. Don’t forget about young Black men and women and Hispanics…because that’s the future of the country and the backbone of his support. And if we don’t convert those people to being enthusiastic Republicans, then if the Democrats were even just a little bit better, they might win an election.”

Miller is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean.

They might—and they did. And now Wiles is out, taking up shop, so Trump himself has said, within his political operation. Last November she hinted that she knew this day might come: “You go to bed at night, you say your prayers, you take stock of what the day was and what your day is tomorrow, and you get up and do it again…. So as long as that’s the case and the president’s pleased…” Wiles paused. “He could fire you tomorrow.”

She’s sensitive about her legacy as the first female White House chief. “I’m not an enabler,” she insisted. “I’m also, like, not a bitch. I try to be thoughtful about what I engage in, and what I disagree [with the president] about. I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

What about Wiles’s successor, Stephen Miller?

Miller is the antithesis of Ronald Reagan’s chief James Baker, a cool pragmatist who could push back on the president’s half-baked ideas. Miller, by contrast, is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean. He believes in a Hobbesian world, he has stated, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” Now he’ll be the last person in the room when Trump makes life-and-death decisions about law and order and war and peace.

The man who decreed that the president’s powers “are very substantial and will not be questioned” is now the official charged with questioning the president’s decisions. It’s hard to imagine Miller doing that without a personality transplant. He’s already alienated the House minority leader, and soon to be Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” insisting, “I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

At the White House last November, after a Vanity Fair photo session, I spoke with Miller at length about the midterms, still a year away; about his portfolio in the Trump administration; and about the role of the White House chief of staff. Perched on a chair in the Roosevelt Room, he eyed me warily. He seemed impatient to get back to work. “I understand that your need for me is quite limited, right?” he said.

I asked Miller about his interactions with the president—specifically an Oval Office meeting in which he and Trump reportedly talked about blowing up boats in the Caribbean. “I would never talk about…whether a meeting occurred or didn’t occur,” he said, “or whether it was in a meeting that did occur, or was not in that meeting if it occurred, which I would never say either way.”

Miller was more forthcoming about Wiles’s prediction—that Trump and the GOP would triumph at the polls in 2026. “What about you?” I asked him. “I am confident that we’ll win the midterms,” he replied. History might be against them, he said, “but we have every expectation that we’re going to defy that history.” “Why?” I asked. Miller replied, “Because of the president’s unprecedentedly successful first nine months in office.”

What followed was a black-is-white, up-is-down litany of Trump’s accomplishments, a revisionist history that might have made Karoline Leavitt, another world-class propagandist, blush. “In no particular order,” Miller said, “the taming and defeating of inflation. As you know, we inherited record double-digit inflation and the president made his first priority to bring down the cost of living…cutting the price of energy by high double digits. For many Americans, gas prices have been cut in half since we took over.” None of this, of course, has proved true—but Miller was just warming up.

“And the passage of the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Fully securing the Southern border, the most secure border in history, zero illegal crossings, four months in a row. And also the largest number of deportations in American history…. The president has…achieved more in foreign policy than any president in our lifetimes, ending eight wars in eight months—which includes, but is not limited to, securing the historic peace deal between Israel and Gaza, Thailand and Cambodia, Congo and Rwanda, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Israel and Iran, and so on…”

Miller still wasn’t done. The president, he said, “has executed on every promise he’s made to the American people and that includes also taking back our culture and fighting against whether you call it radical leftism or woke or Marxism—a lot of people just call it plain crazy—but taking back our culture and restoring sanity to American life.

“It is my extraordinary privilege and blessing,” Miller added, “to be able to work for the president of the United States, to implement an agenda that I believe in wholly and completely and with every fiber of my being.”

I was there, of course, because I was writing a story on Susie Wiles and her West Wing team. I asked him, point-blank: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?”

“No, I wouldn’t say that,” Miller replied, finding fault with my framing of the question and insisting that this president wants to hear everything. “The chief of staff would never have to encounter the scenario you’re describing.” Miller said. “President Trump craves, he loves the every-minute detail of management, having every piece of information, having every side of everything, having inputs into the Oval Office from every square, every quarter, every person.”

As for the president’s staff, Miller said, their job is “implementing the president’s vision, the president’s directions, the president’s agenda, the president’s plans for the future…. We’re just here on his behalf to see that that is done.”

As the great political columnist Molly Ivins once wrote, “It probably sounded better in the original German.”

Chris Whipple is a contributing writer at Vanity Fair and a Fall 2026 Resident Fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School Institute of Politics. You can follow him on Substack.

#3530. Jennifer Lawrence's R-Rated Spy Movie Is One Of HBO Max's Biggest Streaming Hits

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

An R-rated spy thriller starring Jennifer Lawrence is finding new life on HBO Max. The Oscar-winner's 2018 movie "Red Sparrow" has become one of the streamer's biggest hit movies, nearly a decade after its original release.

Directed by Francis Lawrence, who had previously worked with Jennifer Lawrence on "The Hunger Games" movies, "Red Sparrow" is currently the eighth-biggest movie on HBO Max right now, per FlixPatrol. It sits just above "The Wolverine" and just below "The First Purge." Olivia Wilde's comedy "The Invite" is still HBO Max's biggest streaming hit, but the fact that an eight-year-old thriller is right up there with the streamer's current biggest movies is meaningful.

"Red Sparrow" sees Lawrence play a deadly Russian spy. The film centers on Dominika (Lawrence), a former ballerina forced to enter Sparrow School, a government program that thrusts her into a treacherous espionage game. She emerges as a lethal agent, but is trapped in a world she desperately wants to escape. Joel Edgerton ("Warrior"), Matthias Schoenaerts ("Rust and Bone"), Charlotte Rampling ("Broadchurch"), Mary-Louise Parker ("Weeds"), and Ciarán Hinds ("Rome") also star.

The movie is based on the novel of the same name by Jason Matthews. Before it turned into a Lawrence and Lawrence "Hunger Games" reunion, "The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" director David Fincher and Rooney Mara were poised to reunite for "Red Sparrow." Darren Aronofsky ("Black Swan") was also set to direct at one point. But after much back and forth with a revolving door of A-list talent coming and going, it became a Lawrence starring vehicle. The results were viewed as underwhelming at the time.

Critics weren't terribly kind to the thriller upon its initial release. It currently holds a not-so-great 45% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. /Film called "Red Sparrow" an "overlong waste of Jennifer Lawrence's talent" in our review from 2018. It also didn't resonate as well as Fox had hoped it would at the box office at the time.

Against a relatively steep $69 million budget, the movie pulled in $151 million worldwide. It was by no means a hit, especially relative to expectations. Keep in mind that Francis Lawrence and Jennifer Lawrence had a great track record together. "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" ruled the box office just a few years earlier, capping off a multi-billion-dollar run for that franchise. Not to mention that Lawrence was just a handful of years removed from her Oscar win for "Silver Linings Playbook."

Maybe it's because Lawrence remains a big star, with viewers seeking out stuff they haven't seen of hers before. Maybe it's because this sort of action/thriller is the perfect kind of "watch it on the couch" movie. Either way, what was once a disappointment is finding new life all these years later.

You can also grab "Red Sparrow" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.
