#3510. Why Prince William Is Reluctant to Become Head of the Commonwealth

Following King Charles’s successful nine-day tour to the Caribbean, the future of the Commonwealth has become a much debated subject. At last week’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, Charles, who was designated Head of the Commonwealth, a role he assumed after his late mother Queen Elizabeth, told assembled leaders he found the voluntary union of 56 nations to be a “source of enormous encouragement and pride.”

However, Buckingham Palace has made it clear this weekend that Charles will only serve as monarch in the Caribbean realms “for as long as they wish” and that the monarch is open to change. According to The Times, Charles is “fully open” to those realms removing him as head of state.

While Charles was in the Caribbean, there was ongoing debate about slave trade reparations, which the monarch addressed in his speech to CHOGM. Describing it as a “monstrous injustice” he expressed his “profound personal sorrow” but fell short of making a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. (Since King Charles is a ceremonial head of state, he is unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless the government sanctions it.)

Amid calls for reparations, there are questions about the future of the Commonwealth and who its next head should be. In conversation with Vanity Fair, constitutional expert Ed Owens, author of After Elizabeth: Can the Monarchy Save Itself?, discusses what’s in store for the future.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

King Charles reacts near Antigua and Barbuda flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda on November 2, 2026 in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda.

Vanity Fair: Prince William has made it clear that he does not necessarily expect to follow his father as head of the Commonwealth, saying that the decision belongs to the Commonwealth itself.

Ed Owens: Prince William hinted after his difficult 2022 tour of Belize, the Bahamas, and Jamaica that he wasn’t focused on following his father as head of the Commonwealth. A couple of weeks ago The Times of London confirmed that the prince’s position was unchanged on this issue. Crucially, the position of head of the Commonwealth is not hereditary. King Charles got the role because his mother and predecessor, Queen Elizabeth II, actively lobbied Commonwealth heads of state to ensure that the role would pass to him when he became monarch, following her death. But it will not automatically transfer to William when Charles dies.

What is the Commonwealth and how significant is that statement?

The Commonwealth of Nations (as it’s officially known) is a voluntary association of 56 independent member states. Most of these member states were once colonies in the British empire. Decolonization began after World War II and most newly independent states—though no longer part of the empire—became part of the new Commonwealth. This new international body represented change but also continuity, enabling Britain to maintain a global (but mostly symbolic) presence at a time when its real geopolitical power was rapidly in retreat. The Commonwealth also provided a stage for the monarchy to continue to exercise an important international role. George VI was the last emperor and first Head of the Commonwealth. The latter role was invented by the British government to replace the former and allowed the monarch to maintain a semblance of global prestige while helping to facilitate the process of decolonization.

Although most member states have historical ties to Britain, any country can apply to join the Commonwealth—exemplified by recent members like Rwanda, Mozambique, Gabon, and Togo. Members commit to shared principles outlined in the Commonwealth charter, including democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and sustainable development. In reality, though, many member states have failed to live up to these principles, and the Commonwealth has, in recent years, felt morally directionless.

William’s reluctance to take on the mantle of Head of the Commonwealth isn’t that surprising: He and his advisers want to future-proof his reign. One way to do this is to identify potential problems in order to avoid them. The Commonwealth is one such potential problem, and William seems to have calculated that the headship of this organization likely represents more trouble than it is worth.

Does it represent a fundamental shift in the monarchy’s attitude toward the organization, or simply an acknowledgement that the old imperial relationship is no longer sustainable?

We have to remember that 15 members of the Commonwealth (including the UK) are also “realms”—i.e. their head of state is King Charles. I think it’s clear even to the current king that his position as monarch of the 14 realms beyond Britain is unsustainable. Eventually all 14 nations, and perhaps the UK too, will opt to become republics, cutting their ties with the crown. Those nations most likely to become republics soonest—owing to the fact that they have surging republican movements—are the Caribbean realms, two of which (the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda) King Charles visited during his recent tour to the Caribbean. Indeed, we can even interpret the tour as the king and his courtiers preparing the ground for this transition to republics. This is because, though former realms will no longer have as their head of state the incumbent monarch, they will almost certainly remain members of the wider Commonwealth.

What King Charles was trying to do with his latest tour was to inject energy and meaning into the idea of the Commonwealth, more than attempt to reinvigorate the personal bonds that connect him to his peoples in the Caribbean. In loudly acknowledging the injustices of the slave trade in which Britain was, for a long time, complicit, while also reminding his hosts that Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish and oppose slavery—the king has sought to address and ease concerns in ways that might enable the Commonwealth to function more cohesively in the future, irrespective of whether the UK’s monarch remains in post as head of the Commonwealth.

When Charles eventually leaves the throne, could the Commonwealth decide that it no longer needs a British monarch as its figurehead? What might replace that role? Will the Commonwealth continue?

I absolutely think [the] Commonwealth nations will look to replace the British monarch with a new figurehead. My sense is that many nations would already prefer to have a different kind of figurehead, for example a head who belongs to one of the 56 member states and is elected by member states for a set term. Alternatively, there could be some kind of “rolling” headship, whereby every member nation is invited to elect an official who will take a 12-month turn as head of the Commonwealth.

Whether or not the Commonwealth will continue is more difficult to say. Certainly one of the reasons it has survived until now is because of the energy and engagement of two British monarchs—Charles and Elizabeth II—who have viewed it as a potential force for good in the world. Without its connection to the British monarchy, it may lose what is left of its momentum. However, its survival also depends on wider geopolitical shifts: If individual governments within the Commonwealth view it as [a] useful arena for bringing together states who could benefit from closer association—be that economic, political, or military association—then it may continue long into the future.

There is an increasingly difficult conversation about Britain’s colonial past, slavery, and reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over the slave trade, but the question of a formal apology remains politically and constitutionally complicated. How much freedom does the king actually have to address these issues, and could William take a different approach?

The king has very little freedom to apologize unless his government specifically sanctions and encourages such an apology. As the recent Caribbean tour made clear, I think Charles would prefer to strike a more nuanced line, reminding audiences that, despite the UK’s colonial past and its involvement in the horrors of slavery, Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish slavery and that it played an important role in bringing to an end the maritime trade in human chattel. Whether William takes a different approach will depend entirely on the UK government’s approach to formal apologies and reparations. My sense is that no government—at least not now or in the near-to-medium-term future—will agree to financial reparations, because historians, philosophers, and politicians are increasingly pushing back on such a solution, questioning why UK taxpayers (already under huge strain) should fork out huge sums for the wrongs committed by some of their ancestors more than two centuries ago.

What would Queen Elizabeth II make of this? She saw the Commonwealth as her father’s legacy and her second family.

I think she would probably be relatively relaxed, recognizing that times change and institutions have to evolve. Let’s not forget that as queen she oversaw many key alterations in the way both the monarchy and Commonwealth functioned through her long reign, as was required by shifts in politics, economics, culture, and social norms. While the Commonwealth was of emotional importance to her—not least for the way it connected her back to her father and predecessors—by the end of her reign it was already a shadow of what it once had been and she would have known that it was likely to continue on a trajectory of decline. William has decided that given the challenges and changes of the mid-20th century the monarchy and royal family’s future is likely to be stronger without the post-imperial baggage of the Commonwealth. I think his grandmother would have respected the way he is putting the family firm first in this instance.

For over 20 years now, the 2003 Mike Myers version of The Cat In The Hat has been the only version of the classic Dr. Seuss book to watch. However, this past weekend, it got the animation treatment, and it’s a blast of an adaptation. I even have an idea for a spinoff, and I ran it by some of the cast. SPOILERS ahead!

Look, I like The Cat, especially because he’s voiced by Bill Hader years after he played the character on SNL. But to me, the real highlight of the film are The Things. In my opinion, they are like much more likeable Minions, and the movie even explores what can happen to one when they get villainous. As we learn at the end of The Cat In The Hat, the reason why Thing 2 was missing is that he became The Something due to overusing the Go-Backer device. Oh, and of course there’s that meta line where The Cat tells The Things to wait for their own movie.

The Things are pretty mysterious characters, but I thought The Cat in the Hat did an excellent job of making them so fun and intriguing. I think it would be so much fun to see them on their own adventure after this movie earned a thumbs-up with audiences through an “A” CinemaScore. Though it’ll have to earn more money at the box office after Godzilla Minus Zero won the weekend.

When CinemaBlend spoke to the cast of The Cat In The Hat, I brought up the topic of a Things spinoff. Here’s what Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson, a.k.a. Sherrie from HR in the movie, had to say:

I wanna learn everything about them. This movie opening the crate, so to speak, on The Thing world, made me wanna know way more. I still have a lot of questions. Like, are they related? Are they from a planet? Is there offspring? Do they fall in love? Do they get married? I have a lot of questions. Why are they numbered? Do they have names beyond the numbers?

I love all these questions she has about The Things, because I had many of them myself. The Things have always been a memorable part of The Cat In The Hat book, but it would be so fun for a spinoff to explore who they are without The Cat. Here’s what Mr. Hoogeboom voice actor Giancarlo Esposito added:

I'm fascinated by The Things. I think they're on some advanced level of intellectual and emotional feeling. I just think that they're simpler, and somehow they communicate in a way that's clearer than any words could ever get.

I feel like a lot of kids are going to start learning Thinglish as is, and I wanted my own Thing plushy the moment I finished the movie. I even brought it up to the writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni. Here’s what Carloni had to say about my idea:

If we're so lucky that the audience wants more of the characters we created, that would be very flattering. Give them what they want.

We’ll have to wait and see if this becomes a reality! For now, you can watch The Cat In The Hat only in theaters.

Sarah El-Mahmoud has been with CinemaBlend since 2018 after graduating from Cal State Fullerton with a degree in Journalism. In college, she was the Managing Editor of the award-winning college paper, The Daily Titan, where she specialized in writing/editing long-form features, profiles and arts & entertainment coverage, including her first run-in with movie reporting, with a phone interview with Guillermo del Toro for Best Picture winner, The Shape of Water. Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

#3508. VisionQuest: The Identity Of The Client, Explained

Spoilers ahead for "VisionQuest" Episode 8, "Forever."

Ultron (James Spader) may have no strings on him anymore, but someone has been manipulating the events of "VisionQuest" like a puppetmaster. That someone is The Client, who hired the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to capture Vision (Paul Bettany). We've gotten glimpses of The Client all season, but only as a digitally altered voice or a faceless avatar ... until Episode 7, "Immolation."

At the episode's end, Vision and Ultron's gynoid lover Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) are delivered to The Client's doorstep. Out of said door walks ... someone who looks just like Ultron's human avatar. Huh?

"Forever" clarifies it. "The Client" is Virgil Horton, grandson of Phineas Horton (Bettany), the scientist who created the Synthetic Man/Human Torch (Bettany again) in the 1940s. As Virgil explains, the Synthetic Man's uncontrolled fire powers mean that Dr. Horton was considered a failure. Years ago, Virgil joined with Dr. Josephine Carrington (Miller) to perfect AI in hopes of redeeming the Horton family legacy. They scanned their own brainwaves to create the genesis of what Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) completed.

Horton and Carrington also fell in love. After Carrington's death from a terminal illness, Horton revived her as Jocasta. As Virgil explains, he was one of the engineers hired by SWORD to rebuild Vision back in "WandaVision." After that, he created a robotic body for Carrington's mind-scanned AI. Jocasta being a recent creation helps explain why she looks like feminine Ultron, but why did Virgil then erase her memories of him and her creation?

Virgil believes the only worthy lover of a "goddess" like Jocasta is a god. So, he intends to delete Vision's personality and then upload himself into Vision's shell, so he and Jocasta can rule an Earth infected with Jocasta's hive mind nanites.

Virgil's borderline-incestuous romance plan echoes the central influence of Ultron: "Frankenstein," specifically when the Creature asks Doctor Frankenstein to make him a companion. Virgil's plan is rather similar to Kenneth Branagh's 1994 "Frankenstein" film adaptation, where Victor Frankenstein (Branagh) tries to resurrect his dead wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) through the same process by which he made the Creature (Robert De Niro).

There's an implication that Virgil scanning his brainwaves for his and Josephine's AI embedded his personality into the AI code. That's why Ultron basically has his same flamboyant personality, his voice, and why Ultron wears Virgil's face as his human avatar. "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas has said giving Ultron a human form in "VisionQuest" was about getting the most out of Spader's performance. Now, we know, it was also essential to the pay off of this twist about the Client's identity. But "Forever" breaks out Ultron's robotic form, too.

Virgil's plan fails because Jocasta has fallen for Ultron and wants him to be her eternal partner. Using the nanites, Ultron recreates his physical form and crushes Horton to death with a hug. It's a very Oedipal move: Ultron's defining goal has always been killing his father, whether it be Hank Pym (in Marvel's comics) or Tony Stark (in the Marvel Cinematic Universe). He comes close to that by killing the man of whom he's an artificial echo.

Ultron being based on Virgil also explains why fell for Jocasta in the first place. This restores some of the mirroring of the creator and creation that's present in comics Ultron. In the "Avengers" comics, Ultron created Jocasta from the brainwaves of Hank Pym's wife: Janet van Dyne, the Wasp, and his spiritual mother. Since Ultron is based on Hank's personality, he inherited his father's affections for Janet though extremely twisted means. The same logic applies to Spader's Ultron falling for this Jocasta.

Now, it's worth noting that while Phineas Horton and his Human Torch originated in Marvel Comics, Virgil did not. Rather, he's an original creation of this series, and "VisionQuest" seems to be using him as a proxy for the original Dr. Horton. Previously, Steve Englehart and George Tuska's "Avengers" #135 tied Horton and the Ultron-Vision lineage together, with the issue revealing that Ultron had abducted Phineas Horton and forced him to rebuild the inert Human Torch into the Vision.

Keep in mind, Ultron and Vision debuted in 1968. At that time, it was plausible that a scientist active in World War II would be living in retirement. But not so much in 2026, where it makes much more sense to use a descendant of Horton in the present day. It's the same time creep that led to Captain America originally missing only two decades of time while frozen to awakening almost a century later.

#3506. Loose Lips Sink Chips: Silicon Valley Reacts to the (Alleged) Spy Who Shagged Jensen Huang

I remember asking my parents when I was a child why it was such a big deal for a politician to have an affair. They explained to me the many layers of possible compromise beyond the simple breach of morals and propriety. Extramarital affairs, my parents explained, could expose politicians to blackmail, undue influence, and the temptation to give up vital state secrets over pillow talk.

Maybe someone should have that explain-it-to-me-like-I’m-five conversation with investors like Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman, who rushed to the defense of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this weekend following his shocking confession that he’d been involved in an affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. (A Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson has called the spy allegation “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”)

Sure, Jensen Huang is not a head of state. But he’s arguably someone even more powerful. He’s the man in command of the world’s largest company—and its most coveted technological infrastructure: high-performance GPUs required to train artificial intelligence systems.

For years, tech-world observers scratched their head when he insisted again and again that his company should have the right to supply those elite chips to China—even as Americans were told that letting our most formidable adversary gain any advantage in the AI race would spell doom for the Western world. When Huang took the number four spot on our New Establishment list this fall, I wrote that his commitment to fighting these export controls could become his Achilles’ heel. And boy, has it. Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into his affair, while the government continues to assess the blast radius of the scandal.

There are “three big national security implications from this,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me this week. “The first question is whether Chinese intelligence has succeeded in obtaining any sensitive nonpublic information about Nvidia, about its products or—I think what’s being overlooked—its customers of massive quantities of GPUs, like large AI labs.” The second, he said, “is whether Chinese intelligence may have succeeded in indirectly obtaining information about President Trump or people close to him,” given Huang’s unusually close relationship with the president. And third is “the question of whether Mr. Huang’s personal relationship with his customer might have motivated the company’s decision to sell large numbers of computer chips to Megaspeed, a company that has been under investigation by the Commerce Department for violations of American law.” (A Megaspeed rep told The New York Times that the company was “conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion,” the subject of the US probe, and that it had “repeatedly offered to cooperate with the US government.”)

According to the Times, the US government has been aware of Huang’s relationship since at least 2025, prompting many more questions about why this knowledge was not made public until it was uncovered piece by piece by the killer investigative team at the Times—notably, right after the midterm elections.

“Someone in the national security establishment clearly decided that they were sick and tired of the president playing this game with Jensen,” said Dennis Wilder, a former senior intelligence official who now teaches at Georgetown’s School of Foreign Service.

Of course, investors have plenty of reasons to turn a blind eye to Huang’s misdeeds. His company has also played a keystone role in keeping the entire economy afloat, taking many investors’ portfolios along for the ride on its seemingly never-ending bull run since 2023. Many are wondering if dethroning him from the company he built from the ground up could also send our entire economy over the edge.

Fedasiuk thinks the decision is worthy of a bit more nuance. “I think investors and the American people have to remember that there is actually a distinction between the personal interests of Mr. Huang and the corporate interests of Nvidia, a $4 trillion company that is the backbone of the intelligence revolution,” he said.

Mentioned in this issue: Dario Amodei, Sherrod Brown, Whoop, Culper Research, Daniela Amodei, Holden Karnofsky, Brian Chesky, Ramp, Sean Parker, Tilt, Kalshi, Modal Labs, Lina Khan, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren.

Buried in The New York Times’ excellent deep dive into the ideologies that influence Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei was a link to the archived wedding website of his sister, Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei, and Anthropic staffer Holden Karnofsky. However weird you expect it to be, triple that.

I’ve always felt a kind of kinship with short sellers—would-be investigative journalists who’ve decided to use their skill set to make real money. Kudos to the investment-research firm Culper Research for publishing a brief back in May detailing its short position on Nvidia, taken, in part, due to Jensen Huang’s “uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang.”

Next time you log your weekend party habits, remember that Whoop sees you, and it’s judging you. “LSD and ketamine use were associated with bedtimes over an hour later and Recovery scores about 9 points lower. Psilocybin showed smaller changes: 33 minutes later and 2.9 points lower,” the company posted over the weekend. Tsk tsk.

Let the road show begin. Anthropic has proposed pricing its IPO shares at $70–$78 a pop, seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation for the AI company. The offering is expected to start trading on November 19.

Just the other day, a source was venting to me about how Silicon Valley billionaires have failed to use their wealth to improve their own surroundings. Was Airbnb cofounder and CEO Brian Chesky listening in on our call? He just announced a $100 million donation to benefit San Francisco parks—the largest single-donor gift to the city in its history.

Silicon Alley, I was not familiar with your game! New York City start-ups raised a record $4.94 billion this October, driven by giant funding rounds for Ramp, Kalshi, and Modal Labs.

One of the strangest stories to come out of the midterms: California’s Prop. 38, which reportedly granted $4.2 billion in state bonds to a three-person immunology nonprofit that counts Sean Parker as a board member. (The proposition was put on the ballot by the institute’s cofounder Gary K. Michelson.)

$140 billion+: Jensen Huang’s personal net worth. That would be one expensive divorce.

#3505. 5 Funniest Quotes from 'Calvin and Hobbes’ Babysitter Rosalyn

To put it mildly, Calvin got on the nerves of a lot of people in Calvin and Hobbes. First off, there was his mother, who Calvin fought with over her terrible cooking and going to school in the morning. He also frustrated his father, particularly when Calvin would break something costly, like a pair of fancy binoculars or part of the family car. Calvin ticked off his neighbor Susie, too, and even his teacher, Miss Wormwood.

But nothing compared to just how much Calvin would enrage his babysitter Rosalyn. With antics like locking her out of the house, pretending to flush her science notes down the toilet, and regularly jumping on her calls with her boyfriend to tell him she’s a child-hating monster, Calvin knew how to get under Rosalyn’s skin.

Rosalyn wasn’t helpless, however. She knew how to get back at Calvin with a snappy comeback, or an over-the-top threat in an effort to terrify the boy into compliance. She also knew how to squeeze more cash out of his parents to make up for her pain and suffering.

Here are Rosalyn’s five best quotes from the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes, courtesy of cartoonist Bill Watterson.

Just about every appearance of Rosalyn features some variation of the line above. She’s always asking for more money, saying her rates have gone up, or talking about the cost of college tuition. They’re always funny and they help to define who she is and why she puts up with Calvin at all. This line just happens to be the best of her many money-oriented interactions she has with Calvin’s parents.

Just to drive her crazy one night, Calvin is insulting the way Rosalyn has prepared his dinner, complaining about how she set the table wrong and how bad the food smells. Rosalyn, who isn’t in the first two panels, jumps in and shouts in his face that she’s not his mom, proving she’s got zero chill left for this kid.

I’m not even sure what a “drip” is, but man is it a funny insult. It comes when Calvin pretends to hear a noise outside one night when Rosalyn is babysitting. When she steps outside to find the source of the sound, Calvin slams the door behind her, locking her out. She isn't let back in until Calvin’s parents get home.

Needless to say, Calvin gets in big trouble.

Rosalyn’s relationship with Calvin was defined by how combative it was. They both hated each other and insulted each other and that’s where all the comedy came from. But for Rosalyn’s final story, which came just a few months before Bill Watterson concluded Calvin and Hobbes on Dec. 31, 1995, we got to see another side of Rosalyn.

When she kicks off her babysitting night with Calvin, she tells him he can stay up a half hour late and they can play whatever game he wants, as long as he goes to bed after that. It's surprising to hear, at first, but it seems like Rosalyn is just trying a new tactic to get Calvin to behave. She even seems to momentarily regret the idea when Calvin proposes they play Calvinball, a nonsensical game where the rules are constantly changing.

To Rosalyn’s surprise, she actually enjoys the game and has a pleasant evening with Calvin. She even says “Ha! This is fun!” when she starts to get the hang of the game. While it’s hardly a distinct quote, it’s notable because of how genuine it is. Rosalyn was all about the rivalry — and the cash — but this gentle little moment shows a whole other side to her.

There's just nothing better than this. While Rosalyn insulted Calvin all the time, this line takes the cake as her all-time best. It’s from the time when Calvin steals Rosalyn’s science notes and is threatening to flush them down the toilet. He’s locked the door to the bathroom and Rosalyn demands he open it with the funniest threat possible.

#3504. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3503. VisionQuest's Finale Finally Pays Off A Story Marvel Started In Avengers: Age Of Ultron

What is grief if not spoilers persevering? This article discusses major plot details from the season finale of "VisionQuest."

An argument could be made that the "VisionQuest" finale was a confrontation over a decade in the making. Clearly, the well-received Disney+ series has marketed itself as a "WandaVision" sequel and a trilogy-capper to the story continued in "Agatha All Along." But there's no way around its biggest and most pressing concern: providing a fitting epilogue to the 2015 blockbuster "Avengers: Age of Ultron." In an inspired choice, "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas understood there was still plenty of unfinished business between James Spader's megalomaniac robot Ultron and Paul Bettany's synthezoid Vision, which finally pays off spectacularly in the eighth and final episode of the show.

Once Vision and Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) realize that the mysterious Client dogging their steps is actually Virgil Horton (also played by Spader), the descendant of Phineas Horton (aka the mind behind the Synthetic Man, as portrayed by Bettany), this sets up the finale's most compelling battle. No, it's not Horton's toxic, twisted love for Dr. Jo Carrington and his desire to inhabit Vision's body so they may live forever together. It's the apparent murder of Ultron's lover Jocasta, setting off Ultron's malevolence towards humanity and one last showdown with Vision.

This is precisely the kind of potential that shared universes were meant to fully realize — not cameos and references for the sake of it or disposable narratives to throw on in the background as white noise, but as meaningful additions to ongoing arcs for viewers willing to take the time to explore them. That may go down as the greatest accomplishment of "VisionQuest" in its finale, delivering the perfect button on the Ultron saga that "Age of Ultron" simply couldn't pull off.

Amazing what eight hours of storytelling can do that studio-meddled blockbusters never could, eh? In spite of its obvious shortcomings and compromises, we here at /Film are long-suffering defenders of "Avengers: Age of Ultron." Arguably the last time the Marvel Cinematic Universe was able to be as weird and messy and introspective as the comics themselves, the movie still managed to find moments of quiet poignancy amid all the mind-numbing spectacle. To no surprise, that's something showrunner Terry Matalas and his writers have carried over into "VisionQuest," and nowhere is that more confidently on display than in the finale.

We're not only talking about the moment when a dying Jocasta merges Ultron with the horde of killer nanobots and allows him to regain his physical form, fighting Vision in a well-staged battle that ought to be many a nerd's dream come to life. What puts the finale over the top is when it somehow combines the best of "Age of Ultron" with "WandaVision." Vision traps Ultron inside a sitcom-set mindscape where the two artificial beings can hash out their differences without throwing hands and trading particle beams at each other. If previous episodes filled in some Ultron-centric plot holes, then this one brings us back to their best moment of all — when, in the midst of Sokovia's destruction, the two land in an idyllic forest to talk about humanity's doomed fate, the grace found in their failings, and the fact that nothing beautiful is meant to last forever.

Here, the big climactic fight becomes a treatise on Ultron's all-consuming grief, his unresolved malevolence towards human beings, and, deep down, his debilitating fear of being alone.

To the credit of "VisionQuest," this season-long epilogue suggests there's more to his emotional journey than a single movie could ever explore. The finale digs even deeper to prove this, completing Ultron's transformation into something much more human by giving him someone to love. Despite the changes made to the comics' origins, the Ultron/Jocasta romance is a defining moment in Ultron's portrayal in the MCU. Finally, he can understand Vision's own progression to becoming an individual in his own right, along with all the joy and loss and humanity that comes with it.

That's probably why, even after he retreats back to his old ways and attempts to cause our extinction again, "VisionQuest" posits that Ultron isn't beyond redemption. Sure, it isn't until he's confronted with his own mortality that he finally decides to spare the world's population. But even that is as human as it gets. Vision helps him come to terms with what life has to offer. And when we leave him, eager to appreciate human art and perhaps even rebuild Jocasta, it's a perfect period to the end of his sentence ... or, perhaps, an ellipsis.

"VisionQuest" is now streaming on Disney+ in its entirety.

#3501. Marvel Studios Officially Resurrects Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for VisionQuest episode 8.VisionQuest has ended, with the final episode of the Marvel Cinematic Universe TV show out on Disney+, and with it come major reveals, shocking deaths, and teases for what might happen in the future of the franchise. VisionQuest was the final live-action MCU series of 2026, and the only project fans will have before Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18. As such, many expected the show to set up the movie or Paul Bettany's Vision to play a role in it in some form. The VisionQuest finale has now come and gone, and there are direct ties to Doomsday.

What did happen in the final episode of the show was the completion of an emotional arc where Vision, Ultron, and multiple MCU AIs found their humanity. With the release of VisionQuest's final episode, the MCU's WandaVision trilogy, which also includes Agatha All Along, has also come to a close, and it was a fitting finale, which had the kind of superhero action and high-stakes Marvel Studios is known for, but not sacrificing character work for it. After VisionQuest episode 7 set up the finale through the debut of James Spader's The Client, the finale fully explained the character's past and goal.

Many fans hoped that Elizabeth Olsen would return as the Scarlet Witch in VisionQuest, reuniting the Maximoff family in the final release of the WandaVision trilogy. As Tommy and Vision talked following the twin brothers saving their dad, the MCU show teased that Wanda could still be out there with a hopeful line from Vision, who says, "We might say hello again." VisionQuest's second post-credits scene then brought back Olsen's Scarlet Witch, with Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom awakening her after the fall of Mount Wundagore, saying, "Your power will be mine."

This is how VisionQuest sets up Avengers: Doomsday, with Olsen's Scarlet Witch almost certain to appear in the movie and closely tied to Doctor Doom. While Wanda has yet to be confirmed for the film, a set of mysterious Latverian Witches will appear in the upcoming MCU movie, and one of the masked magic users wears red robes. She could be the Scarlet Witch in disguise after her VisionQuest resurrection.

Many fans grew used to following Vision and Wanda Maximoff's love story in the MCU, but VisionQuest set up a new one between Spader's Ultron and T'Nia Miller's Jocasta. However, the latter was killed when Virgil Horton, aka Phineas Horton's grandson and the real identity of The Client, shot a big role out of her chest. This led to Ultron killing Virgil and nearly killing humanity with Jocasta's nanites in retaliation.

However, by the end of the hour, Vision forced Ultron's hand, getting him to back down. In VisionQuest's post-credits scene, Ultron is set up to live like a human in the MCU, taking on Virgil's identity, given that the original died, and he was Ultron's human persona all along, as Horton's brain was buried in the foundational AI code. Ultron has Jocasta's hard drive, which means he could reassemble her, and as he experiences life as a human, there is a chance the MCU might be setting up Ultron to return as an anti-hero down the line.

The biggest surprise in the VisionQuest finale was the MCU return of Joe Locke's Billy Maximoff, aka Wiccan. Ruaridh Mollica's Tommy tried to find his brother, with the two briefly interacting through dream-binding and hugging before their connection broke. That scene also marked the return of Kathryn Hahn's Agatha Harkness, albeit off-screen, as it was implied that Billy was hearing advice from someone about portals, which Tommy questioned, but he wrote it off.

Given how Agatha died at the end of Agatha All Along, this connects with her appearing as a ghost that only Billy can see. Later in the VisionQuest finale, Billy came back in a triumphant return, having mastered the portal spell, and helped save his father, Vision, alongside Tommy. As such, by the end of VisionQuest, Bettany's Vision is finally back with his two sons, now teenagers with their souls reincarnated, and all that is left is one final reunion.

So, Ultron is off to experience life as a human and try to rebuild Jocasta, while Vision now has both of his sons back and has embraced all of his memories and the emotions linked to them. Virgil and Jocasta were the two major deaths of the episode, with the latter killed by the former, and Ultron murdering Virgil with a bear hug after using the nanites to manifest his physical robotic body.

As for the others, all the AIs have left Vision's Mindspace to live their own lives, which includes E.D.I.T.H., who warned Paladin and saved him from the RPG at the end of episode 7, which was revealed in the finale, now working alongside him and the super-powered Lisa Molinari as bounty givers, not hunters, helping people. After Ultron seemingly killed her in episode 7, it was also revealed that F.R.I.D.A.Y. was alive and well, now off to find her own place.

Marvel Studios ended the WandaVision trilogy with an exciting segment in the finale called UltraVision, which brought back the sitcom template as Vision tried to convince Ultron to call off the nanites. Given how time moved differently inside Ultron's mind, Vision could go for as many UltraVision episodes it took to get Ultron to stop.

Eventually, he realized it was futile and there was no longer time, so he went for a kamikaze move, burning both of their cores. In order to survive and also keep Vision, whom he sees as a son after all, alive, Ultron relents, triggering the nanobots' self-destruction, but keeping just enough to survive.

Finally, after seven episodes of teases and a shocking reveal last week, the VisionQuest finale fully explained who The Client was. He is Virgil Horton, the grandson of Phineas Horton, who created the Synthetic Man. Virgil was Josephine Carrington's husband, being responsible for bringing her back as Jocasta, which he deleted from her memory, and resurrecting Vision as White Vision while he worked for SWORD during the events of WandaVision.

Virgil was also Ultron's human avatar, which came as an effect of his brain scan being buried in the AIs' code. Virgil is dead for good in the MCU, with Ultron now taking his place. That is all for VisionQuest, with the MCU TV show not making it clear when fans will get to see its characters again, but at least players like Vision, Tommy, and Billy should return for a reunion with Olsen's Scarlet Witch in one of the upcoming Avengers movies or elsewhere.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

#3499. macOS 27.3 Golden Gate public beta 1 now available, here’s everything new

Following the release of macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, Apple is now rolling out the first test build for users enrolled in the public beta. Here’s what’s coming

Contrary to macOS 27.2, it looks like Apple had quite a bit in store for macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

In addition to expanding Siri AI to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also introduces several new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode for websites, and the ability to organize and manage tabs using Siri AI.

macOS 27.3 also adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look, allowing users to preview .md files with proper formatting instead of raw Markdown syntax.

The update also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

Users who enjoyed the wallpaper introduced with the new touchscreen MacBook Pro will also find a new screensaver called Pro Lighteensaver, which features light moving along the metallic-looking lines that form the word “PRO.”

Earlier this week, Apple also confirmed that macOS 27.3 will introduce new checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links. Starting with the update, files and photos shared using the “Anyone with the link” option will be checked by Apple, which may remove flagged content or take action against accounts that violate its policies.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 1 is 26C5035r, which is the same as the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

#3497. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3494. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3492. Report: Apple’s planned $7 billion bond sale attracts four times as much demand

Apple has filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds. Here are the details.

Over the past week, several Big Tech companies have turned to the bond market to raise billions of dollars amid growing investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta, for instance, just raised $15 billion through a US bond offering, followed by another €9 billion (roughly $10 billion) in European bonds. Earlier this week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (approximately $6.7 billion), while Microsoft completed a $25 billion bond sale last week, its first since 2017.

Apple has also turned to bond sales in the past to raise billions of dollars.

Previous offerings include those in 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Most recently, Apple raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond offering in May 2025, which attracted approximately $10 billion in investor orders.

Earlier today, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

However, while other Big Tech companies have been borrowing heavily amid growing AI infrastructure investments, Apple’s filing makes no specific mention of AI.

Instead, the company says it intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, potentially including stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment, as it has done in previous bond offerings.

And while the prospectus didn’t specify how much Apple intends to raise, Bloomberg reported soon after that the company is targeting approximately $7 billion, with investors already placing orders totaling around $31 billion.

According to Bloomberg, strong investor demand has also helped Apple secure more favorable borrowing terms, with investors willing to accept lower interest rates than those offered by Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle in their recent bond sales.

All of this is happening amid a massive tech sell-off, which saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge more than 6% at one point today, with Nvidia shares falling about 8% and the S&P 500 dropping nearly 4%.

Apple’s own stock is also taking a hit, trading down 1.49% at the time of publication, but it is faring better than those of its Big Tech peers, whose stocks have become more closely tied to the AI spending boom.

Be that as it may, Apple is expected to finalize the size and pricing of its bond offering soon, potentially as early as later today, after which the company will file the definitive terms with the SEC.

#3491. ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

The so-called villains of our childhood stories aren’t so bad when you look at things from their points of view. It’s a lesson that 21st century pop culture has taught us on a constant loop ever since “Wicked” kicked off an Oppenheimer-esque chain of tragedy that has seen everyone from Maleficent to Cruella de Vil humanized with their own origin story. It was inevitable that Cinderella’s allegedly wicked stepsisters would get their own mainstream version of the formula at some point (the Norwegian body horror movie exists in a separate, more ambitious category). If Hollywood can try to make us emphasize with someone who lives to kill puppies, anyone could have guessed that someone would slap a generational trauma label on literal children who grew up under the same evil matriarch as Cinderella. Related Stories ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy ‘Ink’ Trailer: Guy Pearce’s Rupert Murdoch Builds His Tabloid Empire in Danny Boyle’s Fleet Street Thriller

We’re long past the point where reimagining the classics from other characters’ perspectives earns you any credit for originality. If anything, those of us who have lived through the past two decades of pop culture might feel like stories where fairy tale side characters get to reclaim their agency are more omnipresent than actual fairy tales. But those original stories have endured in part because there’s always a new generation arriving to be wowed by them, and there’s no reason that the same principle can’t apply to the reimaginings, too.

Nobody whose age contains multiple digits needs to seek out “Steps” for any reason other than potentially entertaining their own children. But those young enough to be unfamiliar with the tropes it employs might be entertained or even moved by the material. “Cinderella” was an appropriate story to use for the purpose, as the beloved story of wish fulfillment doesn’t contain nearly as much emotional depth as better fairy tales like “Beauty and the Beast” or “The Little Mermaid.” Maybe it’s all part of a healthy cycle in which young kids can watch “Cinderella” and slightly older ones can watch “Steps” before graduating to stories and re-imaginings that have more to say. But on its own terms, the animated film comes across as little more than disposable corporate entertainment.

Directed by Alyce Tzue & John Ripa from a script by six credited writers (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, and Felicia Ho wrote the screenplay and Kate Micucci also has a story credit), “Steps” is a well-meaning entry into the subgenre that follows the blueprint competently enough to avoid being offensive or memorable. It literally opens on an old storybook with a stereotypical voiceover narrator reading the text about Cinderella being mistreated by her wicked stepsisters — before Lilith (Ali Wong) slides into the frame yelling “Whoa whoa whoa” and declares that the fairy tale is “character assassination.” From there, it’s only a matter of time before the contemporary pop needle drops start.

“Steps” has no choice but to expand the thin mythology of “Cinderella” before it has a chance to tell the other side of the story. In this version, the stepmother isn’t wicked at all — she’s just an Asian dressmaker who constantly moves her two daughters Lilith and Margot (Stephanie Tsu) wherever the work takes her. When her marriage takes them to the kingdom of Alouette, all three of them see it as a chance for some much-needed stability. More than anything, the girls are excited to hang out with their new stepsister, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried).

Yes, they started out as friends! (Where have you heard that one before?) The initial villain in “Steps” isn’t Cinderella, but the all-Caucasian kingdom where she lives. The newly blended family has fun sharing their cultural traditions, but Lilith and Margot quickly learn that everyone else sees them as outsiders. And when mean girls at school like Nikki Glazer’s Priscilla start freezing them out, Cinderella doesn’t do enough to stand up for them. Thus a sibling rivalry is born — turns out that Cinderella is also the mean stepsister that somebody else hates.

Lilith decides that if she’s not going to be accepted, she might as well rebel. Like a lot of pre-teens, she’s torn between an impulse to reject the social hierarchy around her and the unavoidable fact that she still defines herself by it. She’s more interested in destroying what she hates than figuring out what she likes, so she steals a magic wand from the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler) and sabotages the royal ball, significantly complicating things for the Prince (Daniel Radcliffe) and sending the kingdom into free-fall. It isn’t long before she and her loathed step-sister have to take a journey through the forest to set things right.

From its unpleasantly slick animation to its picture-perfect storytelling — Cinderella thinks Lilith is mean and Lilith thinks Cinderella is dumb and ditzy, but they both learn there’s more to the other than meets the eye — “Steps” is an example of how you can do everything “correctly” and be left with a film that’s too smooth around the edges to resonate. There’s enough for kids to enjoy, but this won’t be one that parents find themselves unexpectedly invested in.

For all its modern cliches, “Steps” still contains a few moments of genuine pathos that tug at the heartstrings. We can all relate to being bullied as kids and the cosmic importance that our young brains assign to being left out, and the film handles those early scenes admirably well. But nothing in the movie is strong enough to transcend the fact that it’s packaged in a tired formula that has lost any subversiveness it once had. These villain-led reimagnings were introduced as a way to counteract the two-dimensional nature of fairy tales, but it’s starting to feel like we replaced those Happily Ever After endings with something equally superficial.

“Steps” streams on Netflix beginning on Friday, November 20.

#3490. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.
