#3488. 'NCIS' Star Katrina Law Warns the Entire Team Will Break in Season 24

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers from NCIS Season 24, Episode 3. NCIS Season 24 has given longtime fans a reason to celebrate Michael Weatherly's return as Tony DiNozzo, but the team won't ride that nostalgia wave forever. According to Katrina Law, the job's emotional toll is about to catch up with Jessica Knight and her colleagues in ways viewers haven't seen before. The actress, who has played Knight since Season 18, tells Collider that the team will face a breaking point this season, with some particularly revealing episodes still ahead.

"I think this season you really get to see a lot of Knight's vulnerability in a way that you've never experienced before," Law says. "This season, you get to see her break in a way that you haven't seen before." And Knight won't be the only one struggling. Law adds that viewers will see "the entire team break" in a way the series hasn't explored before, making the aftermath as important as the moments that lead to it.

Before those emotional storylines unfold, however, the November 10 episode, "Speechless," gives Law a very different reason to remember Season 24. The installment marks the acting debut of her seven-year-old daughter, Kinley Andreen, who plays a young girl caught in the middle of a frightening investigation. It's a family milestone for the actress, but it also brings a personal connection to an episode built around the lengths a parent will go to protect their child.

Knight has spent much of her time on NCIS proving she can handle whatever comes through the doors at headquarters. A former member of the agency's REACT team, she joined the Major Case Response Team after the deaths of several colleagues and the arrest of her former team leader. She's since become an established part of the group, but Law's comments suggest Season 24 will ask something different of her: What happens when the agent who used to hold it together can no longer do so?

Knight has already experienced significant personal and professional upheaval throughout her time on the series. Law's tease, though, points to a more exposed side of the character, one that hasn't necessarily had the same space to emerge amid the team's investigations. The actress is particularly interested in seeing audiences connect with that vulnerability, especially as the other agents face their own emotional struggles.

Law says two upcoming episodes have already been filmed, and she credits writer Scott Williams with understanding how to bring out the characters' emotional depths. "I think Scott Williams does such justice to the characters when it comes to their emotional depths and bringing out the best and the worst in them," she tells Collider. For Law, what makes the story worth watching is how the team comes together and moves forward after reaching that breaking point.

Tonight's episode, "Speechless," gives Law a chance to share the screen with someone she knows better than anyone: her daughter, Kinley. The seven-year-old makes her acting debut as Chloe Sims, an eight-year-old girl the NCIS team discovers hiding alone in her apartment after her Marine mother disappears.

Chloe is frightened and initially reluctant to help, but she has a surprising skill that could give investigators the breakthrough they need. Her fluency in Mandarin becomes an important part of the case, creating an unexpected connection between the young witness and Knight. Law tells Collider that the character's appearance makes that ability all the more striking, describing Chloe as a blonde-haired, green-eyed girl whose talent will surprise viewers.

The casting also makes the episode's central themes hit a little closer to home. The investigation revolves around a missing mother and a child left to navigate a frightening situation, while Law is experiencing the unusual privilege of playing opposite her own daughter. She says watching Kinley move from being her little girl to a young actor stepping into character was unlike anything she'd experienced.

Law's behind-the-scenes experience was just as memorable as what audiences will see on screen. In her Collider interview, she recalls watching Kinley switch into character, suddenly becoming Chloe rather than the little girl she knows at home. "I would literally kind of see my daughter disappear and then this little actress pop up," Law tells Collider. "It was surreal, but then I would also kind of see my daughter peeking through, looking for the validation of like, 'Mommy, am I doing a good job?'"

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Kinley's Mandarin-speaking abilities also connect to Law's family. The actress, who is half Chinese and speaks fluent Mandarin, explains that her mother has been instrumental in passing the language down to the next generation. "Pretty much every day my mom will sit down with Kinley and go over her Mandarin skills and teach her," Law says. "So it's been passed down through generations to Kinley, and she's upholding her family traditions."

One challenge Law hadn't quite anticipated, though, was balancing all her responsibilities on set. She was Kinley's mother, acting coach, scene partner, and fellow performer at the same time. At one point, she tells Collider, she even had to remind her daughter to look at her rather than directly into the camera. Kinley eventually pointed out that she was looking at her mother, prompting a laugh from Law.

The actress also explained why allowing Kinley to act on NCIS doesn't mean she's changing her approach to protecting her daughter. Law has deliberately kept Kinley off social media, but the young girl wanted to take part in the show and was already familiar with its cast and crew after years of visiting the set. With her mother beside her throughout filming, surrounded by people she already knew and trusted, she says it was an especially comfortable introduction to acting.

Of course, Kinley's debut isn't the only major development adding extra excitement to Season 24. Weatherly is back as Tony DiNozzo, and Law is just as enthusiastic about his return as longtime viewers. An original NCIS fan herself, the actress describes the decision to bring Weatherly back as a brilliant move by the network.

She didn't expect Jessica to get involved in Tony's return. Law pitched several ideas for how Knight might interact with Weatherly's character, but never expected Ziva David (Cote de Pablo) to pull her into their history by asking her to keep tabs on him.

"I kind of love it," Law tells Collider, explaining that the unexpected setup creates a fun relationship between Knight and Weatherly. It's an interesting position for Jessica, who now finds herself caught up in a dynamic that predates her time on the team.

Law has a few ideas about where that connection could go. When asked what she'd like to see for Knight this season, she didn't hesitate: she wants Jessica and Ziva to finally share the screen, preferably in an action sequence or an interaction that leaves Tony thoroughly uncomfortable.

For a franchise that's been on television for more than two decades, it has found new ways to bring its characters together while making room for the next generation. Season 24 is doing both, giving viewers the nostalgia of Tony's return while promising a much more vulnerable side of the agents they've spent years following.

"Speechless" offers a particularly personal entry point into that larger story, but Law's comments suggest the emotional challenges ahead won't be limited to one case. With two more character-focused episodes already in the can, Knight and her teammates could be heading into some of their most difficult moments yet. And if Law gets her way, perhaps a certain former Mossad agent will be around to make things even more interesting.

The NCIS Season 24, Episode 5, "Speechless," airs Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at 8 p.m. ET / 7 p.m. CT on CBS.

#3487. ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 21, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

Winifred Notty is the sanest person she knows, or so the heroine (or anti-heroine, depending on how you might see it) of Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” is quick to tell anyone who will listen. Or not, as star Maika Monroe delivers that damning and darkly funny insight into Winifred’s soul via a prim voiceover that seems to exist for her own benefit as much as the audience she seems to imagine.

That’s tangled enough, but there’s also this: Winifred doesn’t really know that many people, mostly because just about everyone she’s come across in her life is dead. Still, sane! Ish. Well, it’s not called “Victorian Psycho” for nothing. Related Stories ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too ‘The Debut’ Trailer: Julianne Moore Goes Full Julianne Moore in Jesse Eisenberg’s Riotously Funny Musical Theater Comedy

Adapted for the screen by novelist Virginia Feito from her own work, the book comes recommended alongside its predecessor, “Mrs. March,” for anyone drawn to entertainment with “psycho” in the title.Beloved scream queen Maika Monroe (“It Follows,” “The Guest,” “Longlegs”) may be switching sides here, offering a twist on who horror fans root for once the blood starts flowing. (Hint: it’s the psycho.)

When we first meet Winifred, the Victorian-era governess is bound for her next assignment to teach the children of Mr. and Mrs. Pounds (Jason Isaacs and a sneaky-great Ruth Wilson, respectively) at their sprawling Yorkshire estate. “This won’t be like the other times,” she tells herself, winking mightily at how all those other times turned out. Our Winifred sports dead eyes and a rictus grin she works so very hard to fix in place. It’s even better when she attempts to imitate those around her, all the better to approximate “being human.”

No question, there’s something very wrong with Winifred. But what? You’ll find out soon enough. Possessed of “a darkness” she cannot shake, Monroe’s Winifred practically vibrates with the need to hold things together. It does not always work for her, but it is nearly always funny, deliciously and dementedly so.

Wigon and Freito don’t balk at the “psycho” promise of their story, as Winifred happily whacks away (often literally) at everyone icky, from gardeners to nurses (Thomasin McKenzie) and, yes, at least one baby. Killing scenes are elegantly, amusingly cut by editors Dustin Chow and Lance Edmands and designed for maximum gasps. Blood flows, then spurts, then pools. Sometimes it gets on Winifred’s face or her collar. She moves on, grimly and happily.

Cinematographer Nico Aguilar brings a similar energy to his work, shooting in and through keyholes, swinging his camera like a clock pendulum, even briefly adapting the perspective of a swallowed (redacted, for spoilers) as it travels into Winifred’s belly. It’s playful and gross, wholly fitting the material. Mostly, it’s so dark and fucked up you can’t help but laugh. OH! Did they do that? Yes, yes they did.

Possessed by the notion that she’s meant to be a part of the Pounds family (who would want to be? these aristocrats are monstrous), Winifred continues to fray. Bloodlusty audiences will be charmed by her go-for-broke attitude (more like go-for-the-throat), plus a steady stream of visual cues as to her current state. Dreams and nightmares merge, she’s haunted by the Pounds’ family mascot of a wild boar (particularly in an ever-morphing tapestry), and she simply can’t stop sneaking into places to stare at people while they sleep.

Clocking in at a tight 90 minutes, some changes to the also-slim book are smart, while others dilute its darkest impulses. Gone is the countdown to a Christmas massacre, which frames the novel; hell, gone is the whole Christmas massacre. Freito’s script leads up to a different sort of celebration, doing away with many of the most colorful supporting characters in the process (Mrs. Fancey, we hardly knew ye!).

That choice isn’t disastrous, although the execution of the big! final! event! is oddly watered down. Here it’s imagined as a battle of Winifred’s wills… but, erm, what wills? The book and the film each offer enough reasons for why our heroine is the way she is, Wigon’s film oddly bisects her spirit by implying she’s not fully on board with all the evil she commits.

For fans of the novel and its wonderfully unrepentant star, this choice might rankle; it’s also odd that Freito would go this route with her own adaptation. “Well, that’s not my ‘Victorian Psycho’ — and she’s not. That’s such a shame because for much of the film, she’s even better. By tempering her impulses and inner monologue, the film ends with less of the giddy gore that makes the rest of it such a dark treat. Dare we say it? We would have loved for this one to go full, ahem, boar.

“Victorian Psycho” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release it in theaters on Friday, September 25.

#3486. The Newest 4K Amazon Fire TV Stick Is Nearly 60% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3484. Ruaridh Mollica Breaks Down What VisionQuest Finale's Epic Reunion Means For His MCU Future

VisionQuest's Ruaridh Mollica discusses the major finale moments of the WandaVision spinoff, the massive MCU reunion, and Tommy Maximoff's MCU future.

WARNING: This interview contains MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8, "Forever."

Since Phase 4, one of the big successes to come out of the Marvel Cinematic Universe was the WandaVision series, bringing Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch and Paul Bettany's Vision together for their own solo adventure. As the MCU timeline was beginning its era of original TV shows on Disney+, the nine-episode project emerged with tremendous success, while also kicking off the beginning of a new trilogy.

After Agatha Harkness' breakout debut in the Phase 4 series, it led to Kathryn Hahn headlining her own spinoff, with Agatha All Along. However, despite Wanda freeing Westview, which seemingly meant the end for her kids that she had created through magic, that was far from the case, as the Phase 5 offshoot revealed that Wiccan had survived.

In true comic book fashion, his soul managed to inhabit Billy Kaplan's body, with Joe Locke playing the teenage version. After managing to save Tommy, it was time for the speedy hero to get his time to shine by becoming one of the central figures in VisionQuest, which serves as the finale to the trilogy, with Ruaridh Mollica being cast as the other Maximoff twin.

With the end of VisionQuest season 1, viewers have been able to follow Tommy's complex journey as both Thomas Shepherd and the son of Vision and Scarlet Witch. A few weeks ago, I was honored to speak with the Scottish actor for ScreenRant about not only giving the MCU audience a lot of payoffs for the WandaVision trilogy, but also bringing a new era to Speed, including some of the pivotal moments in episode 8, "Forever."

Over the last couple of years, the MCU has begun to introduce more LGBTQ+ characters across the big and small screens, with Tommy being canonically bisexual, which made this role a personal one for the star, who is also openly bi. Throughout VisionQuest, it doesn't get explored or established, but as I asked Mollica if there were discussions about whether the Phase 6 drama would address it, he assured comic readers who are seeing him adapted in the franchise that this incarnation of Speed is bisexual.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think Tommy knows he's bi. I think that a specific queer relationship isn't explored in this particular section of his life in the show. I really hope that will be explored in the future. I think as a bisexual actor playing a bisexual role, I do feel there's moments where I'm watching me do something in a scene, and I'm like, 'Oh yeah, that was very queer!' [laughs] I hope that it exists in who he is and in elements of his personality rather than in his specific relationship during the show. But yeah, I do think Tommy's probably been with guys before the show happened, or in other timelines."

The tragic backstory for Thomas, before Tommy's soul got transferred, was a driving factor in how it influenced the dynamic between the orphan and Vision, with Mollica elaborating why it stands out as much as it did.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think it's one of the biggest parts of his backstory. Like, other than the complexities of the Tommy Maximoff side, ultimately, the Thomas Shepherd side of everything is heartbreaking. Thomas has been alone for so much of his life. Life has not been easy for him. He is a hustler and a grifter for a reason. He is out on the streets and stealing things, and he doesn't trust probably anyone other than Lisa that, at this time, he's had a string of foster families that have never understood him. I think, to have the potential promise of finally having a father like that, is all he really wants. [All] Thomas Shepherd wants is to be loved by a parent, and suddenly that is shown to him, and it might be possible. And obviously, then there's all the complexities of the Tommy Maximoff side and the impossibility of that interaction as a whole. But I think his backstory of being an orphan is so important for the yearning and the desire of that father-son relationship, and the desire to have a mother as well."

Similar to how Agatha All Along followed Billy and allowed him to express his perspective on Wanda, that also became the case for Tommy on VisionQuest, but very differently. While Locke's hero shared his conflicted feelings for his mother, Mollica's character is someone who looks at the Scarlet Witch in a very different regard, with past episodes revealing that he can relate a lot to their mom, which became one of the most emotional components throughout these eight episodes. Obviously, everyone is now waiting for the full Maximoff reunion, as Mollica reflected on how he envisions the perfect reunion between Speed and Wanda.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I would obviously love that reunion to happen. I don't know how I would envision it. I think, based on how we've seen the reuniting of Tommy, Billy, and Vision, I would assume that the same feeling [from] that moment would translate into the feeling of reuniting with Wanda."

It was only a matter of time before the twins finally found each other, as Locke reprised his role as Wiccan in VisionQuest episode 8, bringing him and Mollica's Speed together in a heartfelt reunion that viewers have waited to see since 2024. However, little did these actors know that they would work together outside the MCU, as the two of them got cast in West End's Clarkston.

As rewarding as it becomes for viewers, it means just as much for Mollica himself. During our interview, he shared with me how it was a gift to get to bond with his on-screen brother through VisionQuest, while also building a dynamic that would help them on stage in Clarkston.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Filming that moment was amazing. I love the finale of the show, [episode 8] is my favorite episode because it feels like this big moment of everything coming together in this really f-----g epic way. It is a story all about family. And so when we're there trying to save Vision, and I can't do it alone anymore, and my brother finds me again and comes out of his portal, and we do it together - that broke my heart. It was powerful, even when we were shooting it, and then I love that we have this beautiful hug with our father that resembles the comics, when it's Billy and Tommy hugging Wanda.

It really paralleled that for me, and yeah, I just thought it was such a beautiful moment to shoot, but like you said, watching that moment, I teared up, and I, I was there. And in terms of our relationship going forward onto the play, we met for the first time doing this, so we got to spend a lot of time together on set, and I guess, playing brothers, there's a closeness there, and we get along really well anyway. So it definitely helped us bond a lot more before the audition process, and then we spent a lot of time together anyway, leading up to the play, and then got pretty close in rehearsals and everything like that."

There may not have been an official "like uncle, like nephew" mantra, but the VisionQuest finale gave Speed not only his own iconic superhero moment, but also a clever way to nod towards his uncle from another universe. As Tommy is mastering his speed more, the final episode sees him getting to have a very X-Men: Apocalypse-esque scene a la Sweet Dreams. When asked if this was a clever way to pay homage to Evan Peters' Quicksilver, but with their own spin, Mollica shared the following:

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think with that moment, we needed to have Tommy's superhero moment, his moment of, 'I am Tommy Maximoff,' - and that line gave me chills whenever I was reading it before we shot it. I was like, 'That is the epic superhero moment,' and he gets to zoom-zoom off and have his hero moment, and then Terry, what he loves to do as a writer, a creator, filmmaker, is then flip the moment on its head and be able to kind of laugh at it. And I think by slowing it down, it allowed for the family dynamic to exist in the epic moment, and I thought that was just perfectly [descriptive] of the show. It is superhero, and it is epic, but it's a father and son who are still trying to figure out their relationship. So even in the most epic moments, they are bickering, and that moment definitely allowed that to happen, and also just poke fun at the superhero moments that exist."

As Billy got his Wiccan suit in Agatha All Along, I asked Mollica if Tommy was meant to officially get his Speed costume in VisionQuest. It turns out, the MCU spinoff was very close to making it happen, as he had even been measured for a superhero uniform. However, he elaborated on how they decided to hold off on that for a very good reason.

Ruaridh Mollica: "It's so interesting you say that, and actually, I've not told anyone this yet, so this is exciting. Yes, I got completely measured for a full superhero suit. We were gonna make it. It was gonna happen in the finale at some point. But then Terry, exactly like you said, couldn't find a way for [Tommy] to just appear in a suit. He wants the show to be as grounded in reality as possible, especially my character, who really, I feel like grounds everything back to London and the real world and everything like that. There was never a moment where he could just find a superhero suit, or turn up in it, and it breaks that connection [to] reality. We were able to get the superhero goggles because they came from Paladin, and that was a way that could be worked in. And then we changed the costume to be a bit more green and tracksuit-like to reflect the superhero suit, and I think that was a really good choice. I think I like that, and also it leaves us wanting more. "

ScreenRant: "I also took the jacket as a nod to what we saw little Tommy wear in WandaVision as a nice little homage in that way."

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, totally. Sarah Young, our costume designer, she was so on top of making sure there were so many homages to the original characters."

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

By the end of the VisionQuest finale, Tommy has become more comfortable with his powers, as he is learning to discover just how powerful he is. But how powerful would Mollica say Speed is at this point?

Ruaridh Mollica: "I think he's pretty comfortable. I think that was the first time he'd used his speed to that level, and he obviously realized that he needs to eat more before he does that. I think now that he knows that if he carbs up, he could sustain himself for a lot longer. And I think he's probably experimenting with that after that moment. And I think he's still got a lot to figure out, especially about how far does his phasing go? His ability to affect the atomic structure of atoms using his speed. How far does that go? I think his power could be pretty massive, so I think he still [has] a lot to learn."

While VisionQuest completes this trilogy, many have expressed wanting to see the MCU finally adapt Avengers: Children's Crusade. When I asked if a potential spinoff like that is something he, Locke, and the Marvel Studios folks have discussed, while also addressing whether he knows where Tommy is going next, he is just as curious.

Ruaridh Mollica: "I honestly don't know. I don't know. We'll have to wait and find out. I hope to know as well."

Nevertheless, Avengers: The Children's Crusade or maybe even a Young Avengers spinoff is something he would be more than down for.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Totally. I mean, I loved reading it, and it would be a privilege. But I cannot say anything, I don't have that information [laughs]"

At the time of this interview being conducted, Mollica was in London, which is where Avengers: Secret Wars will film in the near future. With the world speculating who is in the Phase 6 finale, when I asked him if Tommy might be popping up in the 2027 ensemble, as it would make sense for Speed to be part of the cast after VisionQuest, the star laughed with a "No comment!" response.

Another crucial figure in Thomas' life is Lisa Molinari, played by Lauren Morais, with the WandaVision spinoff showcasing how important she has been to him. In a lot of storytelling, there is sometimes the scenario where a man becomes a female character's entire world or arc, but VisionQuest instead flips it on its head, where it's almost reversed.

Throughout the season, viewers have been able to see that, prior to reuniting with Vision, Lisa is very much what Tommy's world is heavily dependent on. When asked if that was something that he and Morais consciously worked into that dynamic, or if it was something that they both felt, 'We're gonna flip the script a little bit from what we usually see in these kinds of relationships', he shared the following:

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, I think that was something Terry did really well, just with the writing and the characters. And I think me and Lauren naturally had just a fun rapport, and yeah, I think that was mainly down to the writing, but also kind of where Tommy comes from. Lisa means so much to Tommy in that sense because she is powerful. She is cool, I think she's probably taught him a lot over the years."

ScreenRant: I'm glad she survived, and you guys are both together by the end, and you're with Paladin now. That was a dynamic I was not expecting to see be so much fun. Todd is, obviously, awesome, as you know, so I'm glad that you all made it out alive. I'm hoping that is something that we see more of in the future.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Yeah, that was so cool leaving that dynamic with Paladin and having them together at the end. I thought that was such a beautiful way to tie that section off, as well as our section, and leave things open."

Credit: Anna Maria Tinghino/Future Image/Cover Images

After his big MCU debut, what is next for Mollica beyond the Marvel brand? The Franchise alum is busy with several projects, which happen to involve a few names that are no strangers to the superhero genre.

Ruaridh Mollica: "Right now, I'm filming a Paramount show called Laird, which will be super cool. #3480. 8 Movies To Watch if You Love Ken Russell's 'The Devils'

In 17th-century France, Loudun became the site of the Loudun possessions, a gruesome case of alleged mass demonic possession that is now understood as a landmark study in mass hysteria. The "possessions" were blamed on Urbain Grandier, a charismatic but womanizing local priest who was then executed for political purposes. This event became the inspiration for Aldous Huxley's 1952 non-fiction book The Devils of Loudun, and then John Whiting's 1960 stage play The Devils. In 1971, Ken Russell took both of these works as inspiration and made The Devils.

One of the most notoriously heavily-censored horror movies in film history, The Devils was massively controversial upon release for its graphic sexual imagery and blasphemous content, but has since come to be recognized as one of the greatest films of its time. With the recent release of the 4K restoration of the film's 114-minute director's cut, now's about as perfect a time as any to watch the eight most noteworthy films that feel remarkably similar to The Devils for one reason or another.

As far as deliberately and calculatedly blasphemous films go, it doesn't get much more iconic than Viridiana, made by one of the most notoriously anti-clerical auteurs in film history, Luis Buñuel. Arguably the greatest of Buñuel's Mexican movies, Viridiana is one of the greatest movie classics of 1961, following a devout novice nun who abandons her vows to shelter local vagrants after the suicide of her fetishistic uncle.

Its surrealistic imagery is about as brilliant as you'd expect from any Buñuel film.

A must-see for all those whose favorite part of The Devils is the scathing study of The Profane as a philosophical concept, Viridiana is an unforgiving critique of religious dogma and naive idealism. Its surrealistic imagery is about as brilliant as you'd expect from any Buñuel film, and Silvia Pinal's lead performance is a tour de force. It's definitely more overtly sacrilegious than The Devils, but it's every bit as much of a hyper-influential must-see.

Before The Wizard of Oz came around to revolutionize fantasy cinema forever, there were many fantasy films that are also still remembered among the greatest of all time, including the horror essay film Häxan. This silent Swedish masterpiece is a semi-documentary blends scholarly literature and phantasmagoric horror, charting the history of witchcraft and Satanism from the Middle Ages to the 20th century.

It's one of the clearest and strongest cinematic ancestors to Ken Russell's magnum opus, and one of the most important documentaries in the history of cinema. Insightful without ever feeling didactic and atmospheric without ever sacrificing its scholarly dimensions, Häxan laid the foundations for horror cinema to explore themes of religious hysteria, state control through religion, and institutional persecution. Both through its visuals and its mere premise, it was far ahead of its time.

Robin Hardy's The Wicker Man is one of the greatest and most influential British horror movies of the 20th century, as well as one of the most important folk horror films of all time. It's based on David Pinner's horror novel Ritual, and it follows a devout Christian cop who travels to a remote Scottish island to investigate a young girl's disappearance, only to discover that the local pagan community has lured him there as a human sacrifice for a failing harvest.

Much like The Devils, The Wicker Man explores how sexual repression can be weaponized and exploited by oppressive forces; and much like The Devils, it forces the sacred and the profane to clash visually, narratively, and thematically throughout. It's one of those movies unlike anything you've ever seen before, a genre-defining masterpiece that shows how dogmatic self-righteousness can be little more than a self-destructive trap.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

What better recommendation for people who loved Ken Russell's The Devils than the rest of Russell's impeccable filmography? As it happens, after making one of the best horror movies of the 1970s, he made one of the best hard sci-fi movies of the 1980s: Altered States, based on Paddy Chayefsky's 1978 novel. In it, a Harvard psychophysiologist uses sensory deprivation tanks and powerful tribal hallucinogens to explore alternate states of consciousness, unwittingly triggering a dangerous devolution into a primitive ape-man.

Brilliantly experimental and surrealistic from beginning to end, Altered States is anchored by unparalleled visuals and sound design, creating a true aesthetic supernova further bolstered by John Corigliano's avant-garde score. Like all auteurs worth their salt, Russell had a collection of themes that were most interesting to him over the course of his career, and Altered States thus explores many ideas similar to those found in The Devils. Instead of 17th-century religion and politics, this film explores 20th-century scientific hubris, exploring ideas of repressed biological impulses through intentionally grotesque images.

Chilean-French avant-garde auteur Alejandro Jodorowsky is one of the biggest and most influential names in the history of surrealist cinema, and there are many who would point to The Holy Mountain as his magnum opus. After the underground success of the acid Western El Topo, Beatles manager Allen Klein agreed to produce Holy Mountain, and John Lennon and Yoko Ono also contributed financially. The result is one of the most delectably strange and fascinatingly impenetrable Mexican movies of all time, about seven people led up a sacred mountain by a powerful alchemist so they can steal the secret of immortality.

The Holy Mountain is certainly not for those who prefer their fantasy movies straightforward, and it's probably not the most accessible introduction to cinematic surrealism for those unfamiliar; but it's a must-see masterpiece nonetheless, especially for those who love the provocative blasphemy and hyper-stylized colors of The Devils. One of the best international masterpieces of all time, The Holy Mountain is just as fiercely anti-authoritarian as Russell's masterpiece, rejecting institutional corruption and repressive state control through a bunch of deliberately shocking moments.

There is perhaps no better Ken Russell film for people to watch after seeing (and loving) The Devils than Women in Love, which is also anchored by a powerhouse performance by Oliver Reed. This is not a horror movie, though it is a period piece, this one a romantic drama following the relationships between two sisters and two men in a mining town in post-World War I England. Based on the 1920 novel of the same title by D. H. Lawrence, the film obtained an impressive four Academy Award nominations, including Glenda Jackson's victory in the Best Actress category.

This was the movie that established Russell as a major force in world cinema, and it was its huge commercial and critical success that gave Warner the confidence to give Russell a blank check to make The Devils. These two films couldn't possibly be more different in terms of tone, with Women in Love being an uncompromisingly dense and philosophically profound adaptation of the source material. However, since Women in Love directly preceded The Devils, you can see many of the blueprints for Russell's next film there: eroticism, theatricality, and characters trapped between society's expectations and their own physical and psychological impulses.

Directed by Pier Paolo Pasolini and loosely adapted from the 1785 novel The 120 Days of Sodom by the Marquis de Sade, Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is perhaps one of the most controversial major films in the history of cinema. Taking the basis of the Marquis de Sade's story from 18th-century France to World War II Italy, it's about four wealthy fascists who kidnap a group of teenagers and subject them to 120 days of systemic mental, physical, and sexual torture inside a secluded villa. For its unapologetic approach to topics that continue to be taboo today, the film has been widely banned and censored across the world throughout history.

It isn't the least bit hard to see why. Much like The Devils, this is one of the heaviest movies of the 20th century, an absolutely unrelenting political allegory of fascism's cold cruelty shot with high-art anti-sensationalism that nonetheless doesn't make the film any easier to stomach. It's a remarkable feat that Pasolini was able to take such an inflammatory premise and manage to treat it with such care that it doesn't feel exploitative at all, a compliment that can also be directed at The Devils.

There are only two major feature films directly depicting the Loudun possessions, and the first one came out a decade before The Devils. It is, of course, the Polish horror art film Mother Joan of the Angels, directed by Jerzy Kawalerowicz and based on a novella of the same title by Jarosław Iwaszkiewicz. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 1961 Cannes Film Festival, Mother Joan of the Angels is one of those near-perfect horror movies that nobody remembers anymore, but which should be essential viewing for anyone even slightly interested in the story and context of the Loudun possessions.

Most would agree that the film isn't quite as masterful, timeless, or hard-hitting as The Devils, but it's still very much worthy of praise. With some incredibly striking black-and-white cinematography that stands in stark contrast to the vibrancy of Russell's masterpiece, Lucyna Winnicka's transcendental performance as Mother Joan, and a tremendous level of intellectual and existential depth, Mother Joan of the Angels is to the '60s what The Devils is to the '70s. Both are among the greatest "demonic possession" movies in the history of horror cinema.

#3479. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3477. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3476. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

#3475. ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Review: Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ Series Is Just Going Through the Motions

The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth. Related Stories Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not.) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir (for now, at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door. Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god, these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.

Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang said they continue to think about what new innovation they can bring to the product side, and noted that “Apple as a potential bidder in other markets is helpful” for their business.

#3472. Forget 'Tracker,' Disney+'s Forgotten 13-Episode Crime Series Is a Perfect Weekend Binge

Giovana Gelhoren is a High-Trending Topics Writer at Collider, covering the most-talked-about stars, movies, and TV shows. Before joining Collider, she was a Digital News Writer at People Magazine and served as Associate Editor at SheKnows, where she honed her expertise in celebrity coverage and entertainment journalism.

A proud Latina from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Giovana graduated from Northwestern University with a degree in Journalism and International Studies. She has interviewed countless celebrities, including Anne Hathaway, Halle Berry, Pamela Anderson, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Brenda Song, and is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of film, TV, and pop culture.

For 12 seasons, the Fox series Bones proved to have an unbeatable formula. With the will-they-won't-they main characters played by Emily Deschanel and David Boreanaz, the series delivered years of classic procedural drama with a twist as they look into a corpse's body (and bones) to get to what really happened. But while the series was certainly a hit, Bones' spin-off series never reached the same fate.

In the sixth season of Bones, audiences tuned to an odd backdoor pilot episode titled “The Finder.” In the episode, they were introduced to Geoff Stults's Walter Sherman, a character who inspired his very own spin-off, also titled The Finder. The series premiered on January 12, 2012, but, like many TV shows over the years, was canceled after one season and never had enough time to find its groove.

The Finder is a crime procedural that follows Walter Sherman (Geoff Stults), a character from Bones who's sought for his ability to find anything, from the incredibly important to the mundane, like a pair of socks. Walter's talent was refined after he suffered brain damage from his time serving in the Army in Iraq, which caused him to be incredibly paranoid about the people and the world around him. This brain damage also created an inherent impulse to find missing things, hence Walter's nickname as "The Finder."

Along the way, Walter has the friendship of Leo Knox (Michael Clarke Duncan), a former lawyer who acts not only as a local bar owner, but as Walter's manager, and sometimes, his bodyguard. Walter, who lives out in the Florida Keys, also relies on Willa Monday (Maddie Hasson), a rebellious teenager who becomes his assistant. Together, the unlikely team takes on cases involving missing people, stolen valuables and unexplained disappearances.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

You know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

While fans of Bones might've rejoiced when they heard about a series spin-off, The Finder was never able to achieve the same success. The show was met with significant barriers from its inception; after originally being slated for Thursday night airings, the series was moved to Friday nights and aired out of order. Also important to its lackluster success was The Finder's mid-season premiere. The odd-timed premiere meant that already established and returning shows are midway through their seasons, meaning The Finder's pilot slot had a bigger risk of not gaining the same viewing audience as something premiering in the fall.

The CBS series doesn't let itself become bogged down in too much history.

Overall, while critics were not overly supportive of the series, The Finder did receive a warm reception from audiences, even if not enough to warrant a renewal. On Rotten Tomatoes, the series holds 82% on the Popcornmeter, with reviews calling the series "entertaining and fun." "Good, lighthearted, fun show. Talented and engaging cast," wrote one review. "At every episode I wanted to watch another. Never knowing what unexpected thing Walter was going to be asked to find next." The Finder also marked one of Duncan's last credits before his death on September 3, 2012. He passed just four months after The Finder came to an end.

With all that said, while The Finder never achieved the same success and numbers as Bones, let alone another comparable show, The Tracker, The Finder still makes for an entertaining, light watch. With a fascinating protagonist, an excellent cast of supporting characters, and mind-bending cases, it delivers another well-done procedural, and the perfect weekend binge.

An Iraq war vet suffers a brain injury that triggers the ability to see connections between seemingly unrelated events, objects or people.

#3470. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

#3467. WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

Select WhatsApp users on TestFlight and in the main app are now seeing the option to expand an image in the app’s photo editor. Here are the details.

iPhone users with access to Apple Intelligence have a native AI-powered photo expansion tool called Extend, which lets users pinch or drag to expand an image beyond its original borders.

This feature, which is also present on AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and image-editing platforms like Photoshop, is now also making its way into WhatsApp.

According to WABetaInfo, the platform is rolling out a Meta AI-powered image expansion tool, though it is currently limited to select users, primarily those in WhatsApp’s beta program via TestFlight.

When users select a photo in their chats, WhatsApp opens the drawing editor. Here, they can choose to apply some AI effect to improve it. Among these, users can find a new option to expand their photos. Once users select this option, Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the expanded version. Once the process is complete, WhatsApp shows the expanded photo in the drawing editor, and users can choose to send it. Note that this feature is also compatible with status updates.

The site notes that if the user isn’t happy with the result, they can tap an undo button to revert to the original and then try using the tool again to generate a different result.

As is usually the case with beta features on WhatsApp, there is no telling when it might become widely available.

#3466. How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

Jordan Firstman knew that the success of “Club Kid” hinged on finding the perfect preteen actor to play his character’s long-lost son, Arlo.

It was a demanding role that had a lot of boxes to check off: A British kid, whose hard-partying mother had just committed suicide, finds himself dumped in New York City, where he struggles to break out of his protective shell to bond with his party promoter dad, Peter (Firstman, who wrote and directed the film, in addition to starring in it ). But the perfect candidate had to project an effortless coolness that allows him to organically blend in with his newfound father’s social circle of hard-living, LGBTQ+ clubgoers, whose lives revolve around their love of music, dance, and drugs. Related Stories ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

“[Arlo’s] not just cool, he’s empathetic and wise; there’s a lot of stuff about that kid that was on the page that needed to be there,” said Firstman, who on this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, called the casting search the most “nerve-wracking” part of making “Club Kid.”

“Club Kid” had the right casting director for the job. Carmen Cuba has a legendary track record of finding child stars, including the original “Stranger Things” ensemble. But as Cuba pointed out while participating in IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable of Casting Directors, “Club Kid” was different from those previous assignments.

“I do six-month searches for kids,” said Cuba. “On ’Stranger Things,’ ‘Starfighter,’ you have time and money, and this was a small film.”

The $6 million production could not afford a lengthy search. It didn’t even have the money for Cuba to fly to London with Firstman for auditions. She would be reliant on a UK casting team, working within a limited budget, to help her find a needle in a haystack.

“I was very nervous about just sort of the plan of attack, because I was going to have a UK team, and you need a British kid who looks like he’s half-Jordan,” said Cuba.

Right before jumping into “Club Kid,” Cuba went on her yearly vacation with a group of close casting director friends. As the holiday wound down, Cuba tried to work through her upcoming casting dilemma with some of her closest colleagues.

“I [said], ‘How am I going do this?’ just trying to map it out for myself before I left to go start it,” recalled Cuba of the conversation. “And one of those friends is Lucy Bevan, who had just finished her ‘Harry Potter’ search, so she so generously said, ‘Why don’t I share some of the names.’”

To cast the first season of the $200 million-plus upcoming HBO series — based on the first Harry Potter book, “The Philosopher’s Stone,” in which Harry turns 11 — Bevans had just finished her own six-month search. She had auditioned thousands of young British actors to play the next generation of Harry, Hermione, Ron, and their Hogwarts classmates.

“This is just a testament to our relationship because Lucy would not normally do UK casting on a tiny movie,” said Cuba of the prominent British casting director, whose credits include “Barbie,” “F1,” and “The Batman.”

“She had just seen 40,000 kids,” said Firstman of Beaven, who early on showed him a photo of Reggie Absolom. “I saw his face and I was like, ‘that is the face that I’ve seen in my head.’ Even in the script, he’s supposed to be a quarter Indian – “Innit Babes” [Peter and his friends’ nickname for Reggie’s mom based on her favorite expression] is supposed to be like half Indian — and Lucy [said], ‘Let’s not focus on that. That’s not going happen.’ And Reggie’s a quarter Indian. Every single thing that I had asked God for, this kid came to me in Reggie.”

In total, according to Cuba, Bevan showed Firstman 90 kids, with a wider range of ages — Cuba and Firstman went back and forth about how old Reggie should be, with the character originally skewing younger than 10 — but Firstman never wavered from Absalom, whose résumé included roles in “Silo” and “The Other Bennet Sister.”

“Lucy was so generous. They had no money to fly me to London to do the session in person, so she hosted the callback session there,” said Cuba. “Jordan is incredible with kids, he was like, ‘Let’s not do it in this casting office, let’s take it outside.’ So suddenly Lucy’s assistant is outside with the camera, and they’re walking and talking. I rewatched that audition recently, and it’s just amazing. Jordan’s brain, and how he connects to everyone that he casts. I think that’s what you feel in the movie; it’s so familial.”

On the podcast, Firstman talked about how beyond his decade of drug-fueled clubbing in Europe and New York City, one of the inspirations for “Club Kid” was the bond he formed with one of his close friend’s child, something he felt would be essential to replicate with Absolom.

“The reason kids like me is I don’t treat them as kids,” said Firstman. “They’re surprised at my candor, or the inappropriate things that most adults wouldn’t be willing to say in front of a kid. I know what Reggie sees on the internet. I’m not going to say something too much, but I can push it a little bit.  I think he always appreciated that in me, and once he understood that I liked to be made fun of too, everything shifted. Once he got permission to make fun of me, the whole dynamic shifted, and we just got so much more comfortable around each other.”

Much like his unorthodox, take-it-outside, walk-and-talk callback audition with Absolom, Firstman quickly realized, after casting the young actor, traditional preparation wouldn’t work.

“We tried doing traditional rehearsals, and it was awkward,” said Firstman. “I [said], ‘Let’s just keep hanging out, and keep having pizza together, and keep talking about music, and keep talking about TikTok clips we’ve seen, and send each other TikToks,’ and that’s how we bonded.”

An A24 release, “Club Kid” is now in New York City and Los Angeles theaters, and will expand on Friday, November 13.

#3465. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link. And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro.
