#3464. Geralt of Rivia Officially Returns in New Witcher Expansion

Although there won’t be another season of The Witcher on Netflix this year, fans of the hit fantasy franchise still have a lot to be excited about in the next few years. Many gamers are still working their way through The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt after CD Projekt Red released a new next-generation remaster of the game back at the end of September. It features a slew of added accessibility options, as well as enhancements to make the game feel more like a game that was released in the last few years and not over 10 years ago. CD Projekt Red also has one final expansion for The Witcher 3, Songs of the Past, set to be released sometime next year. It will be The Witcher 3’s final expansion centered around Geralt of Rivia before Ciri takes center stage in The Witcher 4 in 2028.

It’s safe to say The Witcher 4 is one of the most anticipated games currently in development, but there is still plenty of Geralt’s story left to tell before Ciri takes over in a few years. In fact, The Witcher 3 players on PC were treated to a new expansion mod featuring more story for Geralt of Rivia via the new mod, Annals of Duchy, which is described as a “lore-friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt’s life in Toussaint.” Those who have played The Witcher 3 know well that Toussaint is the area in which the beloved DLC, Blood and Wine, takes place. The area is vastly different from other famous Witcher 3 areas such as Skellige or Novigrad. It offers big cities and more rural areas, both flush with color and danger.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

CD Projekt Red has already confirmed that Geralt of Rivia will be in The Witcher 4, but the nature of his role is unclear at this time. Most fans are expecting Geralt to act as more of a mentor to Ciri in The Witcher 4, but a playable section as Geralt also can’t be ruled out, especially considering how many sections of The Witcher 3 required fans to play as Ciri. It would be undeniably cool if CD Projekt Red gave Geralt a big moment as a sort of send-off after playing as him for so many years.

Check out the new Annals of Duchy expansion for The Witcher 3 on PC and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of The Witcher franchise.

#3463. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3462. ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’

Jack O’Connell was feeling a little bashful. Seated outside for coffee, taking in the fresh fall air at the remote Salamander Resort in Middleburg, Virginia, the actor revealed that communication between him and Oscar-winning filmmaker Danny Boyle began long before he was cast as the lead in the director’s latest film, “Ink.”

“I used to write to Danny a lot. I wrote all the directors that I admire,” said the 36-year-old star from Derbyshire, England. “Not cap in hand, trying to get anything out of them, just letters of appreciation, lovely stuff that’s affected me and inspired me. ‘I hope we get to do it someday.’ And, in Danny’s case, we did.” Related Stories How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

Technically “Ink,” in which O’Connell plays influential newspaper editor Larry Lamb after he’s recruited by outcast media magnate Rupert Murdoch to take over The Sun tabloid in 1969, is the second time the actor has worked with Boyle. The pair first officially met when he was brought in to play antagonist Jimmy Crystal in last year’s “28 Years Later,” directed by Boyle, and more prominently in January’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” directed by Nia DaCosta.

“It was right before I went and shot ‘Sinners,’” he said, referencing another major turn as a villain that loomed prominently over cinema this year. “The initial meeting wasn’t an audition. I just didn’t have the role. It was a meeting discussing the role with Danny and Nia.” It was the first time Boyle had acknowledged O’Connell, though he had a sneaking suspicion that he had been on the director’s radar for a while, having starred on the same iconic British teen drama “Skins” from which Boyle had found the star of his Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire.”

“Listen, he cast Dev [Patel]. He knew about ‘Skins.’ I think his daughter put him onto ‘Skins’ in the first place. So whether or not he stuck it out for our generation, I don’t know,” said O’Connell.

It’s been almost two decades since he first played fan favorite Cook as part of the second generation of the trailblazing E4 series, which ran from 2007 to 2013. “Skins” still stands out as an experience that helped shape his ethos as an actor. “I certainly felt like we were on the coolest show around. It was so amazingly written. The directors we had were brilliant. The whole model of the way that you audition en masse and then they find their characters. I love that,” said O’Connell. “It’s really quite pure, isn’t it? People are just getting the roles because of ability.”

The “Ink” star first trained as an actor at a free program in Nottingham called the Television Workshop, which eventually helped lead to his first breakout film role in the coming-of-age drama “This Is England.” However, it was “Skins” that felt like a “crash course” continuing education. “You’re doing all the heavy stuff, the tough stuff, the really laborious side of doing a TV show like that. But also the fun and the joy that gets provoked by all the art, the amazing writing and everything else,” said O’Connell. He’s quick to remind that notable “Skins” alumni include not just Patel, but also writers like Emmy winner Jack Thorne and Tony-nominated playwright Lucy Kirkwood.

But free programs like the Television Workshop are increasingly hard to come by, meaning there are less and less egalitarian-type opportunities in the United Kingdom for an actor from a working-class background like O’Connell’s to find their own “Skins.” Asked what he would tell the next generation of artists, the “Ink” star said, “I wouldn’t know what advice I would give nowadays, which is a shocking indictment.”

What attracted O’Connell to playing Lamb in “Ink,” a role that has brought him to the Middleburg Film Festival to receive the Spotlight Actor Award, was the opportunity to address how the UK, and the world in general, reached this place of inequality. “We see this man just excavate his morals, and his soul, and his decisions, and this newspaper. Being the best-selling newspaper, he’s had to part with what makes people more human. To me, it’s a comment on capitalism,” said the star. “The beginning of hyper capitalism, post-war England, and individual opportunity versus looking after everyone else and your responsibility within society. That was all just getting ripped up.”

“Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s 2017 play of the same name, with Graham also serving as the screenwriter of Boyle’s film. Another major factor in O’Connell’s decision to play Larry Lamb was working with the playwright and the director, who had come from a similar background. With Boyle, “I came to his work as a fan first, before I knew I was going to try and be an actor,” he said. “I remember watching ‘The Beach,’ and that made me want to go and see the world. And watching ‘Trainspotting’ and that made me want to never take heroin. But also the amazing soundtrack that’s in there and the fucking unforgettable performances.”

With “Ink” they were preparing to tell what O’Connell sees as a quintessentially British story, and “what [Danny’s] films have meant for British cinema and British culture as a result is undeniable. Thank fuck for Danny Boyle. He is an artist by every stretch of the word. I would argue that his films have perhaps meant the most to us as a collective growing up. His work at the Olympics opening ceremony makes you tingle to watch it. It is fucking monumental.”

Boyle is why O’Connell, an outsider to the film and TV industry in the same way Lamb was to the publishing industry, could still envision himself becoming an actor one day. “His style has been able to make you feel part of the film. It takes you along. You feel like you’re in the movie somehow. You don’t feel like an observer, like a spectator. They give you a feeling and mood as well,” he said.

As for Graham, “We’re not too far from each other in a particular pocket of the UK. And although my town and his town famously don’t get on — that’s all to do with football and Brian Clough and whatever else — but he is a dramatist. He’s also interested in analyzing culture and the culture around him and examining it,” said O’Connell. “He’s a great spokesman for under-representation in the industry at home because eight percent of the entire industry are from our background.”

The actor added, “Once he knew that I was somebody that could be trusted with his words, not someone who was going to try and fucking destroy them, we really hit it off.”

Here the three were, as what some would call a band of outsiders, telling a story about these insurgents to the distinguished Fleet Street, where the most esteemed newspapers like The Daily Mirror were published. Playing Lamb was a bit of an exercise in what would happen if O’Connell’s comeuppance led him toward the dark side. “The intoxication of power is something that really interests me. And Larry, he began as a socialist, voted Labour, celebrated socialist politicians. He left Fleet Street having been knighted by Margaret Thatcher. … Talk about excavation, a whole U-turn politics there, colluded with Rupert Murdoch in tearing up the unions and workers’ rights. Sold his soul,” said O’Connell.

“There’s a great contradiction with Larry that he begins as an outsider. Even within the duration of our film, he’s trying to become an insider. He wants to be part of that gang. In fact, that’s where he ended up, Sir Larry. So there’s a great contradiction in the man. So I can’t afford to go all the way ‘outsider with a chip on his shoulder,’” said the actor.

With “Ink” following the successes of “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” so quickly, O’Connell has a newfound feeling of security and sense of becoming that sought-after leading man. “It probably is my most mature role to date,” he said. “I look back on my career and I just feel so fortunate. There’s not a single regret. So if this is a new era, yeah, brilliant, bring it on. A lot of my heroes, a lot of their work that I really celebrate, were around my age, so maybe that is inspiring and gives me cause to kick on.”

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters across the United States on Friday, December 11. The film will debut on the streaming service on January 8, 2027.

#3458. Apple confirms $7.5 billion bond sale following strong investor demand

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

#3457. Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Talent labs and mentorship programs are plentiful for aspiring filmmakers — but where do you turn when your career has already started, after your first movie or on the precipice of one, and especially when filmmaking can be such a lonely enterprise?

Enter Square Peg Social, the Austin, Texas-based filmmaking summit launched by Lars and Amy Knudsen and Ari Aster that offers four days of singular community-building: brutally honest advice, commiseration, and idea exchange shared among 35 participants, with the program now in its second year.

A weekend of panels, discussion, and camaraderie designed for filmmakers at the early stages of their career, this year’s talent-incubating event was even crashed by the likes of Zach Cregger and Richard Linklater — both of whom were down to get frank about their filmmaking highs and lows. (In fall 2025, IndieWire did a deep dive into Square Peg Social’s first year, just to show how much the event has already grown.) Related Stories ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’ How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

But the program’s stable of 2026 mentors and panelists — i.e., filmmakers keen not only to open up to new filmmakers about their own struggles, but also to scout new talent — also counted “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” director Lance Oppenheim, “Sing Sing” filmmaker Greg Kwedar, “The First Omen” director Arkasha Stevenson, and “Mother Mary” director David Lowery among them.

The closed-door, off-the-record, noncompetitive summit opened to applicants in May, later unfolding from September 17-21. Partners including the Austin Film Society, Belvedere, and Airbnb offset the cost, besides a modest application fee, for participants to hole up for four days and nights at Soho House that don’t promise job opportunities — but instead, the kind of lasting industry connections that can take years (and many starts and stops) to build. Also, no job opportunities isn’t entirely true. Take last year’s Square Peg Social mentee Yona Strauss, who’s now working for Knudsen and Aster’s Square Peg.

Just a sampling of this year’s participating producers and directors: producer Annie Huang, who worked on franchise IP like “Barbie” and “Wicked” at major studios; Jack Auen, co-founder of the filmmaking collective Cosmic Salon, which this year directed the New York critics’ favorite “Chronovisor”; Emmy-winning director of the Netflix short “The Turnaround,” Kyle Thrash; SXSW 2026 Neon Auteur Award winner Oliver Woolf; and many more who have their foot in the door, but are ready to cross the threshold.

IndieWire spoke to Lars Knudsen and Aster (who also co-founded the production company Square Peg, which this year backed “The Drama” and “Primetime”), plus Stevenson, Oppenheim, and Kwedar, along with three participants, to replay the on-the-ground experience in Austin. Late nights, early mornings, and vulnerabilities abounded across a long (but in some ways too short) weekend of intimate panels, small group sessions, and candid remarks from established filmmakers about the times they were trying to hold their own projects together with Scotch tape and paper clips. Think of it like a mini summer camp devoted to obsessive ambition.

“When you’ve been doing it for this long, sometimes it feels like you’re just a little bit going through the motions. You’re going from movie to movie to movie, and you sometimes forget why we do this thing that we do. We’re in this world working with these artists where they don’t have a plan B. Having now worked with 30, 40 filmmakers, I realized that when my wife brought up the idea of doing something because she has her own aversions to the industry, and that there isn’t really — it sounds cliché — but there just isn’t a lot of kindness or compassion or openness in our industry.

“There’s a lot of fear, there’s a lot of rejection. We wanted to create a space for filmmakers where there’s radical transparency and where it was truly, truly focused on a selfless thing: helping young filmmakers navigate the industry at a time in their career where things can either take off or not, and really demystifying the process of making movies, especially during the stage where they’re often in the back seat, which is financing or casting. Because for all these filmmakers that I work with and all the filmmakers that we’ve invited there, even the producers, it’s the first thing to think about when they wake up and the last thing to think about when they go to bed. Nothing is more important. I wanted to create an event where that is treated with the utmost importance, almost like it’s a life-or-death thing because it is all they want to do.”

“When Lars and Amy first broached the idea with me, I realized that it was something that I wish I had when I got out of school [at AFI], because I really did have to navigate that on my own. I was making a lot of shorts with whatever money I could raise and writing screenplays and trying to get one screenplay going. When that failed, writing something else and really looking for any sort of mentorship or guidance, It’s a very demoralizing process, and it was very, very hard for me to find traction, and it hasn’t gotten easier. It’s as bad as it’s ever been. There’s just so much uncertainty right now in the industry, not just for filmmakers. Even the lives of these studios are suddenly in danger and in question.

“There are a lot of filmmakers that Lars and I have been championing and films that we’ve been trying to get financing for that have proven almost impossible… It felt like a good thing to create a space where filmmakers can come together and commiserate and share experiences and connect. More important than even the connections that are made between the mentors and the mentees here are actually the relationships made among the people who are attending. A lot of them end up working together because we have producers and directors coming in. Last year proved really successful, and I would just say it was refreshing for us, too, that it galvanized us to keep doing this. Because last year it was almost an experiment: Will this work? How will we feel having done this? … Everybody walked away feeling good and feeling like it was a really useful and positive experience.”

“I’ve never really had the opportunity to just hang out with so many great filmmakers, not only just working filmmakers whose work I’ve loved, like David Lowery, who I’ve idolized for so long, but there’s so many filmmakers that were actually in the program as participants whose work I also have really admired. So having a space where we could all just kind of talk and vent and really nerd out on stuff that you never really get the opportunity to do.

“Because this was so filmmaker-driven and filmmaker-led, it encouraged the spirit of vulnerability [where] everyone really went there. I felt like maybe I should go back to therapy or something, but I felt like this was a great opportunity to therapize and also dump all of my feelings into a forum where you could just be open and honest about the process of making films… Most people had made features before, and were in the process of making features. It felt much more like we were at a film festival and everyone was able to connect with each other in a much deeper way, more than anything I’ve been to before.

“The first night I was there, I stayed up till like three in the morning, and I went on one of those electric scooters, the limes with Lars and Christian [Vasquez], my producer, and a producer from the event, too. We went to Whataburger and just kept talking. I think that was sort of the vibe. I don’t know. I guess everyone was encouraged to hang out for as long as they wanted to and to kick back and relax. There was another night we closed down the Soho House lounge bar, and Amy was like, ‘Let’s keep hanging out.’ So we were outside the bar, and everybody pulled together all of the drinks in their mini bar, and we created an ad hoc bar outside of the Soho House, and we kept drinking and hanging.”

“I don’t think you can really do film if you have a plan B because there’s always an escape hatch, and film requires every single atom of your body, mind and soul. It naturally becomes a very therapeutic place. I think because we’re all in this constant state of obsession, that can get really tiring, and it can get really lonely. … [The industry] attracts very sensitive souls. [With Square Peg Social] I didn’t even realize how badly I needed it until the first year. I’d known Amy and Lars before that, and Amy said that she wanted to start a Social. … I thought it would be much smaller, smaller. It ended up being this great big thing where, yeah, it does feel like a therapy circle, really.

“Everyone was really struck by the safety of the event. There was this unspoken agreement that everybody would be checking your egos at the door, and that this would be a very safe place to share your personal vulnerabilities, which is exceptionally rare in film because resources are so limited, and it’s just naturally a very competitive industry. Letting yourself be very, very vulnerable in front of your peers is something you were, in a sense, trained not to do but sometimes desperately need. At Square Peg, also, the line between mentee and mentor blurs quite a bit, which is why I think it’s so beneficial for everybody who goes there.

“It kind of reminds me of summer camp a little bit because you’re up until two or three in the morning talking to people, and then you’re up at eight again.”

“I always think of this term, like, whenever you take an elevator up, if you get to the top floor, send it back down for someone else to get on. [Square Peg] is one of the busiest production companies working today. To dedicate this weekend for emerging artists to have a forum where they can come and feel completely comfortable being very vulnerable with their ambitions, but also the things that they’re afraid of, and to hear that echoed from industry mentors who are being just as vulnerable about their ambitions and the things that they struggle with and the heartbreaks they’ve had, it’s an amazing table that’s set.

“I had ulterior motives in the, in the sense that Clint [Bentley] and I have started this new company, Ethos, and we have a deal at Netflix to finance films from emerging artists, and so I was also there … to look for talent. We’ll be following up with a lot of these artists to just hear more about the films they want to make. One thing that I appreciated about it was that it wasn’t like a pitch fest. You’re not there to pitch your project. You’re there to soak it in and learn.

“It had this healthy blend of these panels, and not the normal kind of panel. One was a panel of filmmakers led off by Ari and Lars, telling a very, very brutally honest story of how hard one of their films was to make. That kind of created a pathway for how the rest of the weekend would unfold.”

“I think the whole reason anyone works in film is that we were once kids making videos in the woods with our friends, making with a shitty camera. And there’s nothing else in this world, and I think I probably speak for everyone, where I can’t imagine film is the only thing that’s our main passion and hobby and something we can also make a career out of. So there was never a plan B at all. Whenever someone asked me, ‘What do you think you’d do if you couldn’t do anything film-adjacent?’ I have literally no idea, maybe a teacher or something. That’s super nice that Lars and the rest of Square Peg was saying that there is no plan B. There’s only: If it takes longer to get to Plan A, then it takes longer to get to Plan A.

“I remember on the very first day before we even properly began, Lars did a little speech with Ari, and Lars was like, ‘We’re going to be 100 percent transparent with you guys.’ And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that’s cool, but I wonder how transparent.’ And by the end of it, I was like, ‘Fuck me, that was transparent.’ There really was nothing off the table.”

“It was definitely something that I’ve never experienced before in this industry, to experience that level of candor and to hear these traumatic experiences that they have gone through in not a sensationalistic way, but almost in a very personal and almost relatable way, despite me having never experienced that level of millions of dollars of movie budget making — but on a personal level of how the heartbreaks had felt for them individually and the hardships of filmmaking. Coming into this program, there are so many people within our cohort who are incredibly talented, who have accomplished so many things. And coming into it, oftentimes you’ll have a fear of: ‘OK, how do I compare in relation to their accomplishments?’ But in hearing Lars and Ari talk about their own hardships, I think that’s what influenced me to really share some of mine coming up in the industry and producing independently.

“Some of the traumatic experiences that I have also faced are ones that I feel like I have to not talk about or hide from people, for fear of them looking like mistakes or of me looking like I’m not good enough to be doing this. And we were able to share that, like Ollie [Woolf] and I, in our own little producer’s therapy session with the mentors, with Lars. That was really healing for me.”

“[Ari, Lars, and the mentors are] on, not a different level, but they’re all going through similar issues and this and that, whether it’s a low budget or a higher budget type of ordeal. Everyone’s going through the same thing in their own way, in a sense. Just to know the people that I’ve been looking up to for a very long time, the reason in large part why I got into making films, to know that they’re going through similar things and just keep going, and it’s fine. No matter what level we’re going to be at, there’s still something to navigate. So I thought it was very cool to see, over the course of five days, to hear these individual experiences and stuff and how you could relate it back to what we’re going through right now and where we are.

“It was information overload in the best way possible. At a certain point, I hope I’m retaining everything that was said over those five days because it was nonstop, all useful information. I wasn’t even taking notes at a certain point because I’m like, ‘I can’t write all this stuff down. I’m just going to try and soak it all in.'”

#3456. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3455. Twelve South’s new Cablesnap charger has a built-in retractable USB-C cable

Popular Apple accessory maker Twelve South is launching a new retractable Cablesnap 65W travel charger this week. It has a built-in USB-C cable, alongside an additional USB-C port and USB-A port.

You can order the new Cablesnap 65W on Amazon today for $49.99.

We’ve seen travel chargers with retractable cables before, and Twelve South’s is similar. It has a 29-inch (75cm) spring-loaded USB-C cable built right in, so you can pull out exactly as much as you need. Then, when you’re ready to pack up, just give it a little pull, and it snaps back into the charging brick.

In addition to the retractable USB-C cable, there’s a separate USB-C port and a USB-A port for charging other accessories. It can charge at up to 65W speeds, shared across each connected device.

You can order the new Cablesnap 65W on Amazon today. This is just the latest in what’s been a busy few weeks for Twelve South. Last month, the accessory maker introduced the popular AirFly Drive adapter that converts wired CarPlay into wireless. A few weeks later it unveiled the AirFly View, an evolution of its wireless audio dongle that’s perfect for planes.

#3454. ‘VisionQuest’ Showrunner Breaks Down the Finale’s Massive ‘WandaVision’ Reunion Scene

Taylor Gates is an Indiana native who earned her BFA in Creative Writing from the University of Evansville. She fell in love with entertainment by watching shows about chaotic families like Full House, The Nanny, Gilmore Girls, and The Fosters. After college, she moved to Los Angeles to pursue a career as a writer, editor, and filmmaker. Today, she’s a sucker for dramedies — especially coming-of-age stories centering around complex female and LGBTQ+ characters. She has been with Collider since May 2022.

This interview contains spoilers for the VisionQuest finale.

James Spader is one of the most beloved and versatile actors working today, with his resume spanning everything from ‘80s classics like Pretty in Pink and Wall Street to the critically acclaimed indie dramedy Secretary. He’s also a staple of TV, earning three Emmys for his work in Boston Legal, becoming a fan-favorite character on The Office, and starring in over 200 episodes of the crime thriller The Blacklist. His newest role is once again a small-screen one, though he reprises the last movie character he played all the way back in 2015: Ultron in Avengers: Age of Ultron and now VisionQuest. Deliciously complex and bitingly hilarious, he’s easily one of the best parts of the show whether he’s flirting with Jocasta (T’Nia Miller) or dealing with his son Vision’s (Paul Bettany) angst.

Though many were anxious when WandaVision and Agatha All Along creator Jac Schaeffer had to leave VisionQuest, Terry Matalas has proven himself worthy of taking up the mantle. He brings a plethora of experience in the sci-fi space, serving as the showrunner of 12 Monkeys and two seasons of Star Trek: Picard. Matalas has shown he has a special talent for combining deep, philosophical themes with witty humor and compelling character work, so it’s no surprise that he absolutely sticks the landing as the writer and director of VisionQuest’s fantastic finale.

Collider got the chance to speak to Spader and Matalas about their work in the final episode. During the conversation, Matalas discussed pulling off that sitcom sequence and emotional reunion, while Spader revealed how he balanced playing those two wildly different yet intrinsically linked characters.

COLLIDER: I thought the idea of Vision using a sitcom to get through to Ultron was such a brilliant full-circle moment. Terry, how and when in the process did that idea come to you?

TERRY MATALAS: That came in the writers’ room. I have a brilliant writers’ staff, and we knew we wanted to honor WandaVision. We knew we were heading towards that territory, and there were a couple of versions of what that might have looked like with UltraVision. There was a version that was him and Jocasta, but ultimately, in the writing, about halfway through, I was like, “No, this has to be about Vision and Ultron. That's what the show really, truly is.” It's a miracle that we pulled it off. We had a writer, Cindy Appel, who has some sitcom background, who helped me shape that, and we have an incredible cast that just got the tone. It is a big swing, and I hope people like it. I'm very nervous about it, but we'll see how it lands.

I loved it, so I imagine everyone else will feel the same way. James, it was so fun to watch Ultron in that sitcom. What was the fun, and then also the challenge of filming those scenes?

JAMES SPADER: The prism through which I saw this show was as the standalone show — the standalone story. I do not have an encyclopedic knowledge of the Marvel universe, so the last time that I'd sort of touched home base with it was when I did Avengers: Age of Ultron. I then went away and did other work for 10 years, and then, all of a sudden, I'm back at it. For me, that was just this incredibly creative and original, and yet completely sensible and irrational but rational idea for what should transpire, or what Vision should grab onto and then for Ultron to take over and hijack. It was lovely and funny, and also scary and sort of disturbing, and that's what I loved about it — it would tonally shift within a scene, really getting pretty dark at times, and then just laugh-out-loud funny.

I was also so thrilled to see Billy back in the finale. Terry, was there any conversation about having Ghost Agatha tag along with him?

MATALAS: I don't know that we could have afforded that. [Laughs] So not really, no. We always knew that reunion was going to be, and how much of it, and how early — what would be right for Tommy, what would be right for Billy, what would be right for the family story. But I feel like we got the proper emotional reunion for them. And I think the way that his return impacts Vision — without being too spoilerific — is important.

And I also really love the complicated love triangle between Jo, Ultron, and Virgil. James, how did you build those two distinct but sort of interconnected relationships with T’Nia?

SPADER: I don't know. [Laughs] I really don't know. Terry said to me, about three-fourths of the way through filming the show, “We really need to sit down and talk about Virgil.” And we did. But I don't know — it's a blur to me now, but it made such sense.

MATALAS: Well, we knew it was a different energy.

SPADER: Yeah, completely different from Ultron. It’s madness.

MATALAS: It's a Wizard of Oz “man behind the curtain.” There's a great Paul delivery – after he's doing this whole monologue, Paul finally just goes, “Who are you?” It's fantastic because I'm sure the audience is wondering the same thing at that point. It was just a joy to be on set and watch that happen after doing four months of Ultron, which is a very specific thing, for James to be let loose with this insane mustache that he designed. It was hard to direct because I wouldn't want to cut — it was like being in front of the TV. I was just entranced by it all.

SPADER: It was a great idea of Terry's that you build up to the Big Bad guy through the whole picture, and then you meet him, and he's incredibly dangerous because he's so mad, yet at the end of the day, he's also so not what you expect from a Big Bad guy.

MATALAS: And yet he's also not the final obstacle. It is truly about Ultron, which is what it always needed to be.

SPADER: Well, that's why Ultron kicked his ass.

All episodes of VisionQuest are now streaming on Disney+.

#3453. After James Gunn’s Shocking Departure, It Looks Like Clayface Will Be DC’s Last R-Rated Movie

Shockingly, yet another major shake-up for DC films is coming with James Gunn and Peter Safran being ousted from their roles as the heads of DC Studios, and it seems likely that Clayface could very well be the last DCU movie of its kind.

After four years overseeing the new DCU, James Gunn and Peter Safran will be stepping away from their leadership positions. While they'll still be working on projects like Man of Tomorrow and The People vs. Gorilla Grodd, it's been announced that Marvel Studios veteran Jeremy Latcham will be taking over as the new, singular head of DC Studios. Naturally, this raises some pretty big questions about the future of the DCU and its overall vision, especially given what is known about Latcham.

Considering that Latcham has publicly discussed his preference for making movies accessible to broad, four-quadrant audiences, it feels very likely that Clayface may very well be the first (and last) R-rated DCU movie.

Announced on November 9, Jeremy Latcham's appointment to DC Studios marks a pretty significant change. Having previously worked at Marvel Studios on films like Iron Man, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, and Spider-Man: Homecoming, Latcham's prior superhero history suggests that Skydance is looking for a major pivot, one that suggests a desire to see the DCU becoming more like the MCU. Meanwhile, Gunn and Safran are returning to full-time creative work, though it remains to be seen just how long they'll be involved with the DCU once their remaining projects currently in development are released.

However, the concerns with Latcham go beyond his Marvel background, as he recently voiced an ongoing focus on making sure films are appealing to as general an audience as possible. He's even cited a personal test in an interview with CBN, one he'd conduct during his early days with Marvel Studios. Apparently, one of his key guiding lights for creative decisions was asking himself whether his grandmother would enjoy certain scenes or narratives.

There are also concerns regarding Latcham's faith and more conservative values having a possible effect on future DCU projects, though that remains to be seen (and has arguably been blown out of proportion). What feels more concerning is that focus on wanting to appeal to all ages, suggesting that R-rated films like Clayface will likely face a major uphill battle to get made in the future that they would have under Gunn, not to mention shows with more mature ratings like Creature Commandos, Peacemaker, and Lanterns.

While nothing has been officially said to suggest that DC Studios will stop making R-rated content altogether, it feels entirely plausible based on Latcham's previous comments that Clayface could very well be the last theatrical DCU movie to receive an R-rating.

Ultimately, DC Studios shouldn't simply chase the exact same audience as Marvel Studios all the time. There's an advantage in offering something different, while also taking advantage of the major differences in its characters. Superman should offer hope and optimism and be appealing to everyone, but that doesn't mean DC Studios should shy away from the DC Universe's darkest corners, if only to benefit one of its biggest characters: Batman.

After all, Gotham is supposed to be one of the most dangerous cities in the entire DC Universe, full of some of the most brutal and horrifying villains in all fiction. The less those foes are sanitized, the better, which is why Clayface felt so encouraging for the DCU's future. The fact that an R-rated movie like Clayface exists in the same universe as Superman is a huge benefit.

DC Studios doesn't need every movie to be R-rated, nor should it sacrifice accessibility just for the sake of distinguishing itself from Marvel. That said, it does need room for all kinds of stories, with some that might not appeal to every single moviegoer. If Latcham's leadership does end up pushing DC Studios toward safer, four-quadrant entertainment across the board, Clayface will undoubtedly become a reminder of the creative possibilities left behind.

Gotham actor Matt Hagen's rising star is destroyed when a local crime boss leaves him horribly disfigured. Desperate to regain his former life, Matt undergoes an experimental treatment that restores his appearance but transforms his body into malleable clay. Now able to reshape himself into other people, Hagen sets off on an increasingly violent campaign of revenge against the ones he holds responsible for his fate.

#3450. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3448. Stacy Keach, ‘Fat City’ and ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Dead at 85

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life.” Related Stories How Nicholas Britell Packs Conflicting Emotions Into the ‘Jay Kelly’ Score Adam Sandler Looks Back on His Early Days in Hollywood at IndieWire Honors

She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

#3447. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3446. The 5 Best Noah Wyle ‘ER’ Episodes of the '90s, Ranked

pNBC began airing ER in 1994, and the show quickly became one of the most believable medical dramas of all time. A reason behind this is the beloved character Dr. John Carter, portrayed by Noah Wyle. Noah's character became one of the best television doctors, and critics noticed his uniqueness by the end of Season 1.

Noah received a string of Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for his portrayal, along with four consecutive Actor Awards. He starred on the show for 11 seasons and returned for other story arcs from start to finish, yet his performances were not enough for award recognition after 1999. Here's a list of Dr. Carter's best ER episodes of the '90s, with stories that made this beloved character prove he belongs in an emergency room.

Every County General employee needs a close friend, and for a short time, Carter's was fellow surgical intern Dr. Dennis Gant (Omar Epps). The pair were prepared to become the best surgeons they could be, and stuck by each other when doing so. Their behavior toward one another began to change as time went on, and it made Carter unable to see the signs Gant was struggling. It wasn't until Gant was struck and killed by a train in the episode prior that Carter realized he didn't see what was right in front of him.

Gant's death was one of the most tension-filled times in Carter's life as he couldn't help but wonder if his late friend jumped in front of the train. The survivor's guilt was eating at Carter, and the lack of care he had when expressing his anger toward co-workers was surprising to see so early in his career. The police ultimately ruled Gant's death an accident, and it made doctors a little bit at ease. The cause of death didn't change what Carter felt, and it was stunning to see him question his behavior as a friend, and not as a fellow intern.

The family lives of doctors have been woven into plot lines before, with Carter's being known for their intensity and privileged background. He did maintain positive relationships with some of his relatives, including his cousin, Chase (Jonathan Scarfe). Carter was shocked to learn his cousin was a heroin addict, but he believed that as a doctor and close relative, he could help him get clean. He put in the time and effort with Dr. Anna Del Amico (Maria Bellow), and thought it worked. Carter's plan backfired, and Chase landed in the hospital from a heroin overdose.

Despite Chase's history, Carter's shock was felt throughout the entire hospital room as he tried to resuscitate his cousin. That shock turned into fear while admitting to his grandparents that he was aware of Chase's addiction, and did not tell them about it. Carter had longed for unconditional love from many family members, yet he always had it from Chase. Chase suffered permanent brain damage from his overdose, but Carter sleeping next to his bedside was enough to know that neurological issues would not make him love his cousin any less.

A normal day at County General turned into chaos following a chemical spill. Employees and patients were unsure of what to do, and Dr. Kerry Weaver (Laura Innes) being exposed to the fumes only made things crazier. Carter put his panic aside, and took charge of the ER without hesitation. He directed staff and patients to rooms based on health status while conducting research and communicating with emergency officials.

Carter brought intensity to a whole new level after he was put in charge, and it showed how much he'd grown as a medical professional. He gained more self-confidence just by doing his job, and didn't even realize it until he knew everyone was safe. Carter's work and determination saved hundreds of lives, but he did take a short pause from his leadership duties after finding out his elderly patient had died. Carter snapped out of commander mode when Weaver recovered from her fume exposure and smiled at the employees praising him, realizing that County General's ER was his home.

It's hard to imagine Carter practicing something other than emergency medicine. After figuring that out himself, Carter fought tooth and nail to convince his superior, Dr. Donald Anspaugh (John Aylward) of the same thing. Anspaugh initially refused due to budgetary reasons and Carter signed a contract to complete the County General's surgical program. He changed his mind once Carter explained why he would never be a great surgeon.

It was tough to predict Anspaugh's final decision. He and Carter's reasons behind their opinions of a specialty change were understandable. Carter obviously wasn't backing down, and even if it meant leaving his surgical mentor, Dr. Peter Benton (Eriq La Salle), he couldn't stop fighting for what was right for him. Carter's fight was inspirational for anyone brave enough to follow their hearts, and it led to him becoming one of the best emergency medicine doctors at County General.

Carter was a third-year medical student anxious to become a surgeon on the first episode of ER. He walked in wearing a "tailored white coat," looking nervous and terrified. Carter was eager to begin treating patients, even though he never learned how to start an IV. Something he wasn't afraid of doing when he walked in was interacting with patients, and threw up outside after doing so.

Carter walked back into the ER with his head held high after talking with Dr. Mark Greene (Anthony Edwards). He continued to be imperfect, but he didn't let that get into his head. It was beautiful to see a young student believing in himself on the first day working in a Chicago hospital ER. That beauty is what helped him become a phenomenal doctor who saved millions of lives worldwide.

#3444. 10 Marvel Mutants Whose Powers Are Actually Horrific Nightmares To Live With

Over decades of publication, X-Men and other Marvel Comics titles have delivered mutants who stand out for their overwhelming abilities, with some able to alter the fabric of reality itself. However, not every mutation can be impressive or an omega-level powerhouse. Some carry consequences that make life difficult to manage on a day-to-day basis, while others can spark fear within their users.

Among these mutations, there are a few that mutants have learned to bear and manage, but that doesn’t make their power or skill any less burdensome when looking at their past history. These range from physical limitations to psychological consequences and more, making each mutation come across more like a curse than anything else.

Hector Rendoza, also known as Wraith, has one of the franchise’s most visually unsettling mutations among Marvel’s mutants. Rather than conventional invisibility, his power turns his skin completely transparent, leaving his bones, muscles, and organs completely visible. To top it all off, when his power first manifested, his appearance was so disturbing that an angry mob tried to kill him.

Luckily, he survived, and while he can temporarily restore his normal appearance by transferring his transparency to someone else through physical contact, doing so comes at that person’s expense. His mutation makes living an ordinary life far more complicated, and constantly having his internal organs exposed is pure nightmare fuel.

Bailey Hoskins is a teenager who discovered that he was a mutant only to find that he had one of the worst mutations possible. He can force his entire body to explode with considerable force, however, he doesn’t have a healing factor, meaning that if he ever chooses to use the power his mutation grants him, it will cause his death.

Unlike other mutants who struggle to contain their abilities, Bailey must never use his own. At the Xavier Institute, surrounded by students with abilities they could freely use and develop, Bailey is left unable to embrace his own mutation. Beyond that, villains have also recognized his potential as a living weapon, turning him into a target for exploitation.

Mordred is an antagonist and an ancient mutant whose history stretches all the way back to the fall of Camelot. He’s known as a witchbreed with the involuntary ability that provokes hostility in those around him, called the aura of hatred. This turns even his allies against him, pushing anyone in his vicinity to feel an urge to attack or resent him.

Given that his mutation is involuntary, Mordred is doomed to live his life in constant isolation or alienation. By simply being alive and around others, he stirs up malice, making any genuine relationship practically impossible. Mordred may be an antagonist, but it's hard not to feel a shred of sympathy for him given the life he’s been forced to lead.

Robert Herman, who is better known as Glob, is one of the strangest additions to the Xavier Institute. Similar to Wraith, his mutation leaves his skeleton and internal organs visible, except rather than transparent skin, his body turns into translucent pink bio-paraffin wax. While this form does grant Glob enhanced durability and strength, his physical appearance is something out of a body horror film.

Although Marvel Studios' X-Men reboot is right around the corner, the MCU is already defining what will set mutants apart from other heroes.

At first, Glob hated his mutation and all other mutants. For years, he was projecting his insecurities on others, and while he did grow to embrace his identity over time, that doesn’t erase the hardships of his early life and the internal struggles he suffered for years due to the nature of his mutation.

Marrow’s true name is Sarah, a young woman whose mutation lets her manipulate her own skeleton, forcing her bones to grow through her skin and shaping them into armor and weapons. She was initially a member of the Morlocks before beginning her redemption by becoming one of the X-Men and working as a hero.

While her mutation also grants her an accelerated healing factor, that doesn’t mean that her ability doesn’t have a high physical toll. It's been shown that her bones can grow unpredictably, painfully piercing through her body and leaving her visibly disfigured. Even when she is deliberately using her power, she has no other choice but to endure the pain.

Jonothon Starsmore, best known as Chamber, is a mutant whose powers manifested with severe consequences. When they first emerged, the explosion completely destroyed his lower face and chest, as well as vital organs, replacing them with an ever-burning reservoir of energy in their place.

By some miracle, Jonothon survived and eventually went on to join Generation X, but he has never been able to restore his body. Due to the severity of his injuries, he was rendered unable to eat, drink, breathe, or speak like others normally can. While he does have great power, its original manifestation came at too high a cost, robbing him of the life he once knew.

Japheth, or Maggott, is one of the most unconventional mutants in Marvel. He hides two sentient, slug-like creatures named Eany and Meany in his abdomen, and these creatures can be expelled from his body, consume pretty much anything imaginable, before ultimately returning to Maggott’s body and transferring the energy they absorb.

The fact that Eany and Meany must physically leave his body to consume food before burrowing back into his abdomen to merely sustain him is horrific to think about.

While this mutation does grant him extraordinary abilities, it remains incredibly unsettling. The fact that Eany and Meany must physically leave his body to consume food before burrowing back into his abdomen to merely sustain him is horrific to think about. And yet, without them, Japheth wouldn’t be able to survive.

When Rogue’s mutation first revealed itself, it was during an innocent kiss that ultimately left her boyfriend permanently comatose. From that moment onward, Anna Marie’s ability to absorb another person’s memories, life force, and powers through skin-to-skin touch became a major source of fear in her early life.

Before she learned to control her power, Rogue struggled with the physical and psychological toll of her mutation. Not only could she not safely touch another person, but when she did, she risked losing or blurring the lines between her own identity and someone else's. While she does have one of the most impressive mutations, its early cost was dangerously high.

Kevin Ford’s mutation makes physical contact potentially fatal. Also known as Wither, Kevin can cause any organic matter to decay and disintegrate with touch alone. More horrifyingly, his mutation first manifested in an accident that killed his father. He was sent to the Xavier Institute in the hopes of learning control, but the power never ceased to be a threat to those around him.

Due to the nature of his mutation, Kevin has little other choice but to remain isolated to prevent disaster. One of the most devastating moments was after M-Day, when he mistakenly believed his powers were gone and reached for the girl he loved, only to immediately wither her arm. The moment proved the cruel reality that his mutation forced him to remain physically separated from others.

ForgetMeNot, whose real name is Xabi, has a mutation that makes him impossible to remember. The moment someone stops looking directly at him, they immediately forget he exists, along with any previous interactions. Despite serving with the X-Men for years, he remained largely unknown by his teammates, with only a handful of exceptions.

This mutation is most horrific given that Xabi can never make lasting relationships, but also has an incredibly hard time simply maintaining basic stability. Allies forget him when they look away, and all records of his existence never hold, no matter if they’re physically written or input into a computer, making his life an endless uphill battle and terrifyingly isolated.
