#3442. iOS 27.2 adds Apple Photos invisible watermark feature, here’s how it works

iOS 27.2 arrived last week, and among its changes for Apple Photos, the update adds an invisible watermarking feature when you use certain editing tools. Here’s how it works.

In the age of AI, what looks like a genuine photo might actually be a fake—or partly fake. That’s why tools like SynthID have been used to apply invisible watermarks to AI-generated content.

Starting with iOS 27.2, Apple now uses SynthID watermarks when you make AI-generated edits to photos in Apple Photos, or create all-new images with Image Playground.

Starting with iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2, some Apple Intelligence tools will add an invisible SynthID watermark to images that you create or edit:

Image Playground generates entirely new images, so it’s more what the average person would consider an “AI image.”

However, as Apple notes, the SynthID invisible watermark is also applied to genuine photos in your Apple Photos library if you use the AI-powered Clean Up, Extend, or Spatial Reframing tools to edit them.

It’s worth emphasizing the word “invisible” here. You won’t see evidence of a watermark anywhere on your photos, nor will others unless they explicitly check the image with a SynthID detector.

If you do want to check for the watermark, Apple recommends going to synthid.com, where you can upload an image and see its result.

How do you feel about Apple Photos adding SynthID watermarks in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3439. Rocky’s Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

Sylvester Stallone’s 1976 Oscar-winner Rocky carved itself into Hollywood history thanks to its timeless tale of underdog spirit, and a catalog of memorable moments. Stallone’s script was filled with lines that are quoted to this day – the triumphant cry of “Adrian!," Mickey (Burgess Meredith) declaring, “You’re gonna eat lightnin’ and you’re gonna crap thunder!” or Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers) joking “Apollo Creed versus the Italian Stallion. Sounds like a damn monster movie.” There’s one quote, however, that stands out among the rest, one that sums up everything about Rocky Balboa, and the franchise that tells his story, is all about. It’s not said in the ring, or on top of the famous steps, but in one of the boxer’s most private moments.

The scene in question comes the night before the climactic fight against Creed. Rocky (Stallone) walks around the arena, then back home to his girlfriend Adrian (Talia Shire). Sitting on the edge of the bed, he quietly confesses that he can’t beat Apollo, before adding: “It really don't matter if I lose this fight. It really don't matter if this guy opens my head, either. 'Cause all I wanna do is go the distance. Nobody's ever gone the distance with Creed, and if I can go that distance, you see, and that bell rings, and I'm still standin', I'm gonna know for the first time in my life, see, that I weren't just another bum from the neighborhood.”

At that one moment, The Italian Stallion’s journey comes into perspective. He is a fighter from the street, going up against the heavyweight champion of the world. The odds are against him, and even he can’t see himself knocking out a man who is at the peak of a sport when he had only ever been a manager. However, there’s a way to win even if he loses. That speech becomes the key question of the movie, and every sequel that came after it: can you go the distance?

Anthony Ippolito's uncanny performance and a heartwarming script make this an unmissable film.

Rocky isn’t the story of the preparation for a boxing match. It is the story of personal triumph, of one man who seemed like he didn’t have a future, whose own trainer called his choices “a waste of life,” betting on himself to go toe-to-toe with the best in the world. It’s about becoming more than you thought you could be, pushing the limits of what people expect of you, and shocking the world not by winning or losing, but by going the distance.

It’s a mindset that has prevailed in the six Rocky movies. Rocky II, arriving in 1979, saw the boxer strive to prove the first fight wasn’t a fluke. The third film saw him made complacent by money and fame, having to recapture his underdog spirit when he comes up against a fighter as hungry as he used to be. The fourth film deals with personal grief and revenge, while the fifth sees Rocky turning away from his life’s work in order to be a father and husband. Even his final fight, in 2006’s Rocky Balboa, is less about stepping into the ring than it is proving he still has something to give. Whether on the top of the mountain or haunted by the past, going the distance was always the goal.

It’s easy to assume every Rocky movie ends in glorious victory, but some of the key moments in the franchise are moral victories where someone else’s hand is raised. The first film sees Apollo win on a points victory, with the press and fans surrounding the champion, while Rocky and Adrian embrace each other as if they had won, because the underdog went the distance. Rocky III ends with a victory, but it is defined by a loss, as Rocky underestimates Clubber Lang (Mr T.) and the resulting defeat reignites the spark. Rocky IV sees Apollo die in the ring, a devastating end to a defining relationship, while Rocky Balboa comes full circle as, now in his 60s, he still finds victory in defeat, going all 12 rounds with a much younger champion.

While he stood across formidable men in the ring, Rocky’s most formidable opponent was always himself. Going the distance meant overcoming flaws and demons and becoming who he knew he could be. In the first two Creed movies, where Rocky becomes the trainer of Adonis Creed (Michael B Jordan), the son of his old rival-turned-friend, he imparts that same wisdom onto his protégé. Making Adonis stand in front of a mirror, Rocky points to the reflection and says: “That's the toughest opponent you're ever going to have to face.”

It all comes back to that one moment in Rocky’s small apartment, and a speech that would encapsulate everything that matters about the world’s most famous boxer. Winning and losing are secondary to the personal mountains we have to climb, and the knowledge that we have gone the distance against the odds can be better than any championship.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. #3437. 7 Far Side Comics That Expose The Funniest Truths About Human Nature

Humanity is incredibly weird and paradoxical, with us showing a collective lack of understanding of ourselves much of the time. Gary Larson frequently takes aim at that with The Far Side, drawing up hilarious bite-sized comic strips readers can frequently appreciate by pointing out the funny truths about human nature. True to Larson's style, he can even convey this with non-human animals, as seen all across its 15-year run. But The Far Side's funniest comics can sometimes also be just the most true, observing the many flaws or absurdities of humanity while keeping these observations loaded with levity, so it never feels like it goes too far.

Larson's legendary comic strip thus explores bullying and social pressure to conform, humanity's frequently troubling sense of self-preservation, and intrusive thoughts winning battles of the mind. While some of the best of The Far Side has frequently explored potentially humbling or modestly relatable strips like "Midvale School of the Gifted", others expose practically universal truths about the human experience, even if not displayed by creatures resembling humans at all. That's the magic of The Far Side, in that it adds just enough whimsical perspective to make something truly weird, hilarious, and entertainingly true.

There's something to be said about maintaining a professional image while working a job in psychology, especially when dealing with patients undergoing any number of sources of mental distress. But there's never a shortage of jokes suggesting that mask slips when they're "jotting notes" as their patients speak. Doodles of places they wish they could be, mental notes for anything they need to do before they get home, anything would be perfectly unprofessional in the place of a proper diagnosis.

But for this poor patient, the doctor has concluded, in the broadest layman's terms, that there's no sugarcoating or label necessary. It's hardly a helpful diagnosis, and will likely not help the patient in any way whatsoever. But at that moment, the therapist gives in with his intrusive thoughts to say what many might think but not dare put into writing.

Good stories and a life worth living sometimes make the presence of conflict vital, as something to overcome or persist in spite of their presence. For humans, that is the case of jerks, treated as a twisted spice of life in that they inject just the wrong sort of variety into everyday life. A world without jerks can certainly be a wonderful place, but it begs the question whether humanity have a reason to push and rise above its limitations without them. It's hard to imagine a reality without jerks, and whether such a world would indeed be much blander, but they're here now, and show no sign of going away.

An early example of The Far Side's tendency to poke fun at humanity's flaws while acknowledging classic and relatable experiences, particularly for bespectacled people, glasses-wearers can readily relate to finding out firsthand how much damage their eyewear can take.

They'll also, potentially, be stubborn or slow-moving about when they might need a new pair. As embarrassing as it may sound, walking straight into a wall is surprisingly common despite being given prescription gear to prevent these exact things from happening. Given the pile of destroyed glasses to the left, it appears these testers have a long day ahead of them before they settle on the most durable pair.

The Far Side's tendency to go to dark places is well-documented, and even in its earliest year alone, Gary Larson released a mountain of macabre gems.

Sensitivity about one's appearance is a classic example of a relatable human experience, this time reflected in beavers as they share in a round of jeers and taunts toward their peer who sadly has no buck teeth. The lack of subtlety certainly evokes more of an elementary or high school vibe, though, with the bully beavers zeroing directly in on the most noticeable difference. If anything, the funniest bit about this is just the sheer lack of creativity in their insults. But maybe don't put too much stock in that beaver's woodcutting work anytime soon.

Everybody gets a little bit on edge when driving, and the last thing anyone needs in a highway driving situation is for somebody to merge onto the left lane and continue to putter on. The idea of putting them in a special room in Hell alongside terrorists, homicidal maniacs, and other presumable images of classically horrible people is a hilarious touch. For what it's worth, another spot similar to this should go to people dumping a bag full of change at the checkout counter, expecting the cashier to sort what's there for them.

Mocking the human tendency to lean into mischief at any chance given, the idea of rubber bands being brand new, and not immediately turning one's hands into rubber band shooters, feel utterly incompatible. It doesn't matter what line of work one might be in, or whether someone else might even get mildly hurt. People will see the potential for fun at the expense of others and be presented with the option to have that instantly. For the scientist on the right, he simply had to know per the scientific method. It's his job, after all.

When in trouble, humanity activates their fight-or-flight mechanism just as any animal would. But by anthropomorphizing a pair of bears under the gun in this strip from The Far Side, Larson mocks how quickly people will turn on one another. The most tragic bit about this is that the nervously smiling bear is perfectly happy to sell their friend down the river as they look on, utterly unaware of the hunter's rifle potentially being pointed at them next. The worst part for that scapegoating bear is, there's no guarantee, even after the first shot is taken, that they'll be safe. But they'll happily take those odds and make their getaway from there.

#3434. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3433. Ex-Swinger Reality Star Tony McCollister Facing Life In Prison For Bestiality

Tony McCollister, the former reality TV star convicted of charges related to child rape and sex with dogs, is headed to prison ... with a judge sentencing him Tuesday to 15 years to life behind bars.

McCollister learned his fate in an Ohio courtroom ... where the judge handed down the sentence for raping a child under 10 ... and he won't be eligible for parole for at least 15 years.

And that wasn't his only punishment ... McCollister also received prison time for gross sexual imposition, child endangerment, and charges involving child sexual abuse material ... along with jail sentences for sexual conduct with animals.

The judge ordered those sentences to run concurrently with his rape sentence ... and McCollister will also be required to register as a Tier 3 sex offender.

McCollister and the 5-year-old victim's father both addressed the court during the hearing ... and the judge credited McCollister with 322 days already served.

His defense team says it plans to appeal the conviction.

As TMZ previously reported ... McCollister, who appeared on A&E's short-lived reality show "Neighbors with Benefits," was arrested in December 2025 after investigators accused him of possessing child sexual abuse material and sexually abusing his dogs.

He was later convicted of raping a child under 10 and other offenses ... while his former partner, Erica Grove, was convicted of separate child sex-related charges but acquitted of rape.

Now, McCollister faces the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison.

#3432. iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

#3430. The 10 Best Alternative Rock Songs of All Time, Ranked

While rock music doesn’t seem to dominate pop culture the way it did, in various forms, throughout much of the 1960s, ‘70s, ‘80s, ‘90s, and even the 2000s (to some extent), people do still get passionate about rock music. It can be classic rock, or alternative rock, or maybe even some other kind of rock, but if you write about rock, people will feel strongly about it. It has been happening lately.

So, here’s some more writing about rock. It’s not done to make anyone angry, but if you do get angry, hey, it’s not really all that surprising to the person who put all this together. These are a selection of tracks that are worthy of being considered the best alternative rock songs of all time. And sure, alternative rock was most dominant in the 1980s and 1990s, so maybe this is really a “best alternative rock songs of the 1980s and 1990s” kind of thing, but still, “all time” sounds a little better/fancier, doesn’t it?

It is easy to make fun of Pearl Jam, and honestly sometimes quite fun to make fun of Pearl Jam. In hindsight, they sound a bit like hyper-grunge, or even like some sort of accidental parody of grunge, but early on, they were doing grunge very well. Grunge is a type of alternative rock, and you get some good grunge and/or alternative rock on Ten.

Ten was Pearl Jam’s debut album, and though it frustratingly contained 11 tracks, one of those tracks was “Black,” and that makes the numbers not lining up a little easier to forgive. There’s a real desperation and passion to this song that can make it a hard listen, depending on your frame of mind at the time, but that is also a testament to the undeniable emotional kick (or punch? Whichever one’s more likely to hurt more) it delivers.

“Unsatisfied” is another angsty and hard-hitting song, which are qualities you're probably going to have to get used to experiencing/noticing if you listen to enough alternative rock. This song’s by The Replacements, and it is a track about feeling that titular emotion. That’s it. That’s all it needs to be, of course, when the execution is this good, but it is very straightforward.

The Replacements had a knack for exploring emotions well, though, be they the kinds you often feel while listening to music, or maybe not so often. And another track from the same album (Let It Be) is quite ahead of its time: “Androgynous,” which doesn’t feel like it was recorded over 40 years ago, especially with what it deals with lyrically, and how it deals with it. That’s a very honorable mention, but “Unsatisfied” is placing just ahead of it here because it’s more of a rock song, while “Androgynous” is far gentler and more of a ballad.

Radiohead might still be an alternative rock band, though from Kid A onward, there has been more of an electronic sound/focus. Not exclusively, but still undeniably. OK Computer might be the last properly “alternative rock” album of the band’s, even if it flirts a little with where they'd go sonically on Kid A, and so it feels right to include something from OK Computer here.

It is not the album with “Creep.” Sorry. That’s always been the most famous Radiohead song. But it is the album with “Let Down,” and hopefully you're not feeling too let down that “Creep” isn't here, you creep; you weirdo. No, but truthfully, “Let Down” is such a beautiful and perfect song, not really rocking or feeling as loud as most of the other songs here, but that final minute or so (the big release) makes it more than worthy of inclusion.

“Smells Like Teen Spirit” might be Nirvana’s “Creep,” but it’s also a much better song than “Creep,” so its overwhelming popularity feels a good deal easier to comprehend. And as a band, Nirvana feels less easy to mock than Pearl Jam, even with them being very distinctive and also tied up with the same genre/movement. Nirvana is grunge, and Nirvana did not last long enough to sell out or run the risk of becoming a parody of itself.

The tragic nature of the band is always hard to overlook, which is what can also be said about going back and listening to Joy Division, knowing the truth about things. The anger found in much of Nirvana’s discography becomes more intense, in hindsight, but with “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” there is still that sense of toeing the line of selling out; doing something catchy but it nonetheless still “Sounds Like Nirvana.”

There is a cover of “Downtown Train” by Rod Stewart that isn't alternative rock, and if you can count it as rock, then it’s about as soft, mushy, and bland as rock gets. It’s kind of terrible. Stewart does not seem to get what makes the song special, or maybe he just doesn't. Tom Waits does get it, though. And he should, because he wrote it, but this is Waits at his absolute best, keeping his distinctive style while throwing himself into a song that’s more immediate and moving than the vast majority of his songs.

And those other songs are great in other (not to mention usually more unusual) ways, so “Downtown Train” is possibly to Waits what “Smells Like Teen Spirit” was to Nirvana: both artists at their respective “poppiest.” There is still just the right amount of edge to this original version of “Downtown Train,” thankfully, and Waits doesn’t compromise on his vocal style, with the song being interesting because it’s moving, sweeping, and kind of grimy, all at once, and somehow not in a contradictory manner.

This song really moves. “She Bangs the Drums” is perfect, and it’s perfect on the album it belongs to (more or less the ideal second track for an energetic rock album), and then it’s also perfectly enjoyable on its own, if you feel like you don’t have the time to listen to all of the debut album by The Stone Roses. You should give that album a listen, though.

The band’s discography is easy to churn through, truth be told, just because there are only two studio albums by The Stone Roses. The first is the one that is essential, and the other… well, it exists. It’s there. But there’s nothing that’s anywhere close to as good as “She Bangs the Drums” to be found on that one.

Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness is a difficult album to look past if you want to judge something by its sheer ambition, because The Smashing Pumpkins did go for broke there and made something absolutely massive. It was twice as long (and you might argue less consistent) than the band’s previous album, Siamese Dream. Okay, sure, Siamese Dream could well be stronger just because the songs there do all fit together a little more coherently.

It’s a very sad song that also manages to sound big and potentially even cathartic in some ways, or perhaps more cathartic if you don’t dig too deep into the lyrics.

There are highlights on both albums, undoubtedly, with “Today” being the strongest track on Siamese Dream, and then it also could well be the band’s best song overall, too. It’s a very sad song that also manages to sound big and potentially even cathartic in some ways, or perhaps more cathartic if you don’t dig too deep into the lyrics… that aspect of “Today” is the properly soul-crushing part.

This song’s quite a bit nicer than “Today,” and from The Cure, who are a typically moodier band, perhaps even more so than The Smashing Pumpkins. “Just Like Heaven” is The Cure at their most romantic and sweeping, so there might well be an argument to be made that it’s more of a pop song than a rock one, but too bad, because this was an opportunity to shout out “Just Like Heaven,” and that opportunity has now been seized.

It’s potentially cheesy to describe a song as feeling like something that captures the sensation of the early stage of being in love, but that is what “Just Like Heaven” does indeed do, just as effectively as some of the best love songs of all time (plenty have been more poppy than any other genre, and so many come from the 1960s, too). It is great, however you want to define or describe it. And that’s all that really matters, for now.

This is some more angst now, and it’s angst on an unusually epic scale, not to mention it’s all that by a band not really known for putting out too many long songs. That band’s The Smiths, and a lot of songs by The Smiths manage to do a lot with just two, or maybe three-ish minutes. “This Charming Man,” for instance, is a rather perfect two minutes and 41 seconds, and “Please Please Please Let Me Get What I Want” is hugely emotional while clocking in at 10 seconds shy of two minutes.

But it’s “How Soon Is Now?” that’s going to get included here, partly because it feels about as close to “hard” rock as The Smiths ever got, and also because it definitely feels strange in some ways, and thereby fulfills the “alternative” part of “alternative rock” alongside also doing the “rock” thing very well. This song is heavy on the ears, and then the lyrics cut very deep, even by the standards of The Smiths (an endlessly miserable – but largely in a good way – band).

Like with The Stone Roses (the self-titled album, not the band), Doolittle is an alternative rock album from 1989 that you really should listen to from start to finish. But if you're as pressed for time here as you were for The Stone Roses, for whatever reason, then just sample “Here Comes Your Man,” either before or after “She Bangs the Drums.” Not at the same time; not one playing into one ear and the other into the other. You're not THAT pressed for time, surely?

And then the trend of shouting out an artist’s most immediate song continues here, since “Here Comes Your Man” is a little less intense than a fair few other songs by Pixies… though to be fair, many of those intense songs are still very catchy. Also, sure, some songs were picked here for reasons other than them being very immediate, so there’s been little consistency. Apologies, but alternative music should do things a little differently than mainstream/pop music, so the inconsistency was, uh, spiritually in line with the sub-genre of rock being discussed. Yeah, let’s go with that. That’ll do.

#3428. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.

Now, to close out the year in grand fashion, Elden Ring is returning on December 1 with the official launch of Path of Shadows, taking players back to the Shadow Realm and the dreaded Abyssal Woods for a final tumultuous journey.

Bandai Namco is closing out 2026 with Path of Shadows, the fourth and final installment in its ongoing Elden Ring Community Quests initiative. Running from December 1 through December 28, the event challenges players to return to Shadow of the Erdtree and work together toward several ambitious goals, including revisiting some of the expansion's most memorable locations.

Unlike a traditional DLC questline, Path of Shadows is a community-wide event, meaning individual players contribute toward shared objectives rather than completing every challenge themselves. Bandai Namco has outlined five specific goals for the December event:

Fortunately, participation is straightforward. Players simply need to play Elden Ring on their preferred platform during the event, with progress updates and reminders available through the game's official Discord server.

As for rewards, Bandai Namco has confirmed exclusive commemorative artwork by Crisppyboat, alongside a special St. Trina Twitch chat badge designed by Carsondrewit. For anyone unfamiliar, Twitch badges are small icons displayed beside usernames in livestream chats, allowing viewers to showcase achievements, affiliations, and other distinctions.

Path of Shadows follows three earlier community quests, each celebrating a different aspect of FromSoftware's acclaimed RPG. The first, Path of the Tarnished, ran from September 1–28, challenging players to summon Sorcerer Rogier and collect various items. Rewards included artwork by Shimhaq and a Sorcerer Rogier Twitch badge.

October's Path of the Cardinal Sin resulted in commemorative artwork by Dan Mumford and a Festering Bloody Finger badge, while November's Path of the Elden Lord, running November 2–28, will feature artwork by Louis Gibiard and a Warrior Jar Alexander badge. All three badges were designed by Carsondrewit.

Bandai Namco is also hosting a separate Discord emote contest, giving artistic fans another opportunity to participate in the celebrations. With Path of Shadows bringing the festivities to a close, there's no better excuse for Tarnished to revisit the Shadow Realm in Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree before the year is out.

#3426. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3424. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

#3423. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3419. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3418. The 10 Greatest Fantasy Books Released Since 'The Lord of the Rings,' Ranked

J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings trilogy exists as only a small part of his extensive lore and history collectively known as Middle-earth. The books came out in the 1950s, with a masterfully crafted movie trilogy released in the 2000s. The books are considered some of the most foundational works that shaped high fantasy and completely revolutionized fantasy as a whole. In fact, they are widely considered the best fantasy novels ever written.

In the years since, Tolkien has influenced many other writers with his work. The result is that several fantasy novels have come out that actually come quite close to the inherent quality Tolkien produced in every one of his works. These are the best fantasy books to come out since The Lord of the Rings trilogy was released seven decades ago.

The Name of the Wind is book one of the unfinished Kingkiller Chronicle trilogy. Kvothe runs an inn under the alias of "Kote," but reveals his true identity when he meets a Chronicler who is interested in his life story. Over three days, Kvothe recounts the tales from his youth: how he studied magic at the university, became an accomplished musician, and achieved great feats.

This book really knows how to keep readers hooked. It provides quite a few mysteries regarding a peculiar sealed door at the university, the mystical group of villains known as the Chandrian, and more. Sadly, it looks like Patrick Rothfuss never intends to finish the series. However, that doesn't change the fact that this ambitious work is truly spectacular, establishing a fascinating character while only providing hints about the conclusion, prompting widespread theories and speculation.

Dungeon Crawler Carl is a title that has been absolutely blowing up lately. It's sort of becoming a household name for how popular it is, and for good reason. Quite simply, the books are just very fun. They are unabashedly silly, quirky, and absurd, but this gives them so much more personality and really sets them apart from other fantasy stories. The book opens up in the near future, where aliens have invaded Earth, abducting a man named Carl and forcing him to endure an 18-level dungeon crawl out of classic RPGs.

Author Matt Dinniman has been quite prolific with his writing, producing eight books in the series within a seven-year span. Each entry proves to be just as wacky as the original, almost as if it is trying to one-up itself. While it's more of a science-fantasy rather than a traditional fantasy, Dungeon Crawler Carl is among the most singular and influential fantasy works to come out in a long time. There's just nothing else like it out there.

Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice is the first book in The Farseer Trilogy, which exists as part of the Realm of the Elderlings shared universe. It was a pleasant surprise, as it was the first novel to debut under the Robin Hobb pseudonym, so people didn't know quite who she was, but ended up loving it anyway. The plot follows a young boy who is forced to become an assassin at a young age, only to find out he is the illegitimate son of the king.

Assassin's Apprentice quickly became a favorite and oft-recommended novel in internet fan circles, with readers praising its character development, immersive world, and overall storytelling. Assassin's Apprentice was just conclusive enough to serve as a stand-alone, but just open enough to warrant sequels if people wanted them (which they did). The book was so deep and moving that it became a highly influential piece of literature.

Prince of Thorns is the first in the Broken Empire trilogy, which is set in Europe, centuries after it has been decimated by nuclear war and reverted humanity back to the Dark Ages. Ghosts prowl the landscape, and mysterious necromancers are gathering strength in the mountains. In the Rhineland, a young prince named Jorg Ancrath is desperately trying to escape his father's legacy. Jorg is a self-described sociopath who commits horrific acts of violence at only 14. Leading a band of mercenaries across the devastated wasteland, he begins hatching a plan to earn a kingdom of his own.

This is one of the most disturbing fantasy books ever read. The evil that Jorg is capable of at such a young age is something as morally repulsive as it is intriguing. The story itself provides a unique setting and an extremely bleak atmosphere, but it really feels like a character study of Jorg himself — it's where the book truly shines. Prince of Thorns is certainly not for the faint of heart, but it's excellent for fans of grimdark fantasy.

The Lies of Locke Lamora is an urban fantasy. The central city is more medieval, technologically speaking, which is why it is crisscrossed with a series of canals and resembles Venice, though it is in a completely fictitious world. However, beyond the ancient architecture and picturesque canals lies a dark criminal underbelly. Deep within the city's darkest corners is a crew of thieves and con artists.

The Gentleman Bastards are similar to stereotypical heist crews from crime thrillers. Each has a distinct role, personality, and talents, which they must use to overcome a new threat rising in their criminal underworld. Alternate chapters serve as pieces of lore, establishing the history of the Gentleman Bastards and of the city itself. This is such a good book not only due to its setting and character development, but also because its story is so different from other fantasy novels. It's not about warring kingdoms, and it's not about royal politics or magical mishaps; it's about the hidden machinations of each fantasy world.

Gardens of the Moon is the first novel in the 10-volume epic, Malazan: Book of the Fallen. The main series may be 10 books, but it has since expanded to form a shared universe, including other sub-series and stand-alones. The story opens up in the Malazan Empire, an oppressive regime which has expanded via conquest to encompass basically an entire continent. But hey, when has any tyrant ever looked at what they had and said, "this is enough?" The Empire then sets its sights on a continent across the sea, planning to invade and execute a series of political maneuvers to bend them to the will of the regime.

Malazan is a very depressing series: extremely violent, cynical, and doesn't shy away from showing the full extent of what war can do to people. Even in fantasy worlds, war remains a harrowing and nightmarish experience for all those involved. The world of Malazan is not just fascinating; it's meticulously detailed, with extensive lore that is always developing. It wouldn't be shocking if it eventually morphed to be just as detailed as Tolkien's legendarium.

A Memory of Light is the epic conclusion to The Wheel of Time series, being the 14th entry (15th if you count the prequel novel). This saga is truly a monster to tackle, with a long, complex plotline, hundreds of characters, and a massive world to absorb. The payoff is totally worth it, though. The SparksNotes version of the story is that it's about a Chosen One called the Dragon Reborn who has a split destiny: either he will save the world from the Dark One, or he will help him destroy it.

In this hefty volume, the long-awaited Last Battle finally reaches its boiling point. Though it technically started in the book prior, it really comes to a head in this one. The main chapter focusing on the Last Battle is well over 200 pages long. The book can be a big commitment and can feel daunting or exhausting for some people, but the bittersweet ending, major character deaths, plot developments, and cinematic scale make the effort worthwhile.

Ursula K. Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea has become a favorite for fans of fantasy literature, mainly due to its setting and overall plot. The worldbuilding is where the book shines the most. It is set on the eponymous oceanic planet of Earthsea. However, there is a small archipelago of islands in which the story takes place. Everything about the world feels so realistic. Even though the cultures, religions, and politics presented within the tale don't have any real-world comparisons, they all feel like they could feasibly exist.

As if all that weren't enough, the book also features dragons, which is always great in fantasy. The story is fairly small-scale, including a boy's journey to escape his literal demons after a spell goes awry. However, it's strangely relatable as it presents itself as a coming-of-age story, wherein the protagonist must endure the hardships and awkwardness of adolescence and growing up. The short version is, A Wizard of Earthsea is just a brilliant work of fantasy, and an all-time classic that will be remembered for generations.

A Storm of Swords is the third book of A Song of Ice and Fire, an unfinished series which famously became the HBO smash-hit Game of Thrones. The longest novel in the series, the book picks up where the previous entry left off: nine noble families begin squabbling over the throne of the realm while an ancient, supernatural threat begins preparing an army far to the North, preparing to bring about the end of the world.

The series became famous (or perhaps infamous) for its unflinching violence, brutality, and cynical worldview. It shows the absolute evils that humans are capable of, often sought out in the pursuit of wealth, power, love, or fame. It's a pretty bleak book, but one that has such an interesting plot that it's hard not to love. Moreover, George R. R. Martin became renowned for how well he writes his characters. With how unique each and every player in Game of Thrones is, it's actually quite easy to follow who's who, even if there are hundreds of them. This is an epic fantasy that became legendary for a reason.

Oathbringer is the third book of Brandon Sanderson's critically acclaimed epic, The Stormlight Archive. This series is part of his larger literary universe known as the Cosmere. Set on the barren planet of Roshar, Oathbringer follows Dalinar Kholin, a highprince of Alethkar, as he leads a war against the cristacean Parshendi. The war has escalated from petty squabbles to a full-on fight for survival, with both sides resurrecting ancient forms of magic to aid their conquests. Throughout the story, flashback chapters detailing Dalinar's life and personal traumas build upon the character's history and his relationships with others.

Oathbringer has one of the most thrilling and emotional climaxes fantasy has ever seen, or at least since The Lord of the Rings came out. The great thing about Sanderson is that not only does he write great stories; there's some genuine moral wisdom to be found within, too. Featuring multiple battle sequences, a complex magic system, a fascinating exercise in worldbuilding, and some phenomenal character development, Oathbringer stands as one of the greatest fantasy books ever written.

#3417. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

#3415. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3414. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.
