Why installing Grand Theft Auto 6 isn’t as simple as hitting download

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After years of waiting, GTA 6 is finally within reach. But with preloads opening and the game demanding up to 212 GB of storage, launch day is already exposing hardware bottlenecks for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S owners.

Since Rockstar has skipped physical game discs entirely, shipping boxed editions as digital download codes, every single player will be pulling this colossal install through a network connection.

To ensure you aren't stranded staring at error codes, download pauses, or an overheated machine, here are the five essential checks to run on your console right now.

A 212 GB install means most players will need to make some tough sacrifices. Before opening your wallet, start with a thorough clear-out: head into your console’s storage manager to purge games you haven't touched in months, lingering DLC add-ons, and video captures quietly eating up dozens of gigabytes.

If you already own an external USB drive, you can temporarily offload old titles there as a "cold storage" archive, but current-gen performance demands mean you cannot play GTA 6 directly from an external USB port.

If deleting your backlog still doesn't free up enough space, upgrading your high-speed storage is your only remaining option:

Xbox Series X|S: Slot an official storage card like the WD Expansion directly into the port on the back.

PlayStation 5: Install an approved internal M.2 NVMe SSD into the expansion bay beneath the faceplates.

Preload timing varies significantly between platforms, with release windows shaped by whether your console operates on a unified global rollout or a regional schedule:

Xbox Series X|S: Preloading unlocks simultaneously worldwide, going live first in the US on Monday, November 9 at 7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT (which corresponds to midnight GMT on Tuesday, November 10 for UK players).

PlayStation 5: Downloads roll out on a strict regional basis, unlocking at midnight local time on Tuesday, November 10 across each player's respective time zone globally.

If you opted for a physical boxed edition, keep in mind that these packages rely entirely on an enclosed digital voucher rather than a physical disc. These boxed versions will not arrive on store shelves until Thursday, November 12.

While players with digital pre-orders get a two-day head start over physical buyers to clear that massive 212 GB download, physical buyers will still have a full week to download the files before servers officially open on launch day.

Nothing kills download momentum like an unexpected system lockout. If an essential operating system update is pending, your console will pause your queue and cut off background network services until it is installed.

Power up your console manually ahead of launch day, check for any pending firmware updates, and install them so your machine is clear to download uninterrupted:

Xbox Series X|S: Press the Xbox button on your controller to open the guide, then navigate to Profile & system, Settings, System, and Updates. If your console is fully up to date, you won't see an available update.

PlayStation 5: Head to Settings, System, System Software, System Software Update and Settings, and run any pending updates.

Both consoles can quietly pull down the entire 212 GB package overnight, but only if your standby settings actually allow it:

Xbox Series X|S: Check Settings, General, and Power options. While the default "Shutdown (energy saving)" mode allows basic auto-updates, switching your power mode to Sleep ensures an uninterrupted network connection so queued preloads won't stall overnight.

PlayStation 5: Head to Settings, System, Power Saving, and Features Available in Rest Mode. Ensure Stay Connected to the Internet and Enable Turning On PS5 from Network are toggled on, then check under Settings, Saved Data and Game/App Settings, and Automatic Updates to confirm auto-downloads are active. You can switch back to energy-saving mode once the install finishes.

GTA 6 will push the PS5 and Xbox Series X processors harder than almost any title this generation. If your console has accumulated a carpet of dust inside its vents over the past few years, extended play sessions will quickly trigger thermal throttling or abrupt emergency shutdowns.

Pop off your faceplates and vacuum the dedicated dust catchers on the PS5, or use a soft brush and compressed air around the Xbox vent grills.

And, as is standard practice, ensure your console sits in an open space with at least 4 to 6 inches of clearance on all sides, free from enclosed entertainment cabinets, deep carpets, or tight wall corners.

#3411. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

#3410. Forget 'Tombstone,' Kurt Russell's Most Intense Action Western 'Bone Tomahawk' Is a Start-to-Finish Masterpiece

Kurt Russell is the epitome of cool—look no further than his roles as R.J. MacReady in The Thing and Snake Plissken in Escape from New York as proof. And then, there's his portrayal of Wyatt Earp in 1993's Tombstone. Rocking a badass mustache, Russell is the hero lawman in the iconic Western, which also features riveting performances from the likes of Val Kilmer and Powers Boothe. Tombstone is one of the most popular entries in the genre, but as great as it is, it can't hold a candle to the suspense created in Bone Tomahawk. Russell returns as the good guy here, this time going up against a group of cannibals in a film that turns into all-out horror.

Bone Tomahawk is the directorial debut of S. Craig Zahler. Despite being his first time behind the camera, he had one heck of an impressive cast to work with: Outside of Russell, who is as big as it gets, the film also stars Patrick Wilson, Matthew Fox, Richard Jenkins, and David Arquette, among many others. Like Tombstone, and even The Thing, Bone Tomahawk is a character-driven film. Zahler knows that, before he pulls back the curtain to show us all the gruesome bits, he must first get us to care about the men who are going to be prey for the villains.

Russell once more seamlessly steps into the authority role of an 1800s lawman, this time as Sheriff Franklin Hunt. When some innocent people are kidnapped by a cannibalistic tribe, it's up to Hunt and his team, made up of characters played by Wilson, Fox, and Jenkins, to track them down. Bone Tomahawk is filled with masterful acting helped along by Zahler's screenplay. Rather than creating trope-heavy characters only there to die and nothing more, he settles in with his protagonists, getting to truly know both their flaws and what makes them tick. They feel like real people inhabiting a real world. The sweeping cinematography of the rugged landscape is also a character unto itself. And with a minimal score, Zahler allows the building tension to be formed around the story, not manipulative music beats.

"You called down the thunder, well, now you've got it!"

In a 2015 interview with Collider, Russell said it was Zahler's script that got him to return to the western genre.

"I started just really enjoying his sparse -He has sparse sort of technique in his writing that I really responded to and I thought that it was an opportunity to do a movie that was in a new category. It’s its own category, I wouldn’t know what to call it. It’s not just a straight western, I’ve heard it referred to as a horror western, it’s not that, that’s kind of a bad call on it, I think. I think it’s a graphic western, I think that’s fair."

Russell has a point. Bone Tomahawk is not your traditional Western. Sure, it's set in the Old West and centers on a lawman hunting down bad guys, but it's not focused on tropes of the genre. These characters could have been dropped in any century; the late 1800s Old West is just where they happen to be. It's also not a traditional horror film per se because it doesn't live in that feeling. It could be labeled as more action and suspense for the majority of its runtime, until the last jaw-dropping act. Then, whether you want to call it horror or a graphic Western, it becomes a terrifying bloodbath.

The majority of Bone Tomahawk tricks the viewer, telling them that it is a traditional Western-type movie with some horror-centric elements. Once Russell shows up, he will take down the bad guys, perhaps losing a few friends along the way, before ultimately saving the day. But that couldn't be further from the truth; after brief moments of violence here and there spread throughout, the movie lets loose with a shocking and very bloody final act.

Zahler doesn't let the camera hold back, especially the scene where a captured Sheriff Hunt is forced to watch the cannibals as they scalp one of his friends right in front of him. The last several minutes turn Bone Tomahawk into something more akin to The Hills Have Eyes. Zahler demands us to be a part of it as witnesses. After seeing the villains here and there, we get to experience what they are truly capable of. What they do to the women they capture and keep as their prisoners is just as torturous. How is an aging Kurt Russell supposed to defeat such collective, unimaginable violence?

In his Collider interview, the actor saw the comparisons between Bone Tomahawk and The Thing, saying, "That thing was just trying to survive and that’s all these guys are doing, they’re just trying to survive, they’re just out there living." In The Thing, paranoia reigns with a monster that can take on the form of its victims. No one can trust anyone. Bone Tomahawk takes away any doubt. The monsters are right there, mere mortals who can immediately be seen for who they are. But just like The Thing, there might not be getting out alive for anyone.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

Apple's somewhat controversial new Audio Intelligence feature, Siri Recap, is now live in public beta for Apple Watch users. Best of all, you can try it yourself by following the five steps listed below.

Siri Recap also never identifies individual speakers or saves any actual audio recordings. Better yet, all your data associated with Siri Recap is encrypted end-to-end.

With that said, here's how to enable Siri Recap on your Apple Watch and generate your own Apple Intelligence daily conversation summaries.

Read on to see full illustrated instructions for each step.

To enable Siri Recap on your Apple Watch, first download and install iOS 27.3 beta on your iPhone. Then install watchOS 27.3 beta on your Apple Watch. Note: Only the latest Apple Watch models support this Apple Audio Intelligence feature, including the Ultra 4 and Series 12.

Next, open the Apple Watch app on your iPhone, scroll down and tap on Siri. Then scroll down and tap on “Set up Siri Recap.”

You'll then be prompted to created a passcode if you don't already have one. Unfortunately, a passcode is mandatory to use Siri Recap. If you need to create one, tap "Turn on" and then enter your passcode of choice twice to confirm it.

After that, toggle the Siri Recap switch to on by tapping on it (it should turn green); then tap on the “Enable Siri Recap” button on the following screen. The feature is nearly ready to go!

The last step is to setup and listening schedule for Apple's Siri Recap feature (or not). To set one, tap on "Times" and select and confirmed your desired listening hours. Or, tap Not now” to set one up later. On the following screen, enable notifications for Siri Recaps or don't by tapping "Not now."

And just like that, Apple's new Siri Recap Audio Intelligence feature is ready to roll. As a reminder, you can view your recaps at any time by opening the Siri app on either your Apple Watch or iPhone.

Of course, this is just one ofer several new Audio Intellegence features found in the best Apple Watch models. Others include Live Rewind and automatic, always-on music recongnition.

#3405. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

“What I love most about making ‘Knife Edge’ is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover. Bethany Joyy re-shared the viral video on Facebook, claiming the girls later apologized ... but also asked if the video was going to be deleted.

She wrote ... "As u can see in the video, there is another ring camera across the hall that remained untouched. After they apologized, one of the first things that was asked was about if the video was going to be deleted or not."

Using AI as your assistant shopper before you take the plunge

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It seems like in recent years, Black Friday sales happen a whole lot sooner than the actual day we all expect them to hit our timelines.

Instead of rushing out of the house as soon as it hits midnight while my Thanksgiving dinner is still digesting, I just have to keep an eye out for all the early online deals in the weeks leading up to that cost-effective holiday. The likes of Best Buy, Amazon, Walmart and Target are already posting up their biggest discounts, which have compelled me to set up an alert with Meta Muse whenever any ones geared toward video games go live.

But before I decide to go all-in on any Black Friday purchase, I’ve promised myself to tag in ChatGPT as my online shopping assistant to do a few things first. And with the following methods, fitting prompts and a bit of outside research, you’ll have a much easier time navigating the bargain-filled waters of Black Friday.

From choosing what’s actually worth purchasing to doing a final audit of everything you’re planning to buy, these are the best ways to use ChatGPT before you spend a single dime on Black Friday.

For the past couple of years, my Black Friday wishlist has been dominated by OLED TVs, gaming headsets, kitchen appliances (I’ve been in the market for a soda maker for far too long…) and anything else that requires it to be plugged in.

But once I actually look over that list and consider what’s worth adding to my already crowded bedroom that’s ruled by every piece of consumer tech you can think of, I start to wonder if I really need all of the items I’m hoping get a major Black Friday sale. ChatGPT can come in to help during this sort of conundrum by helping you decide what items on your wishlist are worth a purchase and which ones should be skipped entirely.

This prompt should make your final Black Friday purchasing decisions a lot easier to deal with:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Here’s my Black Friday wishlist: [list of items]. My total budget is [dollar amount], and I already own [list of items]. Ask me [number] questions about what I actually need, then rank my list into buy, consider, and skip. Explain your reasoning.

Coming across a major price drop for something you’ve been eyeing for a good while hits all the right happiness sensors in my brain. But it’s always good to snap out of that optimistic mode and be more of a realist to see if that price is really that good of a deal.

ChatGPT can step in to check whether the advertised Black Friday sale price you’ve come across is really a steal or if that newly discounted price isn’t as great as it’s being marketed. Doing some price-drop digging with this prompt could propel you to look for a better deal on your most wanted Black Friday item:

This exact model [number or product link] is advertised at [dollar amount], supposedly down from [dollar amount]. Search for documented price history and previous sale prices. Is this unusually cheap or a routine discount? Cite dated sources and say what you couldn’t verify.

I’m prone to balling out on Black Friday, which is a bad habit I’m trying to leave in the past this year. To the point where I’m going to try to stay under $200 while I pick up the discounted items I really need. So, for the types of items that have the best practical uses in my kitchen and mancave, I’ll look up specific products I’ve been keeping a close eye on while also considering cheaper options that may fulfill the same uses as my wish-listed goods.

The following prompt is worth using if you’re approaching your future Black Friday sales from the same viewpoint:

I’m buying a [product name] for [list of specific uses], with a maximum budget of [dollar amount]. Identify my must-have specifications, then compare three suitable options. Include a cheaper or previous-generation alternative and explain what I would actually sacrifice.

For those items that require spending a whole lot more than just the initial entry price, it’s good to know what else you might be putting money toward when that item comes into your possession. Printers, coffee makers, video game consoles and mobile phones immediately come to mind as the products that reach into your pocket for additional charges. Subscriptions, required accessories, replacement parts, delivery and possible installation of said devices spring up as the type of charges I’m alluding to.

Putting the following ChatGPT prompt to good use during Black Friday should give you a clearer picture of everything you’ll possibly be paying for beyond the entry fee for whatever you’re considering buying:

Compare the first-year and three-year costs of these products: [links]. Include required accessories, subscriptions, replacement supplies, shipping, and installation where relevant. Separate optional extras from necessities and label estimates.

I love to go digging for product reviews on Reddit since I feel like the takes on there are usually pretty reliable. Anyone who takes the time out of their day to pen a 2000+-word review of their new SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro gaming headset for free in a dedicated headphone subreddit has to be reliable, right? The same goes for folks who list out all the pros, cons and accompanying pics of whatever product they chose to say a few words about in the Amazon reviews section.

The following prompt should do you a lot of good when it’s time to see if the Black Friday item you’re planning to buy is highly rated or a total bust that comes with a serious cause of buyer’s remorse:

Research independent reviews and owner feedback for [exact model name or product link]. Identify recurring complaints, long-term reliability concerns, and the strongest positives. Distinguish measured test results from anecdotes, cite sources, and explain who should avoid this product.

There are those instances where you come across a price that may be a bit too good to be true once Black Friday sales start taking over your timeline. That highly discounted price may carry some factors that you may have never considered before, such as its actual seller (even if it’s being sold through a major online retailer), its condition (new or refurbished) and everything that comes with its return policy.

Putting the next prompt into ChatGPT should help you get a better understanding of what you’re planning to pick up and what catches (if any) may be attached to it:

Review this listing and its policies: [links or text]. Identify who sells and ships it, its condition, warranty coverage, return deadline, return shipping costs, restocking fees, and exclusions. Flag anything unclear that I should confirm before paying.

Before hitting that checkout button, it might be worth taking one last look at your digital cart full of Black Friday goodies and seeing if you need everything or could do without a few of them. Presenting your cart to ChatGPT and asking it to consider the biggest arguments against actually getting anything inside it is worth a shot. Sometimes you just need a second opinion to talk you out of buying yet another set of kitchen utensils or a blender just because it’s heavily discounted (and because you probably have one already and just want a new one).

Take this final prompt to ChatGPT and let it help you take a closer look at your Black Friday cart to reconsider what you’re buying:

Audit this cart: [items and prices]. My budget is [dollar amount], and my priorities are [priorities]. Make the strongest practical case against each purchase. Flag duplicate functions, compatibility issues, and unnecessary extras. Recommend a final cart within budget, allowing me to buy nothing.

We’re nowhere near Black Friday, but a whole slew of sales have begun littering everyone’s inboxes and timelines in the weeks ahead of that consumer-friendly holiday. With ChatGPT in your corner as a digital shopping assistant, you can use any of the aforementioned prompts to let it help you shop smarter.

Gather the evidence the chatbot has presented to you, do a bit of research of your own to check if its claims are factual and make your Black Friday purchasing decisions from there. Going the extra mile to use AI to help you comprehend what you’re considering buying on Black Friday is certainly worth doing this year and beyond, once you recognize how helpful it can be.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

Apple’s first foldable has issues, but here’s why I love it anyway

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve been pretty vocal about what I don’t like about the iPhone Duo so far, from the lack of a telephoto zoom and missing Face ID to the unoptimized apps and hefty weight. (Why can’t this thing be as light as the Galaxy Fold 8?)

But now that I’ve been living with and testing the iPhone Duo for about a month, there’s some things that I really like about this device that I think puts it at the top of our best foldable phone list. Here are 7 reasons why I think it’s worth the $2,000 price tag.

To say that I’m a Slack power user would be an understatement. As editor in chief of Tom’s Guide, I’m constantly jumping between multiple threads, weighing in on everything from photos and production, to collaborating with other departments. And it’s really nice to be able to quickly scroll through rooms and contacts, while still seeing message content on the right.

The iPhone Duo is even smart enough to adapt the layout as you fold the device. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app isn’t even two columns.

Slack looks pretty slick on the front screen, too, even though the menu items take up a lot of real estate on the right side. You can quickly respond with the wide keyboard without a problem.

Yup, it’s overdue, but I really appreciate being able to run two apps side by side on the iPhone Duo. For example, I can look up what to order in DoorDash while having a chat with the family in Messages.

I also like being able to easily drag and drop images from the Photos app into Google Drive without having to start all over again each time by looking up the folder name. It’s a huge time saver. To be fair, the Galaxy Fold 8 can do three apps at once, plus floating windows on top. But I’m fine with two apps for now.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

You might not be able to run four apps at once, but the Multiview feature in YouTube TV on the iPhone Duo lets you watch four of your favorite shows at the same time in a grid — just like Android foldables. You can tune into the audio on any of the four windows just by taping your finger on the live video thumbnail. And you tap again to watch the show in full-screen mode. It’s one of those things you just can’t do on a regular iPhone.

For me, I like being able to toggle between multiple NFL or NCAA football games on the weekend or ESPN’s First Take and CNN during the week.

iPhone Duo: up to $1,200 off w/ trade-in + unlimited @ T-MobileT-Mobile is knocking up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo when you switch and bring your number or when you trade-in an eligible phone and sign up a qualifying plan. The iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display (1,878 x 2,670) and a 5.4-inch outer display. It houses Apple's A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Rear cameras include a 48MP main and 48MP ultrawide. In our iPhone Duo review, we said it was worth the wait with a stellar design and smart software.

Part of the reason why I don’t make many FaceTime calls is that I don’t really feel like holding up my phone the whole time. That complaint goes away with the iPhone Duo, which lets you fold the phone in half and prop it up like a laptop. When you’re in this view, you can make FaceTime calls hands free, which is nice because I like to talk with my hands anyway.

The 4MP FaceTime camera isn’t the sharpest, but it gets the job done.

If there’s one app that I would show people if I had 30 seconds to explain why the iPhone Duo is cool, it would be Netflix. The app has been developed from the ground up for this foldable, and it shows.

For example, on the cover display you can skim through mobile-friendly shorts that fill the screen, like Instagram or TikTok. As you’d expect, shows and movies look great on the large 7.6-inch display, as I discovered when watching “The Diplomat” on a long flight. But if you want to snack while you’re watching, you can put the Duo in tabletop mode so your video is up top and controls down below. Or, if you prefer, you can watch in tent mode.

Standby is one of my favorite iPhone features from the past few years, because you can turn your device into an alarm clock when you’re ready to go to bed. But the iPhone Duo takes that to the next level. You get a clock when you put the Duo in tent mode, and when it’s time to get up a soft glow emanates from the inside of the foldable to help wake you up.

Plus, there’s another Standby mode. When you put the Duo in portrait mode and fold it half-way standing up on a table or desk, you’ll see a clock and calendar on the left and some of your favorite photos on the right. It’s like a digital photo frame. Plus, you can still easily access Spotify in this mode via the Dynamic Island.

Because the iPhone Duo weighs down my front pocket when walking around, I’ve mostly defaulted to carrying it in my back pocket. And lots of times I’ve sat on this foldable phone — forgetting to take it out first, whether I’m sitting at my desk at the office or just plopping down to watch TV at night.

At least so far, the iPhone Duo has survived my daily use without a scratch or crack. The titanium frame feels super durable to me, and even after a few weeks the crease is not prominent at all when using this device.

#3395. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3394. UK Celebrity Who Fought to Hide Sex Misconduct Allegations Unmasked

The mystery celebrity who spent weeks fighting to keep his name secret amid explosive sexual misconduct allegations has finally been unmasked ... and it's author David Walliams.

The popular British children's book author was previously identified only as "PPT" in court proceedings ... as he battled to stop two major news outlets from revealing his identity and publishing allegations against him. Walliams is also an actor and comedian who starred in the BBC sketch series "Little Britain" and "Come Fly With Me."

As TMZ previously reported ... the celebrity was accused of using his fame and influence to pursue inappropriate and exploitative sexual relationships with numerous girls and young women over the years ... allegations he has denied.

In an hour-long documentary released by ITN, a woman identified as "Alex" recalls meeting Walliams at a "Little Britain" signing in London in 2004 ... when she was just 15 and he was 32. She claims he immediately called her attractive and stared intensely into her eyes.

Another woman alleges Walliams sexually assaulted her at his home when she was 15 ... claiming he kissed her, lifted her shirt and touched her breast with his mouth before attempting to put her hand down his pants. She says she pulled away and told him no.

We also first reported, prior to his identity being revealed, Walliams was pulled from an upcoming UK film project, with a source close to production for "The Road to Nevermore" telling TMZ he was removed from the project after the allegations surfaced and scrubbed from their IMDb profile.

His attorneys argued that making the allegations public could have deadly consequences ... warning he was at serious risk of dying by suicide if his name was revealed.

But lawyers for ITN and The Guardian pushed back ... arguing the allegations were too important to keep hidden and that his mental health concerns should be addressed by medical professionals, not by silencing the press.

Tuesday morning, Judge Matthew Nicklin rejected the celebrity's attempt to block publication ... though his identity remained protected temporarily while a possible appeal was considered.

The legal battle also sparked a wave of online speculation ... prompting Nicklin to warn the public against trying to identify the mystery man, with anyone violating the court order potentially facing jail time.

Now, after weeks of secrecy and courtroom drama ... the mystery surrounding his identity is finally over.

#3392. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

Back pain doesn't always originate from your back. For example, tight or weak hips, core muscles, or glutes can cause lower back pain or stiffness, and your back muscles may under- or overfire if you don't focus on proper posture.

That's why exercises that strengthen the muscles around your spine and pelvis, like your core, hips and back, are crucial — it's not just about stretching. There's a specific two-step exercise tucked neatly away that I like to bring out for this exact moment.

It's technically two moves — one for your posterior chain (your back, glutes and hamstrings) and one for your deep core; together, they can strengthen your postural muscles and reduce pain and stiffness.

It gets met with a groan every time I introduce it to my clients' sessions, but if you suffer from a tight lower body or symptoms of sciatica, this could help.

If you struggle with the intensity, reduce the time spent in each position by 10 seconds and try again. Focus on squeezing through your core as you face upward (known as the hollow hold exercise), then squeeze your back and glutes when you are in the prone position (face down, known as the Superman exercise).

You can softly bend your knees if you need to, but otherwise, try to keep your legs straight and toes pointed in both positions. Once you feel comfortable, try adding a gentle rocking motion, a bit like a rocking horse, to the hollow hold.

There’s no doubt that AI tools are making IT admins faster at writing code, researching issues, etc. As a Mac admin, I’ve seen slow but steady growth in how I’ve used it in my daily work across all aspects of IT. It’s not perfect, though. I’ve used it to write scripts, troubleshoot networking errors, and more. About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For this report, Fleet surveyed more than 250 enterprise IT folks who manage Apple, all with admin access to their device management systems. The folks responding to the survey manage an average of 2,000 devices, and nearly half have 6 to 10 years of Apple admin experience.

The debate over whether IT teams should use AI day-to-day is over. They already are, and in the past 30 days, 68% of those responding reported using AI for troubleshooting or log analysis, 62% used it to write scripts, and 61% used it to author device management profiles or configurations. The log analysis is something that I use AI for often. 86% allow AI-written output into production after some form of review, and only 14% keep it out of their production environments entirely. There simply is no world where IT can operate at the speed needed without AI tools.

69% of respondents can’t roll back a bad configuration change within an hour, and 43% need more than a day. Another 26% of those responding can recover the same day, but only by doing it by hand. This is the biggest red flag of the survey, in my opinion. AI lets you ship anything fast, but AI can ship bugs just like humans can.

Here’s a real scenario that can happen: an IT admin asks an AI assistant to write a configuration profile, takes a quick pass at it, and pushes it to a few thousand Macs in seconds. If something is wrong with it (a bad network setting, a restriction that locks people out of an app they need), unwinding it could take a while.

“Mac admins are basically engineers now, whether their job description calls them that or not.”

Today it’s identity, security, compliance, and app lifecycle, all on top of a macOS release that forces changes every year. IT teams keep getting more and more added to them without additional resources or taking things away.

31% said keeping up with Apple’s release cadence is their single biggest IT challenge, far ahead of everything else on the survey. On the bright side, Apple’s own management architecture is moving in the right direction. 53% already have declarative device management in production.

Apple has done a lot of work here, and it’s not even Apple that is to blame for the frustration. Apple has built the platform for IT to do everything it needs to do. It’s everything else. Security is harder. AI has made it harder. It’s the expectation that IT has to own AI while owning literally everything else.

IT is using AI to help with its work because it’s the only way to survive the onslaught of the AI era. You aren’t getting more help, but you’re expected to do more without anything being taken away from you. Even systems that don’t need as much day-to-day management as they did years ago, you still have to own and secure them. Hosted email is a good example here. Yes, 365 and Workspace have made it easier to keep email running. You aren’t managing servers as you did 20 years ago, but email is still not easy. You traded server management for AI-driven phishing scams, MFA management, and more. It’s two steps forward and one back. We need a period of three steps forward and zero back to get back to where IT needs to be.

#3388. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3386. Remove your personal info from the web (and stop it coming back)

It seems incredible that anyone can legally create a business which involves scraping your personal data from the web and then selling it, yet here we are. There are literally hundreds of data brokers doing just this.

Personal data bought and sold includes everything from your web-browsing habits and interests to your location history. The least-worst case is that your personal data is purchased by companies wanting to target you with ads. In the worst case, hackers gain access to that data, where it is made available to scammers and identity thieves.

You can fight back using what’s known as “takedown requests.” By law, data brokers have to remove your data if you tell them to. However, this is much easier said than done.

First, you would have to contact literally hundreds of different companies. Second, many of those companies deliberately make takedown links hard to find, then force you to jump through all sorts of hoops in order to issue the requests. Some of them even break the law by not providing the links in the first place.

But even if you succeed, the results won’t last for long. Data brokers are constantly buying new data and adding it to your profile. It’s a constant game of whack-a-mole.

That’s where Incogni comes in. Not only do they do all of the hard work for you across literally hundreds of data brokers, genealogy websites, and social media, but they monitor to ensure that it has been done, scan for the later addition of new data, and issue new takedown requests for that.

Unlike other services, Incogni helps remove your sensitive information from all broker types, including those tricky People Search Sites that are often missed.

With the company’s Unlimited plan, you can even send links you’ve discovered yourself and Incogni will take care of it for you.

If you're clued into social media, or terminally online like I am, you may have noticed posts of people realizing that photos shot on iPhone look different if they stick their hand in the frame. Instead of the drab, washed out browns and greens, you end up with a photo with warmer and more vivid colors than before. The only trade-off is that you need to have your hand in frame to get the effect.

Obviously, I was curious about whether this was actually true, and how much of an impact sticking your hand in shot actually makes to the final photo. As it turns out, yes, I could mimic the same effect by putting my own hand between the camera and the foliage.

And there's a very good reason for it, and that reason means iPhone 18 Pro owners can avoid going to these same extremes.

iphone can’t handle anything colorful unless there’s a hand in the frame https://t.co/C8FVp17gkoOctober 31, 2026

The above pictures were taken on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the final pair which were shot with the iPhone 17 Pro Max. As you can see, the coloring in all of the images is pretty washed out with a dreary gray sheen that seems pretty typical of the Old English Autumn. Unlike New England, the leaves aren't nearly as vivid here — but they certainly don't look like that.

Once my hand is in frame (with some help of my white sleeve) the coloring changes for the better. The various shades of red and yellow seem to pop a bit more, and even the greens, which are usually rather unremarkable, seem to look a lot more vibrant.

The effect is more prominent in some photos compared to others. The change is most noticeable with the blackberry bush, to the point that you wouldn't even realize that those photos were taken seconds apart.

You can actually see the change happen in real time with the above video. This screen recording was taken on the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and when my hand pops into frame you can see the color of the preview change. The overall color gets warmer, and the colors start to pop a little more than they had before.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

In other words, if you're having trouble with the color of your fall foliage not looking as nice as you thought, it's possible that sticking your hand (or something in a very light color) might help things along.

There's a very good reason why this happens, and it all comes down to the fact that most iPhones rely on automatic white balance. In fact, only the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max give users the chance to adjust white balance, a feature that is more common (and more robust) on other cameras — including non-Apple smartphones.

Auto-white balance is common enough, and is used by the camera app to compensate for the ambient light in a specific scene or location. However, utilizing it over manual controls does leave you at the mercy of computational photography algorithms. And in the case of some phones, like older iPhones, you don't have any choice in the matter.

PetaPixel speculates that the iPhone camera could be confusing warmer Fall lighting with an unwanted color cast. To compensate, the camera cools down the image temperature and dulls the natural coloring in the process.

But if you stick something white, or close enough to it, the iPhone camera app will automatically adjust the color temperature across the photo to compensate. That also means that the foliage in the background takes on a warmer hue, and the fall colors appear to be a lot more vivid than the original washed-put image.

Obviously this technique is only going to work for people with lighter skin tones. While we haven't done any testing to see what happens when someone with darker skin puts their own hand in frame, logically the effect would be totally different compared to my own pasty-white hands.

But in those cases you could experiment with using white objects to help trick the software into tweaking the color temperature.

That said, anyone with an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max has better control over white balance by tapping the camera menu button on the bottom right of the screen, tapping white balance and then picking one of the five preset options.
